title: Overview
heading: 1.1 Overview
start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”, 
NYSE: JPM), a financial holding company incorporated under 
Delaware law in 1968, is a leading financial services firm 
based in the United States of America (“U.S.”) , with 
operations worldwide.
summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM): a U.S.-based financial holding company (incorporated in Delaware in 1968) with $3.7 trillion in assets and $292.3 billion in stockholders’ equity as of December 31, 2022; leadership across investment banking, consumer and small business financial services, commercial banking, transaction processing, and asset management; operates under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands serving U.S. consumers and global corporate, institutional, and government clients.
- Organizational structure and key subsidiaries: principal bank subsidiary JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (branches in 48 states and Washington, D.C.); principal non-bank subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; significant non-U.S. operating subsidiaries J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.) and J.P. Morgan SE (Germany), both under JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; global operations via branches, subsidiaries, and representative offices.
- Regulatory and investor information access: firm’s and SEC websites provide timely access to 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K filings; important firm information posted on corporate and investor relations webpages; website content not incorporated by reference into the Form 10-K.
- Governance and ethics: adoption of a firmwide Code of Conduct and a Code of Ethics for senior finance-related officers; availability online and in print; commitment to post amendments and executive waivers within SEC-required timeframes.
- Business segments: management reporting organized into four reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment; further details referenced in MD&A and Note 32.
- Competitive landscape: operates in highly competitive markets against a wide range of financial and non-financial firms (including banks, broker-dealers, asset managers, insurance companies, fintechs, and internet-only providers); competition based on product breadth and quality, execution, innovation, reputation, and price; intensity varies by client type, product, industry, and geography, with competition spanning global, national, and regional levels; emergence of new digital and non-traditional competitors that can disintermediate traditional banking services.
text:
Overview
JPMorgan Chase & Co.  (“JPMorgan Chase” or the “Firm”, 
NYSE: JPM),  a financial holding company incorporated under 
Delaware law in 1968, is a leading financial services firm 
based in the United States of America (“U.S.”) , with 
operations worldwide. JPMorgan Chase had $3.7 trillion  in 
assets and $292.3 billion  in stockholders’ equity as of  
D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2. The Firm is a leader in investment 
banking, financial services for consumers and small 
businesses, commercial banking, financial transaction  
processing and asset management. Under the J.P. Morgan 
and Chase brands, the Firm serves millions of customers, 
predominantly in the U.S., and many of the world’s most 
prominent corporate, institutional and government clients 
globally.
JPMorgan Chase’s principal bank subsidiary is JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, National Association (“JPMorgan Chase Bank, 
N.A.”), a national banking association with U.S. branches in  
48 states and Washington, D.C . JPMorgan Chase’s principal 
non-bank subsidiary is J.P. Morgan Securities LLC (“J.P. 
Morgan Securities”), a U.S. broker-dealer. The bank and non-
bank subsidiaries of JPMorgan Chase operate nationally as 
well as through overseas branches and subsidiaries, 
representative offices and subsidiary foreign banks. The 
Firm’s principal operating subsidiar ies outside the U.S. are 
J.P. Morgan Securities plc and J.P. Morgan SE (“JPMSE”) , 
which are subsidiaries of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and are 
based in the United Kingdom (“U.K.”) and Germany, 
respectively.
The Firm’s website is www.jpmorganchase.com. JPMorgan 
Chase makes available on its website, free of charge, annual 
reports on Form 10-K, quarterly reports on Form 10-Q and 
current reports on Form 8-K pursuant to Section 13(a) or 
Section 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as 
soon as reasonably practicable after it electronically files or 
furnishes such material to the U.S. Securities and Exchange 
Commission (the “SEC”) at www.sec.gov. JPMorgan Chase 
makes new and important information about the Firm 
available on its website at https://www.jpmorganchase.com, 
including on the Investor Relations section of its website at 
https://www.jpmorganchase.com/ir. Information on the 
Firm's website is not incorporated by reference into  this 
Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended 
D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2 (“2022  Form 10-K” or “Form 10-K”)  or 
the Firm’s other filings with the SEC. The Firm has adopted, 
and posted on its website, a Code of Conduct for all 
employees of the Firm and a Code of Ethics for its Chairman 
and Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, Principal 
Accounting Officer and all other professionals of the Firm 
worldwide serving in a finance, accounting, treasury, tax or 
investor relations role. The Code of Ethics is also available in 
print upon request to the Firm’s Investor Relations team. 
Within the time period required by the SEC, JPMorgan Chase 
will post on its website any amendment to the Code of Ethics 
and any waiver applicable to a director or executive officer.

title: Business segments
heading: 1.2 Business segments
start_phrase:
For management reporting purposes, JPMorgan Chase’s 
activities are organized into four major reportable business 
segments, as well as a Corporate segment.
summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM): a Delaware-incorporated financial holding company (since 1968) and leading U.S.-based global financial services firm, with $3.7 trillion in assets and $292.3 billion in stockholders’ equity as of December 31, 2022. Operates under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands, serving millions of U.S. consumers and small businesses, and prominent corporate, institutional, and government clients worldwide across investment banking, consumer and small business banking, commercial banking, payments/transaction processing, and asset management.
- Organizational structure and key subsidiaries: principal bank subsidiary is JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., with branches in 48 states and Washington, D.C.; principal non-bank subsidiary is J.P. Morgan Securities LLC (U.S. broker-dealer). Major non-U.S. operating subsidiaries include J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.) and J.P. Morgan SE (Germany).
- Regulatory filings and corporate governance disclosures: firm posts 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K filings on its website after submission to the SEC; additional investor information available online. Website information is not incorporated by reference into the 10-K. The firm has a Code of Conduct for all employees and a Code of Ethics for senior financial leadership; amendments and waivers for directors/executive officers will be posted within required timeframes.
- Business segments: four reportable segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment. Further details are provided in MD&A and Note 32.
- Competitive landscape: operates in highly competitive markets against a broad set of financial and non-financial firms (including banks, broker-dealers, asset managers, credit card and mortgage companies, insurers, private equity, hedge funds, fintechs, e-commerce/internet-based providers, and other specialty finance companies). Competition is based on product/service quality and breadth, execution, innovation, reputation, and price, and varies by client type, industry, and geography (global, national, or regional). Notes emergence of new internet-only and non-financial competitors that can disintermediate traditional banking services.
text:
Business segments
For management reporting purposes, JPMorgan Chase’s 
activities are organized into four major reportable business 
segments, as well as a Corporate  segment. The Firm’s 
consumer business is the Consumer & Community Banking 
(“CCB”) segment. The Firm’s wholesale business segments 
are the Corporate & Investment Bank (“CIB”), Commercial 
Banking (“CB”), and Asset & Wealth Management (“AWM”).
A description of the Firm’s business segments and the 
products and services they provide to their respective client 
bases is provided in the “Business segment results” section 
of Management’s discussion and analysis of financial 
condition and results of operations (“Management’s 
discussion and analysis” or “MD&A”), beginning on page 46 
and in Note 32.

title: Competition
heading: 1.3 Competition
start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase and its subsidiaries and affiliates operate in 
highly competitive environments.
summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase & Co. as a leading U.S.-based financial holding company (NYSE: JPM), incorporated in Delaware in 1968, with global operations, $3.7 trillion in assets and $292.3 billion in stockholders’ equity as of December 31, 2022, serving consumers, small businesses, and prominent institutional/government clients under the J.P. Morgan and Chase brands.
- Corporate structure and key subsidiaries: principal bank subsidiary JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (with branches in 48 states and Washington, D.C.); principal non-bank subsidiary J.P. Morgan Securities LLC; major non-U.S. operating subsidiaries J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.) and J.P. Morgan SE (Germany); worldwide presence through branches, subsidiaries, and representative offices.
- Investor and regulatory disclosures: availability of SEC filings (Forms 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) and firm information on the corporate and investor relations websites; clarification that website content is not incorporated by reference into the Form 10-K.
- Governance and ethics: adoption and posting of a firmwide Code of Conduct and a Code of Ethics for senior financial leadership; commitment to posting amendments and waivers within SEC timelines; print availability upon request.
- Business organization: four reportable business segments—Consumer & Community Banking (CCB), Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB), Commercial Banking (CB), and Asset & Wealth Management (AWM)—plus a Corporate segment; references to MD&A and Note 32 for detailed segment results and offerings.
- Competitive landscape: operation in highly competitive markets against a wide range of traditional and nontraditional financial and technology firms; competition based on product/service quality and breadth, execution, innovation, reputation, and price; competition varying by client, product, industry, and geography; emergence of internet-only and non-financial players that can disintermediate traditional banking services.
text:
Competition
JPMorgan Chase and its subsidiaries and affiliates operate in 
highly competitive environments. Competitors include other 
banks, brokerage firms, investment banking companies, 
merchant banks, hedge funds, commodity trading 
companies, private equity firms, insurance companies, 
mutual fund companies , investment managers, credit card 
companies, mortgage banking companies, trust companies, 
securities processing companies, automobile financing 
companies, leasing companies, e-commerce and other 
internet-based companies, financial technology companies, 
and other companies engaged in providing similar as well as 
new products and services. The Firm’s businesses generally 
compete on the basis of the quality and variety of the Firm’s 
products and services, transaction execution, innovation, 
reputation and price. Competition also varies based on the 
types of clients, customers, industries and geographies 
served. With respect to some of its geographies and 
products, JPMorgan Chase competes globally; with respect to 
others, the Firm competes on a national or regional basis. 
New competitors in the financial services industry continue 
to emerge, including firms that offer products and services 
solely through the internet and non-financial companies that 
offer products and services that disintermediate traditional 
banking products and services offered by financial services 
firms such as JPMorgan Chase.Part I

title: Firm culture
heading: 1.4.3 Firm culture
start_phrase:
The foundations of JPMorgan Chase’s culture are its core 
values and How We Do Business Principles, which are 
fundamental to the Firm’s success and are represented by 
four central corporate tenets: exceptional client service; 
operational excellence; a commitment to integrity, fairness 
and responsibility; and cultivation of a great team and 
winning culture.
summary:
- Emphasizes JPMorgan Chase’s firm culture grounded in core values and “How We Do Business” principles, centered on exceptional client service, operational excellence, integrity/fairness/responsibility, and a great team/winning culture.
- Reinforces an inclusive, respectful workplace through the Code of Conduct, awareness, education, communication, and training, supported by Business Resource Groups and global Diversity, Equity & Inclusion (DEI) centers of excellence focused on increasing equity and strengthening inclusion.
- Aims to attract and retain talent across all roles and career stages, offering internships through executive opportunities; in 2022, roughly two-thirds of roles were filled externally, with the rest internal, and hybrid work models used where appropriate.
- Prioritizes diverse hiring, with initiatives for gender diversity, underrepresented ethnic groups, LGBTQ+ individuals, people with disabilities, veterans, and others; DEI centers drive representation and advancement via coaching and mentorship; offers a returnship fellowship and, where appropriate, skills-based hiring over degree requirements.
- Supports employee development with required onboarding on the Code of Conduct, policies, and cybersecurity, plus extensive training in leadership, change management, analytical thinking, culture and conduct, DEI, and risk and controls; “Leadership Edge” builds a unified leadership culture.
- Maintains market-competitive compensation guided by pay-for-performance, alignment with shareholder interests, and reinforcement of culture and conduct, with processes to promote equitable and competitive pay.
- Provides comprehensive benefits and wellness programs, including healthcare, retirement, insurance, wellness centers, mental health resources, employee assistance, generous leave, backup child care, tuition reimbursement, and financial coaching; in 2022, enhanced U.S. medical coverage and paid time off for parental, caregiving, and bereavement needs.
text:
Firm culture
The foundations of JPMorgan Chase’s culture are its core 
values and How We Do Business Principles, which are 
fundamental to the Firm’s success and are represented by 
four central corporate tenets: exceptional client service; 
operational excellence; a commitment to integrity, fairness 
and responsibility; and cultivation of a great team and 
winning culture. The Firm maintains its focus on its culture 
of inclusion and respect, which is reinforced by its Code of 
Conduct and by increasing employee awareness, education, 
communication and training. An important part of these 
efforts includes the Firm’s Business Resource Groups, which 
are groups of employees who support JPMorgan Chase’s 
diversity, equity and inclusion strategies by leveraging the 
unique perspectives of their members. The Firm has global 
Diversity, Equity & Inclusion centers of excellence that lead 
the Firm’s strategy in supporting its commitments to create 
more equity and lasting impact in communities, and 
strengthen its inclusive culture.

title: Attracting and retaining employees
heading: 1.4.4 Attracting and retaining employees
start_phrase:
The goal of JPMorgan Chase’s recruitment efforts is to 
attract and hire talented individuals in all roles and at all 
career levels.
summary:
- Firm culture: Emphasizes four core tenets—exceptional client service, operational excellence, integrity/fairness/responsibility, and a great team and winning culture—supported by a Code of Conduct, inclusion and respect, Business Resource Groups, and global DEI centers driving equity and an inclusive culture.
- Attracting and retaining employees: Recruitment spans all roles and levels, with about two-thirds of 2022 hires external and the remainder internal; hybrid work models used where appropriate. Strong focus on diversity hiring (gender, underrepresented ethnic groups, LGBTQ+, people with disabilities, veterans), DEI-led coaching and mentorship to advance representation, a return-to-work fellowship program, and skills-based hiring practices.
- Developing employees: Required onboarding covers the Code of Conduct, policies, and cybersecurity. Ongoing training includes leadership, change management, analytical thinking, culture and conduct, DEI, and risk/controls. Leadership Edge fosters a unified leadership culture firmwide.
- Compensation and benefits: Market-competitive, pay-for-performance approach aligned with shareholder interests and risk/control considerations; equitable pay reviews. Comprehensive benefits include healthcare, retirement, life/disability insurance, wellness centers, mental health resources, EAP, generous leave policies, backup childcare, tuition reimbursement, and financial coaching. In 2022, U.S. health and wellness benefits were enhanced, including expanded medical coverage and paid leave for parental, caregiving, and bereavement.
text:
Attracting and retaining employees
The goal of JPMorgan Chase’s recruitment efforts is to 
attract and hire talented individuals in all roles and at all 
career levels. The Firm strives to provide both external 
candidates and internal employees who are seeking a 
different role wit h challenging  and stimulating career 
opportunities. These opportunities range from internship 
training programs for students to entry-level, management 
and executive careers. During 2022, approximately two -
thirds of the Firm’s employment opportunities were filled 
by external candidates, with the remainder filled by existing 
employees. In addition, depending on business needs, and 
where appropriate, the Firm has implemented hybrid work 
models which include a mix of on-site and remote work for 
certain roles .
Diversity is an important area of focus throughout the 
Firm’s hiring process. JPMorgan Chase engages in efforts 
aimed at hiring diverse talent, including initiatives focused 
on gender, underrepresented ethnic groups, LGBTQ+ 
individuals, people with disabilities, veterans and others. 
The Firm’s global Diversity, Equity & Inclusion centers of 
excellence seek to increase representation of and advance 
career opportunities for talented diverse individuals across 
the Firm through initiatives such as career coaching and 
mentorship. 
JPMorgan Chase offers a competitive fellowship program 
that seeks to attract accomplished individuals who have 
taken a career break and wish to return to the workforce. In 
addition, and where appropriate, the Firm’s hiring practices 
focus on the skills of a job candidate rather than degrees 
held.

title: Developing employees
heading: 1.4.5 Developing employees
start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase supports the professional development 
and career growth of its employees.
summary:
- Firm culture: Grounded in core values and How We Do Business Principles, emphasizing exceptional client service, operational excellence, integrity/fairness/responsibility, and a great team/winning culture. Reinforced through a Code of Conduct, training, Business Resource Groups, and global Diversity, Equity & Inclusion (DEI) centers of excellence to build an inclusive culture and create equitable community impact.
- Attracting and retaining employees: Broad recruitment across roles and levels, with about two-thirds of 2022 hires from external candidates and the rest internal. Use of hybrid work models where appropriate. Strong focus on diverse hiring across gender, underrepresented ethnic groups, LGBTQ+ individuals, people with disabilities, and veterans, supported by DEI initiatives such as coaching and mentorship. Includes a return-to-work fellowship and skills-based hiring where suitable.
- Developing employees: Required onboarding covering Code of Conduct, policies, and cybersecurity. Extensive ongoing training in leadership, change management, analytics, culture and conduct, DEI, and risk/controls. Leadership Edge serves as the firm’s global leadership and management development center to foster a unified leadership culture.
- Compensation and benefits: Market-competitive, pay-for-performance compensation aligned with shareholder interests and integrated with risk, controls, and conduct considerations. Equity-focused pay review processes. Comprehensive well-being benefits including healthcare, retirement, life and disability insurance, wellness centers, mental health support, EAPs, leave policies, backup child care, tuition reimbursement, and financial coaching. 2022 U.S. enhancements expanded medical coverage and paid time off for parental, critical caregiving, and bereavement leaves.
text:
Developing employees
JPMorgan Chase supports the professional development 
and career growth of its employees. An onboarding training 
curriculum is required for new hires, which covers, among 
other topics, compliance with the Firm’s Code of Conduct 
and information concerning Firm policies and standards, including those relating to cybersecurity. In addition, the 
Firm offers extensive training programs and educational 
resources to all employees, covering a broad variety of 
topics such as leadership, change management, analytical 
thinking, culture and conduct, diversity, equity and 
inclusion, and risk and controls. Leadership Edge, the Firm’s 
global leadership and management development center of 
excellence, is focused on creating one Firmwide leadership 
culture.

title: Compensation and benefits
heading: 1.4.6 Compensation and benefits
start_phrase:
The Firm provides market-competitive compensation and 
benefits programs.
summary:
- Firm culture: JPMorgan Chase’s culture is built on four core tenets—exceptional client service, operational excellence, integrity/fairness/responsibility, and a great team/winning culture—reinforced by a Code of Conduct and a strong focus on inclusion and respect. Business Resource Groups and global Diversity, Equity & Inclusion (DEI) centers of excellence advance DEI strategies, support community equity, and strengthen an inclusive culture.
- Attracting and retaining employees: The firm recruits across all levels with internships through executive roles; in 2022, about two-thirds of roles were filled externally and the rest internally. Hybrid work is used where appropriate. Hiring emphasizes diversity (gender, underrepresented ethnic groups, LGBTQ+, people with disabilities, veterans, etc.), offers career coaching and mentorship via DEI centers, runs a fellowship for career returners, and applies skills-based hiring over degree requirements when suitable.
- Developing employees: Required onboarding covers the Code of Conduct, firm policies, and cybersecurity. Ongoing training spans leadership, change management, analytical thinking, culture and conduct, DEI, and risk/controls. Leadership Edge serves as the global leadership and management development hub to build a unified leadership culture.
- Compensation and benefits: Compensation follows pay-for-performance, aligns with shareholder interests, and reinforces culture with integrated risk, controls, and conduct considerations. Pay equity is monitored through review processes. Comprehensive benefits include healthcare, retirement, life/disability insurance, wellness centers, mental health resources, EAPs, generous leave, backup child care, tuition reimbursement, and financial coaching. In 2022, U.S. benefits were enhanced with expanded medical coverage and additional paid leave for parental, caregiving, and bereavement needs.
text:
Compensation and benefits
The Firm provides market-competitive compensation and 
benefits programs. JPMorgan Chase’s compensation 
philosophy includes guiding principles that drive 
compensation-related decisions across the Firm, and 
includes: pay-for-performance practices designed to attract 
and retain top talent; responsiveness and alignment with 
shareholder interests; and  reinforcement of  the Firm’s 
culture and How We Do Business Principles, including the 
integration of risk, controls and conduct considerations. The 
Firm’s commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion for all 
employees includes compensation review processes that 
seek to ensure that the Firm’s employees are paid equitably 
and competitively for the work they do.
The Firm also supports employees’ well-being. JPMorgan

title: Consolidated supervision
heading: 1.5.1.1 Consolidated supervision
start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a bank 
holding company (“BHC”) and a financial holding company 
(“FHC”) under U.S. federal law, and is subject to 
comprehensive consolidated supervision, regulation and

summary:

text:
Consolidated supervision . JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a bank 
holding company (“BHC”) and a financial holding company 
(“FHC”) under U.S. federal law, and is subject to 
comprehensive consolidated supervision, regulation and 
examination by the Board of Governors of the Federal 
Reserve System (the “Federal Reserve”). The Federal 
Reserve acts as the supervisor of the consolidated 
operations of BHCs. Certain of JPMorgan Chase’s 
subsidiaries are also regulated directly by additional 
authorities based on the activities or licenses of those 
subsidiaries.
JPMorgan Chase’s national bank subsidiary, JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, N.A., is supervised and regulated by the Office 
of the Comptroller of the Currency (“OCC”) and, with 
respect to certain matters, by the Federal Deposit Insurance 
Corporation (the “FDIC”).
JPMorgan Chase’s U.S. broker-dealers are supervised and 
regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission 
(“SEC”) and the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority 
(“FINRA”). Subsidiaries of the Firm that engage in certain 
futures-related and swaps-related activities are supervised 
and regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading 
Commission (“CFTC”). J.P. Morgan Securities plc is a U.K.-
based bank regulated by the U.K. Prudential Regulation 
Authority (the “PRA”) and the U.K. Financial Conduct 
Authority (“FCA”). 
JPMSE is a Germany-based credit institution regulated by 
the European Central Bank (“ECB”) as well as the local 
regulators in each of the countries in which it operates. The 
Firm’s other non-U.S. subsidiaries are regulated by the 
banking, securities, prudential and conduct regulatory 
authorities, as applicable, in the countries in which they 
operate.

text:
Permissible business activities . The Bank Holding Company 
Act restricts BHCs from engaging in business activities other 
than the business of banking and certain closely-related 
activities. FHCs are permitted to engage in a broader range 
of financial activities. The Federal Reserve has the authority 
to limit an FHC’s ability to conduct otherwise permissible 
activities if the FHC or any of its depository institution 
subsidiaries ceases to meet applicable eligibility 
requirements. The Federal Reserve may also impose 
corrective capital and/or managerial requirements on the 
FHC, and if deficiencies are persistent, may require 
divestiture of the FHC’s depository institutions. If any 
depository institution controlled by an FHC fails to maintain 
a satisfactory rating under the Community Reinvestment 
Act, the Federal Reserve must prohibit the FHC and its 
subsidiaries from engaging in any new activities other than those permissible for BHCs, or acquiring a company 
engaged in such activities.

title: Stress tests
heading: 1.5.1.4 Stress tests
start_phrase:
As a large BHC, JPMorgan Chase is subject to 
supervisory stress testing administered by the Federal 
Reserve as part of the Federal Reserve’s annual 
Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (“CCAR”) 
framework.
summary:
- Scope: Outlines the extensive supervisory and regulatory framework governing JPMorgan Chase in the U.S. and internationally.
- Consolidated supervision: JPMorgan Chase & Co. is a bank holding company and financial holding company subject to comprehensive consolidated oversight by the Federal Reserve; various subsidiaries are directly regulated by activity-specific authorities.
- Key U.S. regulators: OCC and FDIC for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; SEC and FINRA for U.S. broker-dealers; CFTC for futures and swaps activities.
- Key non-U.S. regulators: PRA and FCA for J.P. Morgan Securities plc (U.K.); ECB and local EU regulators for JPMSE (Germany); other local banking, securities, prudential, and conduct authorities globally.
- Permissible activities: Bank Holding Company Act limits BHC activities; FHC status permits broader financial activities. The Federal Reserve can restrict activities, require corrective measures, or force divestitures if eligibility or CRA performance falls short.
- Capital and liquidity: Federal Reserve (and OCC for the bank) impose Basel III-aligned capital, liquidity, and leverage requirements; certain non-U.S. entities must meet local standards. Regulators are evaluating implementation of Basel III reforms.
- Stress testing and CCAR: As a large BHC, the Firm is subject to Federal Reserve supervisory stress tests and must run annual company tests and submit an annual capital plan under CCAR. Results determine the Stress Capital Buffer (SCB), with specified 2023 filing and notification timelines; OCC requires similar tests for the bank; the Firm publishes results annually.

text:
Stress tests . As a large BHC, JPMorgan Chase is subject to 
supervisory stress testing administered by the Federal 
Reserve as part of the Federal Reserve’s annual 
Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review (“CCAR”) 
framework. The Firm must conduct annual company-run 
stress tests and must also submit an annual capital plan to 
the Federal Reserve, taking into account the results of 
separate stress tests designed by the Firm and the Federal 
Reserve. The Federal Reserve uses the results under the 
severely adverse scenario from its supervisory stress test to 
determine the Firm’s Stress Capital Buffer (“SCB”) 
requirement for the coming year, which forms part of the 
Firm’s applicable capital buffers. The Firm is required to file 
its annual CCAR submission on April 5, 2023. The Federal 
Reserve will notify the Firm of its indicative SCB 
requirement by June 30, 2023 and final SCB requirement 
by August 31, 2023. The Firm’s final SCB requirement will 
become effective on October 1, 2023. The OCC requires 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. to perform separate, similar 
stress tests annually. The Firm publishes each year the 
results of the annual stress tests for the Firm and JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, N.A. under the supervisory “severely adverse” 
scenarios provided by the Federal Reserve and the OCC.
Refer to Capital Risk Management on pages 86-96  for more 
information concerning the Firm’s CCAR.

title: Enhanced prudential standards
heading: 1.5.1.5 Enhanced prudential standards
start_phrase:
As part of its mandate to 
identify and monitor risks to the financial stability of the 
U.S. posed by large banking organizations, the Financial 
Stability Oversight Council (“FSOC”) recommends 
prudential standards and reporting requirements to the 
Federal Reserve for systemically important financial 
institutions (“SIFIs”), such as JPMorgan Chase.
summary:
- Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s extensive supervision under U.S. federal and state laws and non-U.S. jurisdictions.
- Financial holding company status: consolidated supervision by the Federal Reserve; activity-based oversight of subsidiaries by OCC, FDIC, SEC, FINRA, CFTC; U.K. entities regulated by PRA/FCA; EU entity (JPMSE) regulated by ECB and local authorities; other non-U.S. subsidiaries overseen by relevant banking, securities, prudential, and conduct regulators.
- Permissible activities: BHCs restricted to banking and closely related activities; FHCs may engage in broader financial activities; the Federal Reserve can limit activities if eligibility standards aren’t met; CRA ratings can restrict new activities and acquisitions.
- Capital and liquidity: Federal Reserve and OCC requirements aligned with Basel III, including leverage and liquidity standards; ongoing global refinements to Basel III; some subsidiaries subject to local capital/liquidity rules; cross-references to Capital and Liquidity Risk Management sections.
- Stress testing and CCAR: annual Federal Reserve supervisory stress tests and company-run tests; annual capital plan submission; SCB determined from severely adverse scenario with 2023 notification and effective dates; OCC requires similar tests for the bank; public disclosure of results.
- Enhanced prudential standards for SIFIs: FSOC recommendations implemented by Federal Reserve, including heightened risk management, corporate governance, liquidity, and board oversight requirements.
- Recovery and resolution planning: firm-level and bank-level recovery plans; alternating “targeted” and “full” resolution plans (targeted filed June 28, 2021; full due July 1, 2023); separate bank resolution plan due December 1, 2023; non-U.S. entities subject to local recovery/resolution regimes.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority: potential FDIC-led resolution of SIFIs using a single point of entry strategy, with losses imposed on holding company shareholders and creditors.
- Source of strength: holding company obligation to support depository institution subsidiaries.
- Acquisition regulation: Federal Reserve/OCC approvals required; limits on ownership (>5% voting shares) and market concentration (10% liabilities cap); prior notice for acquisitions of large firms engaged in financial activities; eligibility-based limitations on FHC acquisitions.
- Ongoing obligations: compliance with a 2020 DOJ Deferred Prosecution Agreement related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries markets and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank oversight: OCC authority under the National Bank Act; potential enforcement for unsafe/unsound practices, including activity limits and corrective requirements.
- FDIC deposit insurance: coverage funded by assessments on banks, including JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
- FDIC powers on insolvency: ability to act as conservator/receiver and transfer assets and liabilities without creditor approval.
- Prompt corrective action: mandated interventions for undercapitalized institutions under FDICIA; potential Federal Reserve actions at the parent BHC level and possible guarantees of capital restoration plans.
- OCC Heightened Standards: required risk governance framework for large banks with a clearly distinguishable bank-level risk profile separate from the parent BHC.
text:
Enhanced prudential standards . As part of its mandate to 
identify and monitor risks to the financial stability of the 
U.S. posed by large banking organizations, the Financial 
Stability Oversight Council (“FSOC”) recommends 
prudential standards and reporting requirements to the 
Federal Reserve for systemically important financial 
institutions (“SIFIs”), such as JPMorgan Chase. The Federal 
Reserve has adopted several rules to implement those 
heightened prudential standards, including rules relating to 
risk management and corporate governance of subject 
BHCs. JPMorgan Chase is required under these rules to 
comply with enhanced liquidity and overall risk Part I
4management standards, including oversight by the board of 
directors of risk management activities.

title: Resolution and recovery
heading: 1.5.1.6 Resolution and recovery
start_phrase:
The Firm is required to maintain a 
comprehensive recovery plan, updated annually, 
summarizing the actions it would take to remain well-
capitalized and well-funded in order to avoid failure in the

summary:
- Governance and risk management expectations, including board oversight of risk activities and management standards for large banking organizations.
- Recovery and resolution planning requirements: annual comprehensive recovery plans; alternating “targeted” and “full” resolution plan submissions to the Federal Reserve and FDIC (targeted filed June 28, 2021; full due by July 1, 2023); separate resolution plans for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (due by December 1, 2023); and applicable non-U.S. local planning obligations.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority framework: potential resolution of systemically important firms via the FDIC’s “single point of entry” strategy, imposing losses on BHC shareholders and creditors while keeping operating subsidiaries open, contingent on Treasury/President/FDIC/Fed determinations.
- Source-of-strength doctrine: holding company obligation (JPMorgan Chase & Co.) to support depository institution subsidiaries, including when directed by the Federal Reserve.
- Acquisition regulations: Federal Reserve approval required for BHCs/FHCs acquiring over 5% of an unaffiliated bank’s voting shares; prohibition on acquisitions that push a firm’s total liabilities above 10% of aggregate financial company liabilities; prior notice requirements for acquisitions of companies with over $10 billion in assets engaged in financial activities; Federal Reserve authority to limit FHC acquisitions if eligibility standards are not met.
- Ongoing legal and regulatory obligations arising from a September 29, 2020 Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the DOJ related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries markets, and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank activity limits: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.’s activities constrained by the National Bank Act and OCC interpretations.
- OCC enforcement authority: ability to address unsafe or unsound practices, limit activities, and impose corrective capital or managerial requirements on the bank.
- FDIC deposit insurance assessments supporting insured deposits at JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
- FDIC powers in bank insolvency: appointment as conservator or receiver with broad authority to transfer assets and liabilities without creditor approval.
- Prompt corrective action under FDICIA: mandatory regulatory actions for undercapitalized institutions; potential Federal Reserve measures against the parent BHC; possible requirement for the BHC to guarantee a subsidiary’s capital restoration plan.
- OCC Heightened Standards: requirements for a robust risk governance framework at large banks, ensuring the bank’s risk profile and management are clearly distinguished from those of the parent BHC.
text:
Resolution and recovery . The Firm is required to maintain a 
comprehensive recovery plan, updated annually, 
summarizing the actions it would take to remain well-
capitalized and well-funded in order to avoid failure in the 
case of an adverse event. In addition, JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A. is required to prepare and submit a recovery 
plan as directed by the OCC. The Firm is required to submit 
periodically to the Federal Reserve and the FDIC a plan for 
resolution in the event of material distress or failure (a 
“resolution plan”). In 2019, the FDIC and Federal Reserve 
revised the regulations governing resolution plan 
requirements, and on the basis of those revisions, the 
Firm’s resolution plan submissions will alternate between 
“targeted” and “full” plans.  The Firm’s “targeted” resolution 
plan was filed on June 28, 2021 , and the Firm's next "full" 
resolution plan is due to be filed on or before July 1, 2023 . 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. is also required to prepare and 
submit a separate resolution plan as directed by the FDIC 
on or before December 1, 2023. 
Certain of the Firm’s non-U.S. subsidiaries and branches are 
also subject to local resolution and recovery planning 
requirements.

title: Orderly liquidation authority
heading: 1.5.1.7 Orderly liquidation authority
start_phrase:
Certain financial companies, 
including JPMorgan Chase and certain of its subsidiaries, 
can also be subjected to resolution under an “orderly 
liquidation authority.”
summary:
- Recovery and resolution planning requirements: firm-wide and bank-specific recovery plans updated annually; alternating “targeted” and “full” resolution plan submissions (targeted filed June 28, 2021; next full due July 1, 2023); JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. separate resolution plan due December 1, 2023; non-U.S. units subject to local regimes.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA): potential resolution of the holding company under OLA upon Treasury/President determinations and FDIC/Fed recommendation; otherwise Bankruptcy Code applies; FDIC’s “single point of entry” approach aims to keep operating subsidiaries open while imposing losses on holding company investors by statutory priority.
- Source of strength: JPMorgan Chase & Co. must financially support its depository institution subsidiaries, including as directed by the Federal Reserve.
- Acquisition regulation: Federal Reserve approval needed for BHC/FHC acquisitions exceeding 5% voting shares of an unaffiliated bank; prohibition if post-acquisition liabilities exceed 10% of aggregate liabilities of all financial companies; prior Fed notice required for certain acquisitions of firms >$10 billion in assets engaged in financial-in-nature activities; Fed may limit FHC acquisitions if eligibility standards are not met.
- Ongoing compliance obligations: Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the DOJ (Sept. 29, 2020) related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries markets, and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank oversight: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. activities constrained by the National Bank Act and OCC interpretations; OCC can take enforcement actions for unsafe or unsound practices, including restricting activities or imposing corrective requirements.
- FDIC deposit insurance: coverage funded by assessments on banks, including JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
- FDIC authority upon bank insolvency: potential appointment as conservator or receiver with broad powers to transfer assets and liabilities without creditor approval.
- Prompt corrective action: mandated regulatory intervention for undercapitalized banks; Federal Reserve may act against the parent BHC; BHC may be required to guarantee a subsidiary bank’s capital restoration plan.
- OCC Heightened Standards and governance: large-bank risk governance framework requirements; clear separation of the bank’s risk profile from its parent BHC; management standards include board-level oversight of risk management.
text:
Orderly liquidation authority . Certain financial companies, 
including JPMorgan Chase and certain of its subsidiaries, 
can also be subjected to resolution under an “orderly 
liquidation authority.” The U.S. Treasury Secretary, in 
consultation with the President of the United States, must 
first make certain determinations concerning extraordinary 
financial distress and systemic risk, and action must be 
recommended by the FDIC and the Federal Reserve. Absent 
such actions, the Firm, as a BHC, would remain subject to 
resolution under the Bankruptcy Code. The FDIC has issued 
a draft policy statement describing its “single point of 
entry” strategy for resolution of SIFIs under the orderly 
liquidation authority, which seeks to keep operating 
subsidiaries of a BHC open and impose losses on 
shareholders and creditors of the BHC in receivership 
according to their statutory order of priority.

title: Holding company as a source of strength
heading: 1.5.1.8 Holding company as a source of strength
start_phrase:
JPMorgan Chase & 
Co. is required to serve as a source of financial strength for 
its depository institution subsidiaries and to commit 
resources to support those subsidiaries, including when 
directed to do so by the Federal Reserve.
summary:
- Governance and risk management: Board-level oversight of risk management and adherence to heightened management standards.
- Recovery and resolution planning: Annual comprehensive recovery plan to stay well-capitalized and funded; periodic resolution plans to the Federal Reserve and FDIC, alternating between “targeted” and “full” submissions per 2019 rule changes. Targeted plan filed June 28, 2021; next full plan due by July 1, 2023. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must submit a separate FDIC resolution plan by December 1, 2023. Certain non-U.S. subsidiaries and branches are subject to local planning requirements.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA): Potential resolution under OLA upon Treasury/President determinations and FDIC/Federal Reserve recommendations; otherwise resolution under the Bankruptcy Code. FDIC’s “single point of entry” strategy aims to keep operating subsidiaries open while imposing losses on BHC shareholders and creditors by statutory priority.
- Source-of-strength doctrine: JPMorgan Chase & Co. must support its depository institution subsidiaries and provide resources when directed by the Federal Reserve.
- Acquisition regulations: Federal Reserve/OCC requirements for BHCs and FHCs, including prior Fed approval to acquire over 5% of an unaffiliated bank’s voting shares; prohibition on acquisitions that would raise a firm’s total liabilities above 10% of aggregate financial company liabilities; prior written notice to the Fed for certain acquisitions of firms over $10 billion in assets engaged in financial activities; Fed may restrict FHC acquisitions if eligibility standards are not met.
- Ongoing legal obligations: Compliance with a Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the DOJ (Sept. 29, 2020) related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries investigations, and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank oversight: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.’s activities are limited by the National Bank Act and OCC interpretations; OCC may take enforcement actions for unsafe or unsound practices, including limiting activities or imposing corrective capital/managerial measures.
- FDIC deposit insurance: Coverage funded by assessments on banks, including JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
- FDIC authority in bank insolvency: FDIC may be appointed conservator or receiver with broad powers to transfer assets and liabilities without creditor approval.
- Prompt Corrective Action (FDICIA 1991): Mandatory regulatory actions when capital standards are not met; Federal Reserve may act against the parent BHC based on a subsidiary’s undercapitalization, and the BHC may be required to guarantee a capital restoration plan.
- OCC Heightened Standards: Large bank guidelines requiring a robust risk governance framework and a risk profile clearly distinguishable from the parent BHC’s, with strong board oversight.
text:
Holding company as a source of strength.  JPMorgan Chase & 
Co. is required to serve as a source of financial strength for 
its depository institution subsidiaries and to commit 
resources to support those subsidiaries, including when 
directed to do so by the Federal Reserve.

title: Regulation of acquisitions
heading: 1.5.1.9 Regulation of acquisitions
start_phrase:
Acquisitions by BHCs and their 
banks are subject to requirements, limitations and 
prohibitions established by law and by the Federal Reserve 
and the OCC.
summary:
- Board oversight of risk management standards.
- Recovery and resolution planning requirements:
  - Annual firmwide recovery plan to remain well-capitalized and funded in adverse events.
  - Alternating “targeted” and “full” resolution plans per 2019 FDIC/Fed rules; targeted plan filed June 28, 2021; full plan due by July 1, 2023.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. must submit separate recovery and resolution plans as directed by the OCC and FDIC (bank resolution plan due by Dec 1, 2023).
  - Non-U.S. subsidiaries and branches subject to local recovery/resolution regimes.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA):
  - Potential FDIC-led resolution upon Treasury/President determinations and FDIC/Fed recommendation.
  - FDIC “single point of entry” strategy aims to keep operating subsidiaries open while imposing losses on BHC shareholders and creditors by statutory priority.
- Holding company “source of strength” obligation requiring JPMorgan Chase & Co. to support depository institution subsidiaries when needed.
- Regulation of acquisitions:
  - Federal Reserve approval required for BHCs/FHCs to acquire >5% of an unaffiliated bank’s voting shares.
  - Prohibition on acquisitions that would push a financial company’s total liabilities above 10% of aggregate sector liabilities.
  - Prior written notice to the Fed for acquiring voting shares of companies >$10 billion in assets engaged in “financial in nature” activities.
  - Fed may limit FHC acquisitions if the FHC or its depository institutions fail to meet eligibility standards.
- Ongoing obligations under a September 29, 2020 DOJ Deferred Prosecution Agreement related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries markets and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank regulation (JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.):
  - Activities constrained by the National Bank Act and OCC interpretations.
  - OCC enforcement authority for unsafe or unsound practices, including restricting activities or imposing corrective requirements.
  - FDIC deposit insurance assessments.
  - FDIC powers as conservator/receiver in insolvency, including transferring assets and liabilities without creditor approval.
  - Prompt corrective action under FDICIA if capital standards are not met; Federal Reserve may act against the parent BHC and require guarantees of capital restoration plans.
  - OCC Heightened Standards requiring a formal risk governance framework and a risk profile distinguishable from the parent BHC, with board-level responsibilities.
text:
Regulation of acquisitions . Acquisitions by BHCs and their 
banks are subject to requirements, limitations and 
prohibitions established by law and by the Federal Reserve 
and the OCC. For example, FHCs and BHCs are required to 
obtain the approval of the Federal Reserve before they 
acquire more than 5% of the voting shares of an 
unaffiliated bank. In addition, acquisitions by financial 
companies are prohibited if, as a result of the acquisition, 
the total liabilities of the financial company would exceed 
10% of the total liabilities of all financial companies. 
Furthermore, for certain acquisitions, the Firm must provide written notice to the Federal Reserve prior to 
acquiring direct or indirect ownership or control of any 
voting shares of any company with over $10 billion in 
assets that is engaged in activities that are “financial in 
nature.” Moreover, while FHCs may engage in a broader 
range of activities (including acquisitions) than BHCs, the 
Federal Reserve has the authority to limit an FHC’s ability to 
conduct otherwise permissible acquisitions if the FHC or any 
of its depository institution subsidiaries ceases to meet 
applicable eligibility requirements.

title: Ongoing obligations
heading: 1.5.1.10 Ongoing obligations

title: FDIC deposit insurance
heading: 1.5.2.1 FDIC deposit insurance
start_phrase:
The FDIC deposit insurance fund 
provides insurance coverage for certain deposits and is 
funded through assessments on banks, including JPMorgan

summary:
- Governance and risk management standards, including board oversight of risk management.
- Recovery and resolution planning: an annually updated firmwide recovery plan; OCC-directed recovery plan for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; alternating “targeted” and “full” living will submissions to the Federal Reserve and FDIC under 2019 rules (targeted plan filed June 28, 2021; full plan due by July 1, 2023); a separate bank resolution plan due to the FDIC by December 1, 2023; and local recovery/resolution requirements for certain non-U.S. subsidiaries and branches.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority: potential resolution of the firm under Title II upon determinations by Treasury (in consultation with the President) and recommendations by the FDIC and Federal Reserve; absent such action, bankruptcy would apply; FDIC’s draft “single point of entry” approach would keep operating subsidiaries open while imposing losses on the holding company’s shareholders and creditors.
- Source-of-strength doctrine: the holding company must support its depository institution subsidiaries, including when directed by the Federal Reserve.
- Acquisition regulation: Federal Reserve approval required for BHC/FHC acquisitions of more than 5% of an unaffiliated bank’s voting shares; prohibition on acquisitions that would raise the acquirer’s total liabilities above 10% of aggregate financial company liabilities; prior written notice to the Federal Reserve for certain acquisitions of companies over $10 billion in assets engaged in financial activities; authority for the Federal Reserve to limit FHC acquisitions if eligibility standards are not met.
- Ongoing legal obligations under a September 29, 2020 Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the DOJ related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries markets, and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank oversight: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.’s activities are limited by the National Bank Act and OCC interpretations; the OCC can take enforcement actions for unsafe or unsound practices, including restricting activities or imposing corrective requirements.
- FDIC deposit insurance and assessment obligations.
- FDIC authority upon bank insolvency to act as conservator or receiver and transfer assets and liabilities without creditor approval.
- Prompt corrective action: mandatory regulatory responses to capital shortfalls at depository institutions; potential Federal Reserve actions against the parent BHC and possible requirements to guarantee a subsidiary bank’s capital restoration plan.
- OCC Heightened Standards: large-bank risk governance framework requirements, including clear separation of the bank’s risk profile from that of its parent and defined board-level oversight.

title: FDIC powers upon a bank insolvency
heading: 1.5.2.2 FDIC powers upon a bank insolvency
start_phrase:
Upon any insolvency of 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., the FDIC could be appointed as 
conservator or receiver under the Federal Deposit 
Insurance Act.
summary:
- Board-level oversight: Emphasis on board of directors’ oversight of the Firm’s risk management activities and adherence to management standards.
- Recovery and resolution planning: Annual comprehensive recovery plan to remain well-capitalized and funded; alternating “targeted” and “full” resolution plans with filings in 2021 (targeted) and due July 1, 2023 (full); JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. to submit its own recovery and resolution plans (including a plan due December 1, 2023); certain non-U.S. subsidiaries and branches subject to local regimes.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA): Potential resolution under OLA upon determinations by the U.S. Treasury Secretary (in consultation with the President) and recommendations by the FDIC and Federal Reserve; FDIC’s “single point of entry” strategy aims to keep operating subsidiaries open while imposing losses on BHC shareholders and creditors; absent OLA, resolution proceeds under the Bankruptcy Code.
- Source of strength: JPMorgan Chase & Co. must serve as a financial source of strength to its depository institution subsidiaries, including when directed by the Federal Reserve.
- Acquisition regulation: Federal Reserve/OCC approvals and limits, including approval for acquisitions exceeding 5% of a bank’s voting shares; prohibition on acquisitions that would push a financial company’s total liabilities above 10% of sector liabilities; prior written notice to the Federal Reserve for acquisitions of companies over $10 billion in assets engaged in “financial in nature” activities; the Fed may restrict FHC acquisitions if eligibility standards are not met.
- Ongoing legal obligations: Compliance with a Deferred Prosecution Agreement (Sept. 29, 2020) related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries markets, and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank oversight: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.’s activities are limited by the National Bank Act and OCC interpretations; the OCC may take enforcement action for unsafe or unsound practices, including imposing activity limits or corrective requirements.
- FDIC deposit insurance: Coverage of certain deposits funded by bank assessments, including those on JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
- FDIC powers upon insolvency: If JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. becomes insolvent, the FDIC may be appointed conservator or receiver with broad authority to transfer assets and liabilities without creditor approval.
- Prompt corrective action: Regulators must act when capital adequacy thresholds are breached; the Federal Reserve can take action against the parent BHC; in some cases the BHC must guarantee a subsidiary bank’s capital restoration plan.
- OCC Heightened Standards: Large banks must maintain a robust risk governance framework that clearly distinguishes the bank’s risk profile from its parent BHC; enhanced board and risk management responsibilities.

title: Prompt corrective action
heading: 1.5.2.3 Prompt corrective action
start_phrase:
The Federal Deposit Insurance 
Corporation Improvement Act of 1991 requires the relevant 
federal banking regulator to take “prompt corrective 
action” with respect to a depository institution if that 
institution does not meet certain capital adequacy 
standards.
summary:
- Board-level oversight of enterprise risk management standards.
- Recovery and resolution planning requirements:
  - Annual firmwide recovery plan to remain well-capitalized and funded.
  - Alternating “targeted” and “full” resolution plan submissions to the Federal Reserve and FDIC under revised 2019 rules (targeted plan filed June 28, 2021; next full plan due July 1, 2023).
  - Separate recovery/resolution plans required for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. as directed by the OCC and FDIC (bank resolution plan due December 1, 2023).
  - Certain non-U.S. subsidiaries and branches subject to local recovery and resolution regimes.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA) framework:
  - Potential FDIC-led resolution of the holding company upon systemic risk determinations by U.S. authorities.
  - FDIC’s “single point of entry” strategy aims to keep operating subsidiaries open while imposing losses on holding company shareholders and creditors.
  - Absent OLA, resolution proceeds under the U.S. Bankruptcy Code.
- “Source of strength” obligations requiring the holding company to support its insured depository subsidiaries.
- Acquisition regulations and limitations:
  - Federal Reserve approval for acquiring over 5% of an unaffiliated bank’s voting shares.
  - Prohibition on acquisitions that would cause a firm’s total liabilities to exceed 10% of aggregate liabilities of all financial companies.
  - Prior written notice to the Federal Reserve for certain acquisitions of companies (over $10 billion in assets) engaged in financial activities.
  - The Federal Reserve may restrict otherwise permissible FHC activities/acquisitions if eligibility standards are not met.
- Ongoing obligations under a September 29, 2020 Deferred Prosecution Agreement with the DOJ related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries markets and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank governance and supervisory framework:
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.’s activities limited by the National Bank Act and OCC interpretations.
  - OCC enforcement authority for unsafe or unsound practices, including potential activity limits or corrective requirements.
- FDIC deposit insurance assessments supporting insured deposits.
- FDIC powers in bank insolvency, including appointment as conservator/receiver and broad authority to transfer assets and liabilities.
- Prompt Corrective Action under FDICIA:
  - Mandatory remediation for undercapitalized banks.
  - Federal Reserve authority to act against the parent BHC and require guarantees of capital restoration plans.
- OCC Heightened Standards requiring large banks to maintain a robust, distinct risk governance framework with clear separation of the bank’s risk profile from that of the parent and enhanced board responsibilities.
text:
Prompt corrective action.  The Federal Deposit Insurance 
Corporation Improvement Act of 1991 requires the relevant 
federal banking regulator to take “prompt corrective 
action” with respect to a depository institution if that 
institution does not meet certain capital adequacy 
standards. T he Federal Reserve is also authorized to take 
appropriate action against the parent  BHC , such as 
JPMorgan Chase & Co., based on the undercapitalized status 
of any bank subsidiary. In certain instances, the BHC would 
be required to guarantee the performance of the capital 
restoration plan for its undercapitalized subsidiary.

title: OCC Heightened Standards
heading: 1.5.2.4 OCC Heightened Standards
start_phrase:
The OCC has established 
guidelines setting forth heightened standards for large 
banks, including minimum standards for the design and 
implementation of a risk governance framework for banks.
summary:
- Governance and risk management standards emphasizing board of directors’ oversight of risk activities.
- Resolution and recovery planning: annual firmwide recovery plan; alternating “targeted” and “full” U.S. resolution plans (targeted filed June 28, 2021; full due July 1, 2023); separate bank-level plans for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (including FDIC/OCC-directed plans due by Dec. 1, 2023); local non-U.S. recovery/resolution requirements.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority: potential FDIC-led “single point of entry” resolution for SIFIs, imposing losses on holding company investors while keeping operating subsidiaries open; otherwise Bankruptcy Code applies absent OLA determinations.
- Holding company “source of strength” duty requiring JPMorgan Chase & Co. to support its depository institution subsidiaries.
- Acquisition regulation: Federal Reserve/OCC approvals (e.g., >5% bank voting shares); 10% aggregate liabilities cap for financial company acquisitions; prior notice for acquisitions of firms >$10B in assets engaged in financial-in-nature activities; Fed may restrict FHC acquisitions if eligibility standards lapse.
- Ongoing legal obligations under a 2020 Deferred Prosecution Agreement related to precious metals and U.S. Treasuries investigations and a related CFTC order.
- Subsidiary bank oversight: OCC enforcement authority over JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; FDIC deposit insurance assessments; FDIC powers as conservator/receiver in bank insolvency; prompt corrective action framework (including potential BHC guarantees); OCC Heightened Standards for risk governance and board oversight; restrictions on affiliate transactions; dividend limitations and supervisory veto; depositor preference prioritizing U.S. deposit liabilities and receivership expenses over other unsecured claims.
- Consumer regulation: CFPB oversight of consumer protection, fair lending (including small business lending) and UDAAP; proposed 2023 rule to curb credit card late fees; state-level enforcement; U.K. retail operations (JPMorgan Europe Limited and Nutmeg) regulated by PRA, FCA, Payment Systems Regulator, and subject to U.K. consumer-protection laws.
- Securities/broker-dealer regulation: U.S. broker-dealers (e.g., J.P. Morgan Securities LLC) regulated by SEC, FINRA, NYSE; similar non-U.S. regimes (e.g., J.P. Morgan Securities plc in the U.K.); rules covering trading, offerings, research, client funds, margin, capital, recordkeeping, and conduct.
- Investment management regulation: global rules on safeguarding/managing client assets, fund offerings, and marketing; SEC-registered investment advisers with fiduciary duties under the Investment Advisers Act; OCC oversight of bank fiduciary activities.
- Derivatives regulation: capital and margin requirements; central clearing and trading mandates for standardized OTC derivatives; reporting obligations; registration of key entities as CFTC swap dealers and SEC security-based swap dealers with associated capital and collateral requirements for uncleared instruments.
text:
OCC Heightened Standards.  The OCC has established 
guidelines setting forth heightened standards for large 
banks, including minimum standards for the design and 
implementation of a risk governance framework for banks. 
Under these standards, a bank’s risk governance framework 
must ensure that the bank’s risk profile is easily 
distinguished and separate from that of its parent BHC for 
risk management purposes. The bank’s board or risk 
5committee is responsible for approving the bank’s risk 
governance framework, providing active oversight of the 
bank’s risk-taking activities, and holding management 
accountable for adhering to the risk governance framework.

Restrictions on transactions with affiliates.  JPMorgan Chase 
Bank, N.A. and its subsidiaries are subject to restrictions 
imposed by federal law on extensions of credit to, 
investments in stock or securities of, and derivatives,

JPMorgan Chase & Co. and certain other affiliates. These

title: Dividend restrictions
heading: 1.5.2.6 Dividend restrictions
start_phrase:
Federal law imposes limitations on the 
payment of dividends by national banks, such as JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, N.A.
summary:
- Governance and risk oversight: A board-level committee approves the bank’s risk governance framework, oversees risk-taking, and holds management accountable for adherence.
- Affiliate transactions restrictions: Federal laws limit and condition loans, investments, derivatives, and securities lending between JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (and its subsidiaries) and JPMorgan Chase & Co. and other affiliates, requiring specified collateral and compliance with quantitative and other requirements.
- Dividend limitations: National bank dividend payments are constrained by federal law; regulators (OCC and Federal Reserve) can restrict dividends deemed unsafe or unsound, with references to permitted amounts absent prior approval.
- Depositor preference: In an IDI receivership, administrative expenses and U.S. deposit liabilities (including certain dually payable non-U.S. branch deposits) have priority over other unsecured creditors, including non-U.S. branch depositors and public noteholders.
- Consumer regulation: The CFPB oversees compliance with federal consumer protection and fair lending laws, including UDAAP and small business lending under ECOA; it can take enforcement actions. In 2023, the CFPB proposed significant limits on credit card late fees. State consumer laws also apply.
- U.K. retail oversight: JPMorgan’s U.K. retail bank (JPMEL) and Nutmeg are regulated by the PRA and FCA (and the U.K. Payment Systems Regulator for payments), and are subject to U.K. consumer-protection legislation.
- Securities and broker-dealer regulation: U.S. securities activities (e.g., underwriting, dealing, brokerage) are regulated by the SEC, FINRA, NYSE; similar activities in the U.K. are conducted by J.P. Morgan Securities plc. Rules cover sales/trading practices, offerings, research, customer funds, client financing, capital, recordkeeping, and conduct.
- Investment management regulation: Global asset and wealth management are heavily regulated regarding client asset safeguarding, fund offerings, and marketing. U.S. advisers are SEC-registered and subject to Investment Advisers Act fiduciary duties; bank fiduciary activities are overseen by the OCC.
- Derivatives regulation: The Firm is subject to comprehensive derivatives rules requiring capital and margin, central clearing of standardized OTC derivatives, trading on regulated venues, and reporting. JPMorgan entities are registered as CFTC swap dealers and SEC security-based swap dealers, subject to collateralization, capital, and other compliance requirements.
text:
Dividend restrictions.  Federal law imposes limitations on the 
payment of dividends by national banks, such as JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, N.A. Refer to Note 26 for the amount of 
dividends that JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. could pay, at 
January 1, 2023, to JPMorgan Chase without the approval 
of the banking regulators. The OCC and the Federal Reserve 
also have authority to prohibit or limit the payment of 
dividends of a bank subsidiary that they supervise if, in the 
banking regulator’s opinion, payment of a dividend would 
constitute an unsafe or unsound practice in light of the 
financial condition of the bank.

title: Consumer supervision and regulation

start_phrase:

(“CFPB”) with respect to federal consumer protection laws, 
including laws relating to fair lending and the prohibition of

text:
Consumer supervision and regulation.  JPMorgan Chase and 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. are subject to supervision and 
regulation by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau 
(“CFPB”) with respect to federal consumer protection laws, 
including laws relating to fair lending and the prohibition of 
unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices in connection 
with the offer, sale or provision of consumer financial 
products and services. The CFPB also has jurisdiction over 
small business lending activities with respect to fair lending 
and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. As part of its 
regulatory oversight, the CFPB has authority to take 
enforcement actions against firms that offer certain 
products and services to consumers using practices that are 
deemed to be unfair, deceptive or abusive. In February 
2023, the CFPB proposed a rule that would significantly 
reduce and limit the late payment fees that credit card 
issuers, including the Firm, would be permitted to charge to 
customers. The Firm’s consumer activities are also subject 
to regulation under state statutes which are enforced by the 
Attorney General or empowered agency of each state.
In the U.K. , the Firm operates a retail bank through J.P. 
Morgan Europe Limited (“JPMEL”) and provides retail 
investment management services through Nutmeg Saving and Investment Limited (“Nutmeg”). JPMEL is regulated by 
the PRA, and both JPMEL and Nutmeg are regulated by the 
FCA with respect to their conduct of financial services in the 
U.K., including obligations relating to the fair treatment of 
customers. JPMEL is also regulated by the U.K. Payment 
Systems Regulator with respect to its operation and use of 
payment systems.  In addition, the retail businesses of 
JPMEL and Nutmeg are subject to U.K. consumer-protection 
legislation.

title: Securities and broker-dealer regulation
heading: 1.5.3 Securities and broker-dealer regulation
start_phrase:
The Firm conducts securities underwriting, dealing and 
brokerage activities in the U.S. through J.P. Morgan 
Securities LLC and other non-bank broker-dealer 
subsidiaries, all of which are subject to regulations of the 
SEC, FINRA and the New York Stock Exchange, among 
others.
summary:
- Governance and oversight: A designated committee approves the bank’s risk governance framework, actively oversees risk-taking, and holds management accountable for adherence.
- Affiliate transactions: Federal laws restrict JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and its subsidiaries from certain transactions with JPMorgan Chase & Co. and other affiliates (e.g., lending, investments, derivatives, securities lending) unless secured and compliant with specified requirements.
- Dividend limitations: National bank dividend payments are limited by federal law; the OCC and Federal Reserve may prohibit or restrict dividends deemed unsafe given a bank’s condition.
- Depositor preference: In an IDI receivership, administrative expenses and U.S. deposit liabilities (including FDIC and deposits dually payable in the U.S. and a non-U.S. branch) have priority over other unsecured creditors, including non-U.S. branch depositors and public noteholders.

The Bank Secrecy Act and Economic Sanctions: 
The Bank Secrecy Act (“BSA”) requires all financial 
institutions, including banks and securities broker-dealers, 
to establish a risk-based system of internal controls 
reasonably designed to prevent money laundering and the 
financing of terrorism. The BSA includes a variety of record-
keeping and reporting requirements, as well as due 
diligence/know-your-customer documentation 
requirements. The Firm is also subject to the regulations 
and economic sanctions programs administered and 
enforced by the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets 
Control (“OFAC”) and EU and U.K. authorities which target 
entities or individuals that are, or are located in countries 
that are, involved in activities including terrorism, 
hostilities, embezzlement or human rights violations. The 
Firm is also subject to economic sanctions laws, rules and 
regulations in other jurisdictions in which it operates, 
including those that conflict with or prohibit a firm such as 
JPMorgan Chase from complying with certain laws, rules 
and regulations to which it is otherwise subject.

Compensation practices:  
The Firm’s compensation practices are subject to oversight 
by the Federal Reserve, as well as other agencies. The

Board (“FSB”) has also established standards covering

compensation practices are also subject to regulation and 
oversight by regulators in other jurisdictions , notably the

implemented in the EU and as adopted in the U.K, which 
includes compensation-related provisions. The European

regulators have also instituted guidelines on CRD V

summary:
- Overview of regulatory obligations affecting JPMorgan Chase across the U.S., EU, and U.K., including:
  - Requirements on segregation of counterparty collateral, business conduct, documentation, record-keeping, reporting, and anti-fraud/anti-manipulation under EMIR and MiFID II.
  - Registration status: J.P. Morgan Securities LLC as a CFTC-registered futures commission merchant and NFA member.
  - Global data, privacy, consumer protection, and cybersecurity rules that are rapidly evolving and vigorously enforced.

- Financial crime, sanctions, and anti-corruption compliance:
  - Bank Secrecy Act obligations (AML/CFT programs, record-keeping, reporting, KYC).
  - U.S. OFAC, EU, and U.K. sanctions regimes, and conflicts among jurisdictions.

- Compensation regulation and oversight:
  - U.S. Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC guidance on incentive compensation risk.
  - FSB standards; EU/UK frameworks under CRD V and EBA/UK guidelines.
  - Ongoing evolution of rules that may influence compensation design.

- Key international regulatory initiatives and reforms:
  - MiFID II: trading venue mandates, transparency, reporting, investor protection, commodities position limits; EU proposals for amendments (including a consolidated tape) under review.
  - U.K. Wholesale Markets Review and FSMB changes to secondary markets post-Brexit, with further consultations on transparency.
  - EMIR amendments proposed to enhance EU clearing competitiveness and CCP supervision.
  - CSDR mandatory buy-in regime deferred proposal to November 2025.
  - U.K. “Edinburgh Reforms” spanning retail banking, payments, markets, digital assets, and sustainable finance, with further 2023 consultations expected.
  - Basel III finalization in EU and U.K.: compliance from January 2025 with transitional periods; revisions to credit, operational, and market risk frameworks; reduced reliance on internal models; enhanced supervisory tools; ESG risk management and disclosure requirements; EBA sustainable finance standards (2023–2025); PRA climate risk policies.

    - CSRD expanding ESG reporting scope with phased implementation starting 2024.
