title: MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT - Introduction
heading: 7.8.11 MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
start_phrase: Market risk is the risk associated with the effect of changes in market factors such as interest and foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads or implied volatilities, on the value of assets and liabilities held for both the short and long term.
summary:
MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
Market risk is the risk associated with the effect of changes 
in market factors such as interest and foreign exchange 
rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads or 
implied volatilities, on the value of assets and liabilities held 
for both the short and long term.
text:
MARKET RISK MANAGEMENT
Market risk is the risk associated with the effect of changes 
in market factors such as interest and foreign exchange 
rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads or 
implied volatilities, on the value of assets and liabilities held 
for both the short and long term.

title: Market Risk Management
heading: 7.8.11.1 Market Risk Management
start_phrase: Market Risk Management monitors market risks throughout the Firm and defines market risk policies and procedures.
summary:
- Defines market risk as the potential impact of changes in interest rates, FX rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities on asset and liability values over short and long horizons.
- States Market Risk Management’s mandate: oversee market risks firmwide; set and maintain policies; independently measure, monitor, and control risks across Lines of Business (LOBs), Corporate, and the Firm; define, approve, and monitor limits; perform stress testing and qualitative risk assessments; and provide transparency to senior management, the Board, and regulators.
- Objectives include managing risk, supporting efficient risk/return decisions, and reducing volatility in operating performance.
- Emphasizes a multi-metric measurement approach (no single measure captures market risk): Value-at-Risk (VaR), stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, and other sensitivity-based measures.
- Describes a tiered limit framework at Firm, LOB, Corporate, and legal-entity levels, including VaR and stress limits, supplemented by nonstatistical measures (e.g., P&L drawdowns).
- Limit-setting considers market volatility, product liquidity, client business needs, and management judgment; limits are regularly reviewed and updated, with senior management responsible for approving certain limits. Unreviewed limits are escalated.
- Governance and escalation: LOBs/Corporate must adhere to limits; breaches are reported promptly to approvers; remediation may involve reducing risk or granting temporary limit increases to accommodate client activity or volatility; significant breaches are escalated appropriately.
- Acknowledges model limitations and imprecision, particularly under sudden or severe market shifts; references broader model risk considerations and highlights periodic review and calibration of market risk measures.
text:
Market Risk Management monitors market risks throughout 
the Firm and defines market risk policies and procedures. 
Market Risk Management seeks to manage risk, facilitate 
efficient risk/return decisions, reduce volatility in operating 
performance and provide transparency into the Firm’s 
market risk profile for senior management, the Board of 
Directors and regulators. Market Risk Management is 
responsible for the following functions:
•Maintaining a market risk policy framework
•Independently measuring, monitoring and controlling 
LOB, Corporate, and Firmwide market risk
•Defining, approving and monitoring of limits
•Performing stress testing and qualitative risk 
assessments
Risk measurement

title: Measures used to capture market risk
heading: 7.8.11.2 Measures used to capture market risk
start_phrase: There is no single measure to capture market risk and therefore Market Risk Management uses various metrics, both statistical and nonstatistical, to assess risk including:
summary:
- Defines market risk as the impact of changes in interest rates, FX, equity/commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatility on asset and liability values.
- Outlines Market Risk Management’s objectives: manage and control market risks firmwide, support risk/return decisions, reduce operating volatility, and provide transparency to senior management, the Board, and regulators.
- Details core responsibilities: maintain a market risk policy framework; independently measure, monitor, and control market risk across LOBs, Corporate, and Firmwide; define, approve, and monitor limits; conduct stress testing and qualitative risk assessments.
- Describes the risk measurement toolkit: Value-at-Risk (VaR), stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, and other sensitivity-based measures; notes no single metric fully captures market risk.
- Explains risk monitoring and control via a hierarchy of limits at Firm, LOB, Corporate, and legal-entity levels, using VaR, stress limits, and nonstatistical measures; limits are set considering market volatility, liquidity, client business, and judgment.
- Sets governance and escalation protocols: regular review and approval of limits by senior management; monitoring and reporting of exposures; timely reporting and escalation of breaches; remediation may include risk reduction or temporary limit increases.
- Acknowledges model limitations and uncertainty, especially under sudden or severe market shifts; commits to periodic review and calibration of market risk measures.
- Excerpt is from JPMorgan Chase & Co. 2022 Form 10-K.
text:
Measures used to capture market risk  
There is no single measure to capture market risk and 
therefore Market Risk Management uses various metrics, 
both statistical and nonstatistical, to assess risk including:
•Value-at-risk (VaR) 
•Stress testing
•Profit and loss drawdowns 
•Earnings-at-risk 
•Other sensitivity-based measures

title: Risk monitoring and control
heading: 7.8.11.3 Risk monitoring and control
start_phrase: Market risk exposure is managed primarily through a series of limits set in the context of the market environment and business strategy.
summary:
- Defines market risk as potential losses from changes in interest rates, foreign exchange rates, equity and commodity prices, credit spreads, and implied volatilities affecting assets and liabilities over short and long horizons.
- Outlines Market Risk Management’s mandate: set and maintain the market risk policy framework; independently measure, monitor and control market risk across Lines of Business (LOBs), Corporate, and Firmwide; define, approve, and monitor limits; perform stress testing and qualitative risk assessments; support risk/return decisions, reduce earnings volatility, and provide transparency to senior management, the Board, and regulators.
- Describes risk measurement approach: no single metric suffices; uses a toolkit including Value-at-Risk (VaR), stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, earnings-at-risk, and other sensitivity-based measures.
- Details risk monitoring and control framework: hierarchical limits at Firm, LOB, Corporate, and legal entity levels (e.g., VaR and stress limits, plus nonstatistical measures such as P&L drawdowns); processes for limit setting, periodic review and approvals; responsibilities for adherence; timely breach reporting, escalation, and remediation (risk reduction or temporary limit increases for client activity/volatility).
- Acknowledges model limitations and uncertainty, especially under sudden market shifts; references broader model risk governance and notes periodic review and calibration of market risk measures.
- Summarizes LOB/Corporate activity-to-risk mapping and positions included in key measures:
  - Consumer & Community Banking (CCB): mortgage origination/servicing and deposits; risks include closing probability, interest rate and prepayment risk; positions include mortgage commitments and hedges (derivatives), warehouse loans (fair value option), MSRs and hedges, IO/MBS and hedges, fair value option liabilities; retained loans and deposits; DVA on certain liabilities captured via sensitivities.
  - Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB): market-making in FICC, equities, and commodities; risks include price/volatility, basis/correlation, interest rate and prepayment; positions include trading assets/liabilities and derivatives (including hedges), certain repo/securities financing, fair value option liabilities and loans, CVA and hedges, marketable equity investments; retained loans and deposits; privately held equity/real estate FVO loans; FVA and DVA sensitivities; credit component of CVA for stressed counterparties.
  - Commercial Banking (CB): lending and deposits; interest rate and prepayment risk; marketable equity investments in VaR; retained loans and deposits in earnings-at-risk.
  - Asset & Wealth Management (AWM): seed capital, co-investments, lending and deposits; general market factor risks; positions include trading debt held pre-distribution, seed capital and related hedges, deferred compensation and hedges, co-investments; retained loans and deposits.
  - Corporate: manages liquidity, funding, capital, structural interest rate, and non-USD FX risks; positions include derivatives recognized in noninterest revenue, marketable equity investments, deposits with banks, investment securities and related IR hedges, long-term debt and IR hedges, deposits; privately held equity; FX exposure from non-USD long-term debt and hedges.
- Notes that AWM and CB contributions to Firmwide average VaR were not material for 2022 and 2021.
- Cross-references related sections on investment portfolio risk and model risk for further detail.
text:
Risk monitoring and control 
Market risk exposure is managed primarily through a series 
of limits set in the context of the market environment and 
business strategy. In setting limits, Market Risk 
Management takes into consideration factors such as 
market volatility, product liquidity, accommodation of client 
business, and management judgment. Market Risk 
Management maintains different levels of limits. Firm level 
limits include VaR and stress limits. Similarly, LOB and 
Corporate limits include VaR and stress limits and may be 
supplemented by certain nonstatistical risk measures such 
as profit and loss drawdowns. Limits may also be set within 
the LOBs and Corporate, as well as at the legal entity level.Market Risk Management sets limits and regularly reviews 
and updates them as appropriate. Senior management is 
responsible for reviewing and approving certain of these 
risk limits on an ongoing basis. Limits that have not been 
reviewed within specified time periods by Market Risk 
Management are reported to senior management. The LOBs 
and Corporate are responsible for adhering to established 
limits against which exposures are monitored and reported.
Limit breaches are required to be reported in a timely 
manner to limit approvers, which include Market Risk 
Management and senior management. In the event of a 
breach, Market Risk Management consults with senior 
members of appropriate groups within the Firm to 
determine the suitable course of action required to return 
the applicable positions to compliance, which may include a 
reduction in risk in order to remedy the breach or granting 
a temporary increase in limits to accommodate an expected 
increase in client activity and/or market volatility. Certain 
Firm, Corporate or LOB-level limit breaches are escalated as 
appropriate.
Models used to measure market risk are inherently 
imprecise and are limited in their ability to measure certain 
risks or to predict losses. This imprecision may be 
heightened when sudden or severe shifts in market 
conditions occur. For additional discussion on model 
uncertainty refer to Estimations and Model Risk 
Management on page 148 .
Market Risk Management periodically reviews the Firm’s 
existing market risk measures to identify opportunities for 
enhancement, and to the extent appropriate, will calibrate 
those measures accordingly over time.

title: Value-at-risk
heading: 7.8.11.4 Value-at-risk
start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase utilizes value-at-risk (“VaR”), a statistical risk measure , to estimate the potential loss from adverse market moves in the current market environment.
summary:
- Purpose and framework: JPMorgan Chase uses a single Value-at-Risk (VaR) framework across the Firm to estimate potential losses from adverse market moves, supporting both internal risk management and regulatory requirements. It employs historical simulation using the prior 12 months of data and assumes recent historical changes reflect near-term outcomes.

- Risk Management VaR: Calculated daily with a one-day holding period and an expected tail-loss approach approximating a 95% confidence level. It is used to measure risk profiles, diversification, aggregate risks, set/monitor limits, and report to senior management, the Board, and regulators.

- Model structure: Granular VaR models simulate historical returns for specific risk factors and product types, incorporating portfolio-specific sensitivities and time series. Results are aggregated to the Firm level and run daily for businesses with market risk.

- Model limitations: VaR is imperfect due to reliance on historical data, limited horizons, potential market illiquidity, and sudden regime shifts. Some products lack sufficient data; proxies are used, which may affect results. The Firm supplements VaR with non-statistical measures such as stress testing.

- Data considerations: Daily market data used in VaR can differ from independent third-party data used in the monthly VCG price testing process, and it may be impractical to use VCG data for VaR. Model calculations are periodically reviewed and enhanced as portfolios and market conditions evolve, which can affect historical comparisons.

- Regulatory VaR: Calculated separately under Basel III, with a 10-business-day holding period and expected tail loss approximating a 99% confidence level. It applies to covered positions and differs from Risk Management VaR (e.g., exclusion of certain credit derivative hedges and some diversification benefits). Additional details are provided in Pillar 3 disclosures.

- 2022 VaR results and drivers: 
  - Total average Risk Management VaR rose to $58 million in 2022 from $55 million in 2021; min and max were $34 million and $242 million, respectively (vs. $24 million and $153 million in 2021).
  - Key driver was March 2022 nickel price spikes and volatility, which elevated Credit Portfolio VaR; this was partly offset by lower Corporate and other LOB VaR due to decreased market values of a legacy publicly traded private equity position.
  - Governance changes in 1Q22 removed the credit risk component of CVA for certain counterparties (and related hedges) from Credit Portfolio VaR; exposures moved to other sensitivity-based measures.
  - Diversification benefits are material and non-additive; maximum/minimum diversification metrics may be non-meaningful due to timing differences across components.

- Trend visualization: Daily Risk Management VaR over 2022 shows a pronounced increase in March tied to nickel-related counterparty exposure in the Credit Portfolio.
text:
Value-at-risk
JPMorgan Chase utilizes value-at-risk (“VaR”), a statistical 
risk measure , to estimate the potential loss from adverse 
market moves in the current market environment.  The Firm 
has a single VaR framework used as a basis for calculating 
Risk Management VaR and Regulatory VaR.
The framework is employed across the Firm using historical 
simulation based on data for the previous 12 months. The 
framework’s approach assumes that historical changes in 
market values are representative of the distribution of 
potential outcomes in the immediate future. The Firm 
believes the use of Risk Management VaR provides a daily 
measure of risk that is closely aligned to risk management 
decisions made by the LOBs and Corporate and, along with 
other market risk measures, provides the appropriate 
information needed to respond to risk events.  
The Firm’s Risk Management VaR is calculated assuming a  
one-day holding period and an expected tail-loss 
methodology which approximates a 95% confidence level.  
Risk Management VaR provides a consistent framework to 
measure risk profiles and levels of diversification across 
product types and is used for aggregating risks and 
monitoring limits across businesses. VaR results are 
reported to senior management, the Board of Directors and 
regulators.  
Underlying the overall VaR model framework are individual 
VaR models that simulate historical market returns for 
individual risk factors and/or product types. To capture 
material market risks as part of the Firm’s risk management 
framework, comprehensive VaR model calculations are 
performed daily for businesses whose activities give rise to 
market risk. These VaR models are granular and 
incorporate numerous risk factors and inputs to simulate 
daily changes in market values over the historical period; 
inputs are selected based on the risk profile of each 
portfolio, as sensitivities and historical time series used to 
generate daily market values may be different across 
product types or risk management systems. The VaR model 
results across all portfolios are aggregated at the Firm 
level.
As VaR is based on historical data, it is an imperfect 
measure of market risk exposure and potential future 
losses.  In addition, based on their reliance on available 
historical data, limited time horizons, and other factors, 
VaR measures are inherently limited in their ability to 
measure certain risks and to predict losses, particularly 
those associated with market illiquidity and sudden or 
severe shifts in market conditions.  
For certain products, specific risk parameters are not 
captured in VaR due to the lack of liquidity and availability 
of appropriate historical data. The Firm uses proxies to 
estimate the VaR for these and other products when daily 
time series are not available. It is likely that using an actual 
price-based time series for these products, if available, 
would affect the VaR results presented. The Firm therefore 
considers other nonstatistical measures such as stress testing, in addition to VaR, to capture and manage its 
market risk positions.  
The daily market data used in VaR models may be different 
than the independent third-party data collected for VCG 
price testing in its monthly valuation process. For example, 
in cases where market prices are not observable, or where 
proxies are used in VaR historical time series, the data 
sources may differ. Refer to Valuation process in Note 2 for 
further information on the Firm’s valuation process. As VaR 
model calculations require daily data and a consistent 
source for valuation, it may not be practical to use the data 
collected in the VCG monthly valuation process for VaR 
model calculations. 
The Firm’s VaR model calculations are periodically 
evaluated and enhanced in response to changes in the 
composition of the Firm’s portfolios, changes in market 
conditions, improvements in the Firm’s modeling 
techniques and measurements, and other factors. Such 
changes may affect historical comparisons of VaR results. 
Refer to Estimations and Model Risk Management on page 
148 for information regarding model reviews and 
approvals.
The Firm calculates separately a daily aggregated VaR in 
accordance with regulatory rules (“Regulatory VaR”), which 
is used to derive the Firm’s regulatory VaR-based capital 
requirements under Basel III capital rules. This Regulatory 
VaR model framework currently assumes a ten business-day 
holding period and an expected tail loss methodology which 
approximates a 99% confidence level. Regulatory VaR is 
applied to  “covered ” positions as defined by Basel III capital 
rules, which may be different than the positions included in 
the Firm’s Risk Management VaR. For example, credit 
derivative hedges of accrual loans are included in the Firm’s 
Risk Management VaR, while Regulatory VaR excludes these 
credit derivative hedges.  In addition, in contrast to the 
Firm’s Risk Management VaR, Regulatory VaR currently 
excludes the diversification benefit for certain VaR models.
Refer to JPMorgan Chase’s Basel III Pillar 3 Regulatory 
Capital Disclosures reports, which are available on the 
Firm’s website, for additional information on Regulatory 
VaR and the other components of market risk regulatory 
capital for the Firm (e.g., VaR-based measure, stressed 
VaR-based measure and the respective backtesting).

title: VaR backtesting
heading: 7.8.11.5 VaR backtesting
start_phrase: The Firm performs daily VaR model backtesting, which compares the daily Risk Management VaR results with the daily gains and losses that are utilized for VaR backtesting purposes.
summary:
- VaR backtesting: Daily comparison of Risk Management VaR with backtesting gains/losses that exclude certain revenue components (e.g., intraday trading, fees, commissions, valuation adjustments, net interest), aligned to Basel III. Definition of backtesting exceptions (loss exceeds prior day’s VaR), with an expected frequency of about five per 100 trading days, and caveat that exceptions vary with volatility differences from the 12‑month historical window. For the 12 months ended December 31, 2022: 136 gain days out of 259 and 17 exceptions. A distribution chart shows losses as a percentage of VaR in 50‑point intervals, with exceptions >100%; results differ from Basel III Pillar 3 Regulatory VaR disclosures.
- Stress testing: Complement to VaR assessing losses under hypothetical, simultaneous shocks across market factors (credit spreads, equities, rates, FX, commodities) for LOBs and Corporate. Focus on tail events, cross‑factor impacts, idiosyncratic and basis risks; flexible scenario construction. Governance under Market Risk Management and the Firmwide Market Risk Stress Methodology Committee; models subject to Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy. Results reported to senior management, used in CCAR and other enterprise stress tests, and embedded in the Risk Appetite framework reported to the Board Risk Committee.
- Profit and loss drawdowns: Monitoring tool highlighting trading losses via declines from year‑to‑date peak revenue.
- Earnings‑at‑risk (interest rate risk): Overview of structural interest rate risk from both trading and traditional banking (loans, deposits, debt issuance, investment securities). Policy and limits set by the CTC Risk Committee with Board oversight; Treasury and CIO manage and review the profile; dedicated risk function under the CTC CRO provides independent oversight. Sources of risk include timing and amount mismatches in repricing/maturities, yield curve slope changes, and behavioral maturity shifts. Firmwide management via funds transfer pricing and use of the investment securities portfolio and derivatives. EaR measures sensitivity of net interest income and certain fees to rate scenarios versus a baseline using market rates and deposit pricing assumptions, with simulations across USD and non‑USD exposures.
text:
VaR backtesting
The Firm performs daily VaR model backtesting, which compares the daily Risk Management VaR results with the daily gains 
and losses that are utilized for VaR backtesting purposes. The gains and losses  depicted in the chart below do not reflect the 
Firm’s reported revenue as they exclude certain components of total net revenue, such as those associated with the execution 
of new transactions (i.e., intraday client-driven trading and intraday risk management activities), fees, commissions, other 
valuation adjustments and net interest income.  These excluded components of total net revenue may more than offset the 
backtesting gain or loss on a particular day.  The definition of backtesting gains and losses above is consistent with the 
requirements for backtesting under Basel III capital rules.
A backtesting exception occurs when the daily backtesting loss exceeds the daily  Risk Management VaR for the prior day.  
Under the Firm’s  Risk Management VaR methodology, assuming current changes in market values are consistent with the 
historical changes used in the simulation, the Firm would expect to  incur VaR backtesting exceptions five times every 100 
trading days  on average.  The number of VaR backtesting exceptions observed can differ from the statistically expected number 
of backtesting exceptions if the current level of market volatility is materially different from the level of market volatility 
during the 12 months of historical data used in the VaR calculation.
For the 12 months ended D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2, the Firm posted backtesting gains on 136 of the 259 days, and observed 17 
VaR backtesting exceptions.  Firmwide backtesting loss days can differ from the loss days for which Fixed Income Markets and 
Equity Markets posted losses, as disclosed in CIB Markets revenue, as the population of positions which compose each metric 
are different and due to the exclusion of certain  components of total net revenue in backtesting gains and losses as described 
above. For more information on CIB Markets revenue, refer to pages 70-71 .
The following chart  presents the distribution of Firmwide daily backtesting gains and losses for  the trailing 12 months  and 
three months ended  D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2. The daily backtesting losses are displayed as a percentage of the corresponding 
daily  Risk Management VaR. The count of days with backtesting losses are shown in aggregate, in fifty percentage point 
intervals.  Backtesting exceptions are displayed within the intervals that are greater than one hundred percent.  The results in 
the chart below differ from the results of backtesting disclosed in the Market Risk section of the Firm’ s Basel III Pillar 3

title: Stress testing
heading: 7.8.11.6 Stress testing
start_phrase: Along with VaR, stress testing is an important tool used to assess risk.
summary:
- Focus of the section: “Other risk measures” beyond VaR, specifically stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, and earnings-at-risk (EaR).

- Stress testing:
  - Complements VaR by estimating losses under hypothetical yet plausible stressed scenarios with simultaneous shocks across market factors (credit spreads, equities, interest rates, FX, commodities).
  - Covers market risk–sensitive positions across Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate; includes tail events, idiosyncratic risks, and basis risks; flexible to construct new scenarios.
  - Results are periodically reported to senior management; used to understand exposures, set/monitor limits, and inform Risk Appetite.
  - Governance: overseen by Market Risk Management; models subject to Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy; Firmwide Market Risk Stress Methodology Committee approves methodology/scenario changes; significant changes escalated to senior management.
  - Integrated into CCAR and other firmwide stress tests; results reported to the Board of Directors and Board Risk Committee.

- Profit and loss drawdowns:
  - Tool to flag trading losses that exceed risk tolerance.
  - Defined as the decline in revenue from its year-to-date peak.

- Earnings-at-risk (interest rate risk management):
  - Measures the sensitivity of net income (including certain fees) to interest rate changes versus a baseline using market rates and deposit pricing assumptions.
  - Interest rate risk arises from both trading and traditional banking activities (loans, deposits, debt issuance, investment securities).
  - Governance: CTC Risk Committee sets structural interest rate risk policy and limits (approved by the Board Risk Committee); Treasury and CIO, with LOBs, calculate the firm’s structural interest rate risk profile; independent oversight by a dedicated risk function reporting to the CTC CRO.
  - Management tools: investment securities portfolio and interest rate derivatives; firmwide management via funds transfer pricing that centralizes interest rate risk in Treasury/CIO.
  - Sources of structural interest rate risk: timing and amount mismatches in maturities/repricing, yield curve shifts, and changes in asset/liability maturities as rates move.
  - Simulations cover U.S. dollar and non-U.S. dollar exposures, primarily for rate-sensitive assets and liabilities (e.g., retained loans).
text:
Stress testing 
Along with VaR, stress testing is an important  tool used to 
assess risk. While VaR reflects the risk of loss due to 
adverse changes in markets using recent historical market 
behavior, stress testing reflects the risk of loss from 
hypothetical changes in the value of market risk sensitive 
positions applied simultaneously. Stress testing measures 
the Firm’s vulnerability to losses under a range of stressed 
but possible economic and market scenarios. The results 
are used to understand the exposures responsible for those 
potential losses and are measured against limits.  
The Firm’s stress framework covers market risk sensitive 
positions in the LOBs and Corporate. The framework is used 
to calculate multiple magnitudes of potential stress for both 
market rallies and market sell-offs, assuming significant 
changes in market factors such as credit spreads, equity 
prices, interest rates, currency rates and commodity prices, 
and combines them in multiple ways to capture an array of 
hypothetical economic and market scenarios.  
The Firm generates a number of scenarios that focus on tail 
events in specific asset classes and geographies, including 
how the event may impact multiple market factors 
simultaneously. Scenarios also incorporate specific 
idiosyncratic risks and stress basis risk between different 
products. The flexibility in the stress framework allows the 
Firm to construct new scenarios that can test the outcomes 
against possible future stress events. Stress testing results 
are reported periodically to senior management of the 
Firm, as appropriate.  
Stress scenarios are governed by the overall stress 
framework, under the oversight of Market Risk 
Management, and the models to calculate the stress results 
are subject to the Firm’s Estimations and Model Risk 
Management Policy. The Firmwide Market Risk Stress 
Methodology Committee reviews and approves changes to 
stress testing methodology and scenarios across the Firm. 
Significant changes to the framework are escalated to 
senior management, as appropriate.  
The Firm’s stress testing framework is utilized in calculating 
the Firm’s CCAR and other stress test results, which are 
reported periodically to the Board of Directors. In addition, 
stress testing results are incorporated into the Firm’s Risk 
Appetite framework, and are reported periodically to the 
Board Risk Committee.

title: Profit and loss drawdowns
heading: 7.8.11.7 Profit and loss drawdowns
start_phrase: Profit and loss drawdowns are used to highlight trading losses above certain levels of risk tolerance.
summary:
- Overview of additional risk measures beyond VaR, focusing on stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, and earnings-at-risk (interest rate risk).
- Stress testing:
  - Assesses potential losses under stressed but plausible economic and market scenarios by applying simultaneous shocks to multiple market factors (credit spreads, equity prices, interest rates, currencies, commodities).
  - Covers market risk sensitive positions across Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate, including tail events, idiosyncratic risks, and basis risk; framework is flexible to construct new scenarios.
  - Results are reported periodically to senior management; used in CCAR and other firmwide stress tests; incorporated into the Firm’s Risk Appetite and reported to the Board and Board Risk Committee.
  - Governed by Market Risk Management with models subject to the Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy; the Firmwide Market Risk Stress Methodology Committee approves methodology and scenario changes; significant changes are escalated.
- Profit and loss drawdowns:
  - Used to flag trading losses beyond risk tolerances; defined as the decline in revenue from the year-to-date peak.
- Earnings-at-risk (structural interest rate risk):
  - Measures the sensitivity of net income (net interest income and certain interest-sensitive fees) to specified interest rate scenarios relative to a baseline using market rates and deposit pricing assumptions.
  - Interest rate risk arises from both trading and traditional banking activities (loans, deposits, debt issuance, investment securities).
  - Governance: CTC Risk Committee sets policy and limits (approved by the Board Risk Committee); Treasury and CIO, in partnership with LOBs, calculate and review the Firm’s profile; a dedicated risk function reporting to the CTC CRO provides independent oversight, governance of assumptions, and limit setting/monitoring.
  - Managed primarily through the investment securities portfolio and interest rate derivatives.
  - Key drivers of structural interest rate risk include timing and amount mismatches in repricing/maturities, changes in the yield curve slope/levels, and changes in asset/liability maturities as rates move.
  - Firmwide management via funds transfer pricing that centralizes interest rate risk in Treasury and CIO, reflecting balances, contractual rates, payment schedules, prepayments, reset dates, maturities, reference indices, and rate caps/floors.
  - Simulations are conducted for U.S. dollar and non-U.S. dollar exposures and primarily include retained loans.
  - References a table summarizing earnings-at-risk positions by LOB and Corporate.

title: Earnings-at-risk
heading: 7.8.11.8 Earnings-at-risk
start_phrase: The effect of interest rate exposure on the Firm’s reported net income is important as interest rate risk represents one of the Firm’s significant market risks.
summary:
- Overview of additional market risk measures beyond VaR, focusing on stress testing, profit and loss drawdowns, and earnings-at-risk (EaR).
- Stress testing:
  - Complements VaR by assessing losses under hypothetical, simultaneous shocks across market factors (credit spreads, equities, rates, FX, commodities).
  - Covers market risk-sensitive positions across lines of business and Corporate; includes tail, cross-asset, geographic, idiosyncratic, and basis risk scenarios.
  - Flexible framework to design new scenarios; results measured against limits and reported to senior management.
  - Governance under Market Risk Management and the Firm’s Estimations and Model Risk Management Policy; Firmwide Market Risk Stress Methodology Committee oversees methodology and scenario changes, with escalation to senior management as needed.
  - Utilized in CCAR and incorporated into the Risk Appetite framework; results reported to the Board and Board Risk Committee.
- Profit and loss drawdowns:
  - Used to flag trading losses beyond tolerance levels; defined as the decline in revenue from the year-to-date peak.
- Earnings-at-risk (EaR) and structural interest rate risk:
  - Interest rate risk arises from both trading and core banking activities (loans, deposits, debt issuance, securities).
  - Governance: CTC Risk Committee sets policy/limits (approved by Board Risk Committee); Treasury and CIO assess the Firm’s structural interest rate profile; independent CTC risk function provides oversight, assumptions governance, and limit monitoring.
  - Managed via the investment securities portfolio and interest rate derivatives; interest rate risk is aggregated Firmwide with business units transferring risk to Treasury and CIO through funds transfer pricing.
  - Sources of structural interest rate risk include repricing/maturity mismatches, volume mismatches, yield curve slope changes, and changes in effective maturities as rates move.
- EaR methodology:
  - Measures sensitivity of next-12-month net interest income (and certain rate-sensitive fees) to interest rate scenarios relative to a baseline with market rates and deposit pricing assumptions.
  - Simulations cover U.S. dollar and non-U.S. dollar exposures (retained loans, deposits, deposits with banks, investment securities, long-term debt, hedges, and FTP of other positions).
  - Scenarios include parallel rate shifts, steepeners (long rates up, short constant), and flatteners (short up/long constant or short constant/long down).
  - Key assumptions include instantaneous rate shocks, forecasted balance sheet, modeled mortgage prepayments, reinvestment behavior, deposit forecasts (sensitive to QE reversal, Fed RRP utilization, industry loan levels, and deposit competition), and deposit betas; deposit repricing lags are under evaluation and would meaningfully affect U.S. dollar results (higher rates positive; lower rates negative).
  - EaR is a risk sensitivity, not a forecast of net interest income.
- Results and drivers:
  - Tables present U.S. dollar and non-U.S. dollar EaR sensitivities as of December 31, 2022 versus 2021; certain 2021 down-rate scenarios were not meaningful given rate levels.
  - 2022 U.S. dollar sensitivities reflect a higher-rate baseline, higher modeled deposit betas, and balance sheet changes; parallel and short-rate shocks are driven more by liabilities repricing than assets, while long-rate shocks are driven more by asset repricing.
  - Non-U.S. dollar steepener/flattener scenarios with only long-term rate changes were not material to EaR.
text:
Earnings-at-risk
The effect of interest rate exposure on the Firm’s reported 
net income is important as interest rate risk represents one 
of the Firm’s significant market risks. Interest rate risk 
arises not only from trading activities but also from the Firm’s traditional banking activities, which include 
extension of loans and credit facilities, taking deposits, 
issuing debt and the investment securities portfolio.  Refer 
to the table on page 132  for a summary by LOB and 
Corporate, identifying positions included in earnings-at-risk .
The CTC Risk Committee establishes the Firm’s structural 
interest rate risk policy and related limits, which are subject 
to approval by the Board Risk Committee. Treasury and CIO, 
working in partnership with the LOBs, calculates the Firm’s 
structural interest rate risk profile and reviews it with 
senior management, including the CTC Risk Committee.  In 
addition, oversight of structural interest rate risk is 
managed through a dedicated risk function reporting to the 
CTC CRO. This risk function is responsible for providing 
independent oversight and governance around assumptions 
and establishing and monitoring limits for structural 
interest rate risk. The Firm manages structural interest rate 
risk generally through its investment securities portfolio 
and interest rate derivatives.
Structural interest rate risk can arise due to a variety of 
factors, including:
•Differences in timing among the maturity or repricing of 
assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet instruments
•Differences in the amounts of assets, liabilities and off-
balance sheet instruments that are maturing or repricing 
at the same time
•Differences in the amounts by which short-term and long-
term market interest rates change (for example, changes 
in the slope of the yield curve)
•The impact of changes in the maturity of various assets, 
liabilities or off-balance sheet instruments as interest 
rates change
The Firm manages interest rate exposure related to its 
assets and liabilities on a consolidated, Firmwide basis. 
Business units transfer their interest rate risk to Treasury 
and CIO through funds transfer pricing, which takes into 
account the elements of interest rate exposure that can be 
risk-managed in financial markets. These elements include 
asset and liability balances and contractual rates of 
interest, contractual principal payment schedules, expected 
prepayment experience, interest rate reset dates and 
maturities, rate indices used for repricing, and any interest 
rate ceilings or floors for adjustable rate products.
One way that the Firm evaluates its structural interest rate 
risk is through earnings-at-risk. Earnings-at-risk estimates 
the Firm’s interest rate exposure for a given interest rate 
scenario. It is presented as a sensitivity to a baseline, which 
includes net interest income and certain interest rate 
sensitive fees. The baseline uses market interest rates and, 
in the case of deposits, pricing assumptions. The Firm 
conducts simulations of changes to this baseline for interest 
rate-sensitive assets and liabilities denominated in U.S. 
dollars and other currencies (“non-U.S. dollar” currencies). 
These simulations primarily include retained loans, Management’s discussion and analysis
136 JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-Kdeposits, deposits with banks, investment securities, long-
term debt and any related interest rate hedges, and funds 
transfer pricing of other positions in risk management VaR 
and other sensitivity-based measures  as described on page 
132. 
Earnings-at-risk scenarios estimate the potential change to 
a net interest income baseline  over the following 12 months 
utilizing multiple assumptions.  These scenarios include a 
parallel shift involving changes to both short-term and long-
term rates by an equal amount; a steeper yield curve 
involving holding short-term rates constant and increasing 
long-term rates; and a flatter yield curve involving 
increasing short-term rates and holding long-term rates 
constant  or holding short-term rates constant and 
decreasing long-term rates. These scenarios consider many 
different factors, including:  
•The impact on exposures as a result of instantaneous 
changes in interest rates from baseline rates.
•Forecasted balance sheet, as well as modeled 
prepayment and reinvestment behavior, but excluding 
assumptions about actions that could be taken by the 
Firm or its clients and customers in response to 
instantaneous rate changes. Mortgage prepayment 
assumptions are based on the interest rates used in the 
scenarios compared with underlying contractual rates, 
the time since origination, and other factors which are 
updated periodically based on historical experience. 
Deposit forecasts  are a key assumption in the Firm’s 
earnings-at-risk. The baseline reflects certain 
assumptions relating to the reversal of Quantitative 
Easing that are highly uncertain and require management 
judgment. Therefore, the actual amount of deposits held 
by the Firm, at any particular time, could be impacted by 
actions the Federal Reserve may take as part of monetary 
policy, including through the use of the Reverse 
Repurchase Facility. In addition, there are other factors 
that impact the amount of deposits held at the Firm such 
as the level of loans across the industry and competition 
for deposits .
•The pricing sensitivity of deposits, known as deposit 
betas, represent the amount by which deposit rates paid 
could change upon a given change in market interest 
rates. The deposit rates paid in these scenarios differ 
from actual deposit rates paid, due to repricing lags and 
other factors.
The Firm’s earnings-at-risk scenarios are periodically 
evaluated and enhanced in response to changes in the 
composition of the Firm’s balance sheet, changes in market 
conditions, improvements in the Firm’s simulation and 
other factors. The Firm is currently evaluating the modeling 
of repricing lags for deposits in its earnings-at-risk 
scenarios. Incorporating repricing lags, in the current 
environment, would significantly affect the U.S. dollar 
interest rate scenarios, with higher interest rate scenarios 
expected to result in a positive impact, and lower interest 
rate scenarios expected to result in a negative impact, on 
the Firm’s earnings-at-risk . While a relevant measure of the Firm’s interest rate exposure, the earnings-at-risk analysis 
does not represent a forecast of the Firm’s net interest 
income (Refer to Outlook on page 49  for additional 
information) .

title: Non-U.S. dollar foreign exchange risk
heading: 7.8.11.9 Non-U.S. dollar foreign exchange risk
start_phrase: Non-U.S. dollar FX risk is the risk that changes in foreign exchange rates affect the value of the Firm’s assets or liabilities or future results.
summary:
The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s approach to non-U.S. dollar foreign exchange (FX) risk and its use of sensitivity-based measures for market risks not captured in VaR or earnings-at-risk. It defines structural non-USD FX exposures (from capital investments, projected revenues/expenses, securities, and non-USD debt) and notes that Treasury and the CIO, in partnership with lines of business, manage and may hedge these risks with derivatives. It then describes how the Firm quantifies potential impacts on net revenue, other comprehensive income (OCI), and noninterest expense from changes in market variables, with results presented net of hedges where appropriate and accompanied by caveats that sensitivities are not predictions of future outcomes.

Key sensitivity categories and examples include:
- Asset management exposures (seed capital, fund co-investments, deferred compensation) under a 10% market value decline.
- Other debt and equity holdings (real estate-related fair value option loans, privately held equity, other fair value investments) under a 10% market value decline.
- Credit and funding-related exposures:
  - Cross-currency basis risk on non-USD long-term debt (1 bp tightening).
  - FX revaluation of hedges on non-USD debt (10% currency depreciation).
  - Derivatives funding valuation adjustment spread risk (1 bp increase).
  - Counterparty credit risk (CVA) under a 10% credit spread widening, moved from Credit Portfolio VaR to sensitivity-based measures in 1Q22.
  - Fair value option liabilities’ funding spread and interest rate/own-credit-spread sensitivities (1 bp increases).
The footnotes specify where impacts are recognized (net revenue, OCI, or noninterest expense) and exclusions (e.g., certain equity securities under the measurement alternative).

heading: 7.8.12 COUNTRY RISK MANAGEMENT

title: Organization and management
heading: 7.8.12.1 Organization and management
start_phrase: Country Risk Management is an independent risk management function that assesses, manages and monitors exposure to country risk across the Firm.
summary:
- Defines country risk as adverse financial, economic, political or other developments affecting the value of exposures tied to a country; emphasizes active monitoring and diversification relative to strategy and risk tolerance.
- Establishes Country Risk Management as an independent function overseeing policies, frameworks, sovereign ratings, risk tolerance, measurement and stress monitoring, country limits and breach reporting, surveillance tools (signaling models and indicators), and scenario analysis.
- Identifies sources of country risk across lending, deposits, investing, and market-making activities, both cross-border and locally funded, and covering government and private-sector exposures.
- Describes attribution of exposure to the country where a counterparty/issuer/obligor/guarantor has the largest share of assets or revenue (which may differ from domicile), and aggregation based on immediate default with zero recovery; excludes contingent/indirect exposures (e.g., clearing services, secondary collateral exposure in securities financing).
- Notes the use of assumptions for certain products (e.g., non-linear or index) and counterparties not suitable for single-country attribution; different methods could change reported exposure.
- Details measurement standards:
  - Deposits with banks: cash balances at central/commercial banks and other FIs.
  - Lending: total committed (funded and unfunded) net of allowance for credit losses and eligible cash/marketable securities collateral.
  - Securities financing: receivable balance net of eligible collateral.
  - Debt and equity securities: fair value of long and short positions.
  - Derivative receivables: fair value net of eligible collateral.

- States that internal country risk reporting differs from FFIEC regulatory reporting.
text:
Organization and management
Country Risk Management is an independent risk 
management function that assesses, manages and monitors 
exposure to country risk across the Firm. 
The Firm’s country risk management function includes the 
following activities:
•Maintaining policies, procedures and standards 
consistent with a comprehensive country risk framework
•Assigning sovereign ratings, assessing country risks and 
establishing risk tolerance relative to a country
•Measuring and monitoring country risk exposure and 
stress across the Firm
•Managing and approving country limits and reporting 
trends and limit breaches to senior management
•Developing surveillance tools, such as signaling models 
and ratings indicators, for early identification of 
potential country risk concerns
•Providing country risk scenario analysis

title: Sources and measurement
heading: 7.8.12.2 Sources and measurement
start_phrase: The Firm is exposed to country risk through its lending and deposits, investing, and market-making activities, whether cross-border or locally funded.
summary:
- Defines country risk as potential adverse effects from financial, economic, political, or other developments on exposures tied to a country; monitors portfolio impacts and diversification versus firm strategy and risk tolerance.
- Country Risk Management is an independent function spanning the firm.
- Core activities:
  - Maintain policies, procedures, and standards under a comprehensive country risk framework.
  - Assign sovereign ratings, assess country risks, and set country risk tolerance.
  - Measure and monitor country risk exposure and stress across the firm.
  - Manage and approve country limits; report trends and limit breaches to senior management.
  - Develop surveillance tools (signaling models, ratings indicators) for early warning.
  - Provide country risk scenario analysis.
- Sources of exposure include lending, deposits, investing, and market-making, both cross-border and locally funded, with government and private-sector counterparties.
- Country attribution is based on where the largest share of a counterparty’s assets or revenues reside, which can differ from legal domicile or incorporation.
- Exposure measure aggregates risk to an immediate default with zero recovery of attributed counterparties/issuers/obligors/guarantors; excludes contingent or indirect exposures (e.g., clearing services, secondary exposure to collateral on securities financing receivables).
- Assumptions may be required for certain products (e.g., non-linear or index instruments) or counterparties not suitable for single-country attribution; differing approaches can affect reported exposure.
- Measurement framework:
  - Deposits: cash balances placed with central, commercial, and other banks.
  - Lending: total committed amounts (funded and unfunded), net of allowance for credit losses and eligible cash/marketable securities collateral.
  - Securities financing: receivable balances, net of eligible collateral.
  - Debt and equity securities: fair value of all long and short positions.
  - Derivative receivables: fair value net of eligible collateral.
  - Credit derivatives: net notional protection purchased or sold for the same reference entity, inclusive of derivative fair values, aligned with management practices.
- Internal country risk reporting differs from FFIEC bank regulatory reporting.
text:
Sources and measurement
The Firm is exposed to country risk through its lending and 
deposits, investing, and market-making activities, whether 
cross-border or locally funded. Country exposure includes 
activity with both government and private-sector entities in 
a country. 
Under the Firm’s internal country risk management 
approach, attribution of exposure to an individual country is 
based on the country where the largest proportion of the 
assets of the  counterparty, issuer, obligor or guarantor are 
located or where the largest proportion of its revenue is 
derived, which may be different than the domicile (i.e. legal 
residence) or country of incorporation. 
Individual country exposures reflect an aggregation of the 
Firm’s risk to an immediate default, with zero recovery, of 
the counterparties, issuers, obligors or guarantors 
attributed to that country. Activities which result in 
contingent or indirect exposure to a country are not 
included in the country exposure measure (for exa mple, 
providing clearing services or secondary exposure to 
collateral on securities financing receivables) .
Assumptions are sometimes required in determining the 
measurement and allocation of country exposure, 
particularly in the case of certain non-linear or index 
products, or where the nature of the counterparty, issuer, 
obligor or guarantor is not suitable for attribution to an individual country. The use of different measurement 
approaches or assumptions could affect the amount of 
reported country exposure.
Under the Firm’s internal country risk measurement 
framework:
•Deposits with banks are measured as the cash balances 
placed with central banks, comm ercial banks, and other 
financial institutions
•Lending exposures are measured at the total committed 
amount (funded and unfunded), net of the allowance for 
credit losses and eligible cash and marketable securities 
collateral received
•Securities financing exposures are measured at their 
receivable balance, net of eligible collateral received
•Debt and equity securities are measured at the fair value 
of all positions, including both long and short positions
•Counterparty exposure on derivative receivables is 
measured at the derivative’s fair value, net of the fair 
value of the eligible collateral received
•Credit derivatives exposure is measured at the net 
notional amount of protection purchased or sold for the 
same underlying reference entity, inclusive of the fair 
value of the derivative receivable or payable, reflecting 
the manner in which the Firm manages these exposures
The Firm’s internal country risk reporting differs from the 
reporting provided under the FFIEC bank regulatory 
requirements.
JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K 139

title: Stress testing
heading: 7.8.12.3 Stress testing
start_phrase: Stress testing is an important component of the Firm’s country risk management framework, which aims to estimate and limit losses arising from a country crisis by measuring the impact of adverse asset price movements to a country based on market shocks combined with counterparty specific assumptions.
summary:
- Stress testing: Describes the Firm’s country risk stress testing framework, which estimates and limits losses from country crises by modeling adverse market shocks alongside counterparty-specific assumptions. Country Risk Management designs and runs tailored scenarios for specific countries or groups in response to market events, sector concerns, sovereign actions, and geopolitical risks, using results to inform risk reduction actions.

- Risk reporting: Country exposure and stress are regularly measured and reported to track trends, high usages, and limit breaches. For country risk purposes, exposures to non‑fully autonomous jurisdictions (e.g., Special Administrative Regions and dependent territories) may be reported separately from their associated sovereigns.

- Top 20 non‑U.S. country exposures (as of December 31, 2022, with 2021 comparatives): Presents the Firm’s largest total exposures by country under its internal country risk approach; figures can fluctuate with client activity and market flows. Notable drivers:

Stress testing is an important component of the Firm’s 
country risk management framework, which aims to 
estimate and limit losses arising from a country crisis by

title: CLIMATE RISK MANAGEMENT - Introduction
heading: 7.8.13 CLIMATE RISK MANAGEMENT
start_phrase: Climate risk is the risk associated with the impacts of climate change on the Firm ’s clients, customers , operations and business strategy.
summary: Introduces the Firm’s climate risk management by defining climate risk as the impact of climate change on clients, customers, operations, and business strategy, and as a driver affecting existing risk types. Categorizes climate risk into physical risk—acute (e.g., floods, wildfires, tropical storms) and chronic (e.g., sea-level rise, persistent precipitation changes, higher average temperatures)—and transition risk stemming from societal shifts to a low‑carbon economy, including policy changes, new technologies, and consumer preference shifts, noting that transition risks may be influenced by changes in the physical climate.
text:
CLIMATE RISK MANAGEMENT
Climate risk is the risk associated with the impacts of 
climate change on the Firm ’s clients, customers , operations 
and business strategy. Climate change is viewed as a driver  
of risk that may impact existing types of risks managed by 
the Firm. Climate risk is categorized into physical risk and 
transition risk .
Physical risk refers to economic costs and financial loss 
associated with a changing climate. Acute physical risk 
drivers include the increased frequency or severity of 
climate and weather events, such as floods, wildfires and 
tropical storms. Chronic physical risk drivers include more 
gradual shifts in the climate, such as rising sea levels, 
persistent changes in precipitation levels and increases in 
average ambient temperatures.
Transition risk refers to the financial and economic 
implications associated with a societal adjustment to a low-
carbon economy. Transition risk drivers include possible 
changes in public policy, adoption of new technologies and 
shifts in consumer preferences. Transition risks may also be 
influenced by changes in the physical climate.

title: Organization and management
heading: 7.8.13.1 Organization and management
start_phrase: The Firm has a Climate Risk Management function that is responsible for establishing the Firmwide framework and strategy for managing climate risk.
summary:
- Defines climate risk as impacts of climate change on the firm’s clients, customers, operations, and strategy, treating it as a driver that affects existing risk types.
- Categorizes climate risk into:
  - Physical risk: acute (e.g., floods, wildfires, tropical storms) and chronic (e.g., sea-level rise, changing precipitation, higher average temperatures).
  - Transition risk: financial/economic impacts from moving to a low-carbon economy, driven by policy changes, new technologies, and shifting consumer preferences, and influenced by physical climate changes.
- Establishes a Climate Risk Management function responsible for a firmwide framework and strategy, integrating climate considerations into existing risk frameworks.
- Outlines responsibilities of Climate Risk Management: setting policies/standards/procedures; developing metrics, scenarios, and stress tests to assess potential impacts; and building a firmwide climate risk data strategy and technology infrastructure.
- Assigns LOBs and Corporate units responsibility for identifying, assessing, and managing climate risks within their activities and complying with applicable climate-related laws and regulations.
- Details governance and oversight: climate risk management aligns with the firm’s risk governance; LOBs and Corporate integrate climate risk into governance structures (or create new ones) and, along with Climate Risk Management, provide the Board Risk Committee with information on significant climate risks and initiatives.
text:
Organization and management
The Firm has a Climate Risk Management function that is 
responsible for establishing the Firmwide framework and 
strategy for managing climate risk. The Climate Risk 
Management function engages across the Firm to help 
integrate climate risk considerations  into existing risk 
management frameworks, as appropriate.
Other responsibilities of Climate Risk Management include:
•Setting policies, standards, procedures and processes to 
support identification, escalation, monitoring and 
management of climate risk across the Firm
•Developing metrics, scenarios, and stress testing 
mechanisms designed to assess the range of potential 
climate-related financial and economic impacts to the 
Firm
•Establishing a Firmwide climate risk data strategy and 
the supporting climate risk technology infrastructure
The LOBs and Corporate are responsible for the 
identification, assessment and management of climate risks 
present in their business activities and for adherence to 
applicable climate-related laws, rules and regulations.

title: Governance and oversight
heading: 7.8.13.2 Governance and oversight
start_phrase: The Firm’s approach to managing climate risk is consistent with the Firm’s risk governance structure.
summary:
- Defines climate risk as impacts of climate change on the firm’s clients, operations, and strategy, treating climate change as a driver of existing risk types.
- Categorizes climate risk into:
  - Physical risk: acute events (floods, wildfires, storms) and chronic changes (sea-level rise, precipitation shifts, higher average temperatures).
  - Transition risk: financial/economic effects of moving to a low‑carbon economy, driven by policy changes, new technologies, and consumer preference shifts, and influenced by physical climate changes.
- Establishes a dedicated Climate Risk Management function to set the firmwide framework and strategy, integrating climate considerations into existing risk management.
- Climate Risk Management responsibilities include:
  - Setting policies, standards, procedures, and processes for identifying, escalating, monitoring, and managing climate risk.
  - Developing metrics, scenarios, and stress-testing to assess potential climate-related financial and economic impacts.
  - Building a firmwide climate risk data strategy and supporting technology infrastructure.
- Lines of Business (LOBs) and Corporate are responsible for identifying, assessing, and managing climate risks in their activities and complying with applicable climate-related laws and regulations.
- Governance and oversight align with the firm’s risk governance structure; LOBs and Corporate integrate climate risk into governance or create new frameworks as needed.
- LOBs, Corporate, and Climate Risk Management provide the Board Risk Committee with information on significant climate risks and related initiatives.

Governance and oversight
The Firm’s approach to managing climate risk is consistent 
with the Firm’s risk governance structure. The LOBs and 
Corporate are responsible for integrating climate risk 
management into existing governance frameworks, or 
creating new governance frameworks, as appropriate.
The LOBs, Corporate and Climate Risk Management are 
responsible for providing the Board Risk Committee with 
information on significant climate risks and climate-related 
initiatives, as appropriate.

title: OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT - Introduction
heading: 7.8.14 OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT
start_phrase: Operational risk is the risk of an adverse outcome resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes or systems; human factors; or external events impacting the Firm’s processes or systems.
summary:
OPERATIONAL RISK MANAGEMENT
Operational risk is the risk of an adverse outcome resulting 
from inadequate or failed internal processes or systems; 
human factors; or external events impacting the Firm’s 
processes or systems. Operational Risk includes 
compliance, conduct, legal, and estimations and model risk. 
Operational risk is inherent in the Firm’s activities and can 
manifest itself in various ways, including fraudulent acts, 
business disruptions (including those caused by 
extraordinary events beyond the Firm's control), cyber 
attacks, inappropriate employee behavior, failure to comply 
with applicable laws, rules and regulations or failure of 
vendors or other third party providers to perform in 
accordance with their agreements. Operational Risk 
Management attempts to manage operational risk at 
appropriate levels in light of the Firm’s financial position, 
the characteristics of its businesses, and the markets and 
regulatory environments in which it operates.
