text:
Loans held-for-investment
Originated or purchased loans held-for-investment, 
including PCD, are recorded at amortized cost, reflecting 
the principal amount outstanding, net of the following: 
unamortized deferred loan fees, costs, premiums or 
discounts; charge-offs; collection of cash; and foreign 
exchange. Credit card loans also include billed finance 
charges and fees.

title: Interest income
heading: 8.19.1.1.1 Interest income
start_phrase: Interest income on performing loans held-for-investment is accrued and recognized as interest income at the contractual rate of interest.
summary:
- Defines the Firm’s loan accounting framework and categories: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), loans held-for-sale, and loans at fair value; this section details loans held-for-investment.
- Measurement for loans held-for-investment: recorded at amortized cost (principal net of unamortized fees/costs/premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, and FX). Credit card loans include billed finance charges and fees.
- Interest income recognition: accrue contractual interest on performing loans; amortize purchase discounts/premiums and net deferred fees/costs over the loan’s contractual life as yield adjustments.
- Accrued interest handling: recorded in accrued interest and accounts receivable. For credit cards, accrued interest once billed is included in loan balances with a related allowance; changes in that allowance flow through provision for credit losses and charge-offs reverse interest income. For other loans, generally no allowance is recorded on accrued interest receivables; these are written off no later than 90 days past due by reversing interest income.
- Nonaccrual policy: loans (excluding credit cards and certain U.S. government–insured consumer loans) are placed on nonaccrual when full collection is not expected or when 90+ days past due unless well-secured and in collection; collateral-dependent loans are typically nonaccrual. Upon nonaccrual, reverse accrued but unpaid interest and suspend amortization of deferred amounts. Interest may be recognized on a cash basis if fully collectible; otherwise, cash receipts reduce principal (cost recovery). Return to accrual requires reasonable assurance of repayment and demonstrated performance. Credit card loans are generally exempt from nonaccrual.
- Allowance for loan losses: a contra-asset reflecting expected credit losses on held-for-investment loans at the balance sheet date; changes recognized in provision for credit losses.
- Charge-off policies: consumer loans charged off or written down to net realizable collateral value based on FFIEC delinquency standards—generally no later than 180 days past due for residential real estate, unmodified credit cards, and scored business banking; and no later than 120 days for scored auto and modified credit cards. Earlier charge-offs occur for collateral-dependent TDRs and when borrower-specific events make losses known or highly certain.
text:
Interest income on performing loans held-for-investment is 
accrued and recognized as interest income at the 
contractual rate of interest. Purchase price discounts or 
premiums, as well as net deferred loan fees or costs, are 
amortized into interest income over the contractual life of 
the loan as an adjustment of yield.
The Firm classifies accrued interest on loans, including 
accrued but unbilled interest on credit card loans, in 
accrued interest and accounts receivables on the 
Consolidated balance sheets. For credit card loans, accrued 
interest once billed is then recognized in the loan balances, 
with the related allowance recorded in the allowance for 
credit losses. Changes in the allowance for credit losses on 
accrued interest on credit card loans are recognized in the 
provision for credit losses and charge-offs are recognized 
by reversing interest income.  For other loans , the Firm 
generally does not recognize an allowance for credit losses 
on accrued interest receivables, consistent with its policy to 
write them off no later than 90 days past due by reversing 
interest income.

title: Nonaccrual loans
heading: 8.19.1.1.2 Nonaccrual loans
start_phrase: Nonaccrual loans are those on which the accrual of interest has been suspended.
summary:
- Defines the Firm’s loan accounting framework by management’s strategy, with three categories: originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (retained), loans held-for-sale, and loans at fair value; provides detailed policies primarily for loans held-for-investment (HFI).
- Measurement for HFI (including PCD): recorded at amortized cost net of unamortized fees/costs, premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, and foreign exchange; credit card loans include billed finance charges and fees.
- Interest income recognition: accrual at contractual rates for performing HFI; amortization of purchase discounts/premiums and deferred fees/costs into interest income over the loan’s life. Accrued interest is recorded in accrued interest and receivables; for credit cards, once billed it is included in loan balances with related allowance and changes booked to provision, and charge-offs reverse interest income. For other loans, generally no allowance on accrued interest; write-off by 90 days past due via reversal of interest income.
- Nonaccrual policy: loans (excluding credit cards and certain U.S. government–insured consumer loans) placed on nonaccrual when full collection isn’t expected or when 90+ days past due unless well-secured and in collection; collateral-dependent loans typically nonaccrual. Upon nonaccrual, reverse accrued but uncollected interest and suspend amortization of deferred amounts. Interest on nonaccrual recognized on a cash basis if fully collectible; otherwise apply cost recovery method. Return to accrual requires reasonable assurance of repayment and demonstrated performance. Credit card loans are generally exempt from nonaccrual and continue accruing until paid or charged off.
- Allowance for loan losses: contra-asset reflecting expected credit losses on HFI at the balance sheet date; changes recognized in provision for credit losses (with further detail referenced in a separate note).
- Charge-off policies: consumer loans charged off or written down to net realizable collateral value based on FFIEC delinquency criteria—generally by 180 days past due for residential real estate, unmodified credit cards, and scored business banking; and by 120 days for scored auto and modified credit cards. Earlier charge-offs occur for collateral-dependent TDRs and when loss is known or highly certain, with charge-offs recorded against the allowance.
text:
Nonaccrual loans are those on which the accrual of interest 
has been suspended. Loans (other than credit card loans 
and certain consumer loans insured by U.S. government 
agencies) are placed on nonaccrual status and considered 
nonperforming when full payment of principal and interest 
is not expected, regardless of delinquency status, or when 
principal and interest has been in default for a period of  90 
days  or more, unless the loan is both well-secured and in 
the process of collection. A loan is determined to be past 
due when the minimum payment is not received from the 
borrower by the contractually specified due date or for 
certain loans (e.g., residential real estate loans), when a 
monthly payment is due and unpaid for  30 days  or more. Finally, collateral-dependent loans are typically maintained 
on nonaccrual status. 
On the date a loan is placed on nonaccrual status, all 
interest accrued but not collected is reversed against 
interest income. In addition, the amortization of deferred 
amounts is suspended. Interest income on nonaccrual loans 
may be recognized as cash interest payments are received 
(i.e., on a cash basis) if the recorded loan balance is 
deemed fully collectible; however, if there is doubt 
regarding the ultimate collectibility of the recorded loan 
balance, all interest cash receipts are applied to reduce the 
carrying value of the loan (the cost recovery method). For 
consumer loans, application of this policy typically results in  
the Firm recognizing interest income on nonaccrual 
consumer loans on a cash basis.
A loan may be returned to accrual status when repayment is 
reasonably assured and there has been demonstrated 
performance under the terms of the loan or, if applicable, 
the terms of the restructured loan.  
As permitted by regulatory guidance, credit card loans are 
generally exempt from being placed on nonaccrual status; 
accordingly, interest and fees related to credit card loans 
continue to accrue until the loan is charged off or paid in 
full.

title: Allowance for loan losses
heading: 8.19.1.1.3 Allowance for loan losses
start_phrase: The allowance for loan losses represents the estimated expected credit losses in the held-for-investment loan portfolio at the balance sheet date and is recognized on the balance sheet as a contra asset, which brings the amortized cost to the net carrying value.
summary:
- Scope: Note 12 outlines the Firm’s loan accounting framework and policies.
- Loan categories: (1) originated or purchased loans held-for-investment (including PCD), (2) loans held-for-sale, and (3) loans at fair value.
- Held-for-investment measurement: recorded at amortized cost (principal net of unamortized fees/costs/premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, and FX). Credit card loans include billed finance charges and fees.
- Interest income recognition: accrued at contractual rates on performing HFI loans; purchase discounts/premiums and deferred fees/costs amortized into interest income as yield adjustments.
- Accrued interest policy: accrued interest (including unbilled credit card interest) is recorded in accrued interest and accounts receivable. For credit cards, once billed it is included in loan balances with an associated allowance; changes flow through provision for credit losses and charge-offs reverse interest income. For other loans, generally no allowance on accrued interest; written off no later than 90 days past due by reversing interest income.
- Nonaccrual loans: placed on nonaccrual when full payment is not expected or 90+ days past due (unless well-secured and in collection); collateral-dependent loans typically nonaccrual. Upon nonaccrual, accrued but unpaid interest is reversed and amortization of deferred amounts suspended. Interest may be recognized on a cash basis if fully collectible; otherwise cash receipts reduce principal (cost-recovery). Loans may return to accrual when repayment is reasonably assured and performance is demonstrated. Credit card loans are generally exempt from nonaccrual.
- Allowance for loan losses: contra-asset reflecting expected credit losses on HFI loans; changes recognized in provision for credit losses; additional policy details referenced to Note 13.
- Charge-offs: consumer loans charged off or written down to net realizable value per FFIEC delinquency standards—generally by 180 days past due for residential real estate, unmodified credit cards, and scored business banking; by 120 days for scored auto and modified credit cards. Earlier charge-offs occur for collateral-dependent TDRs and when events indicate losses are known or highly certain.
- Note: Loans held-for-sale and loans at fair value are identified categories, with detailed accounting discussion implied outside this excerpt.
text:
Allowance for loan losses  
The allowance for loan losses represents the estimated 
expected credit losses in the held-for-investment loan 
portfolio at the balance sheet date and is recognized on the 
balance sheet as a contra asset, which brings the amortized 
cost to the net carrying value. Changes in the allowance for 
loan losses are recorded in the provision for credit losses on  
the Firm’s Consolidated statements of income. Refer to 
Note  13 for further information on  the Firm’s accounting 
policies for the allowance for loan losses.

title: Charge-offs
heading: 8.19.1.1.4 Charge-offs
start_phrase: Consumer loans are generally charged off or charged down to the lower of the amortized cost or the net realizable value of the underlying collateral (i.e., fair value less estimated costs to sell), with an offset to the allowance for loan losses,
summary:
- Scope: Note 12 outlines the Firm’s loan accounting framework by management strategy and measurement category: loans held-for-investment (including PCD), loans held-for-sale, and loans carried at fair value (fair value option), with cross-references to Notes 2, 3, and 13.

- Loans held-for-investment:
  - Measurement: Amortized cost (principal net of unamortized fees/costs/premiums/discounts, charge-offs, cash collections, FX). Credit card loans include billed finance charges/fees.
  - Interest income: Accrued at contractual rate; premiums/discounts and deferred fees/costs amortized into interest yield.
  - Accrued interest: Recorded in accrued interest and accounts receivable. For credit cards, accrued interest moves to loan balance once billed with related allowance; changes flow through provision; charge-offs reverse interest income. For other loans, generally no allowance on accrued interest; written off by 90 days past due via reversing interest income.
  - Nonaccrual policy: Loans (excluding credit cards and certain government-insured consumer loans) placed on nonaccrual when full payment isn’t expected or 90+ days past due (unless well-secured and in collection); collateral-dependent loans typically nonaccrual. Accrued interest reversed and amortization suspended at designation. Interest recognized on cash basis if fully collectible; otherwise cash reduces principal (cost recovery). Return to accrual upon demonstrated performance and assured repayment. Credit card loans generally exempt from nonaccrual; interest accrues until charge-off or payoff.
  - Allowance for loan losses: Contra-asset for expected credit losses on held-for-investment loans; changes recorded in provision for credit losses (see Note 13).
  - Charge-offs:
    - Consumer: Generally per FFIEC—residential real estate, unmodified credit card, and scored business banking by 180 days past due; scored auto and modified credit card by 120 days. Earlier for collateral-dependent TDRs, bankruptcy (e.g., residential real estate and auto within 60 days of notification), and auto upon repossession. Government-guaranteed portions typically not charged off.
    - Wholesale: Charged off when loss is highly certain, considering bankruptcy priority, expected workout/restructuring, and collateral/equity valuation.
  - Collateral valuation: Liquid securities via quotes; illiquid assets via DCF. Residential real estate uses broker price opinions/appraisals/AVMs (exterior) updated at least annually; interior appraisals upon taking possession; values discounted for liquidation experience and state factors. Commercial real estate appraisals internal/external, typically updated every 6–12 months; frequency may increase based on borrower/market conditions.

- Loans held-for-sale:
  - Measurement: Lower of cost or fair value; valuation changes in noninterest revenue (consumer on a portfolio basis; wholesale individually).
  - Interest income: Accrued at contractual rate.
  - Fees/costs/premiums/discounts: Deferred in a contra account until sale; included in LCM adjustments and gain/loss on sale.
  - No allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies apply; nonaccrual policies do apply.

- Loans at fair value (fair value option):
  - Measurement: Fair value with changes in noninterest revenue.
  - Interest income: Accrued at contractual rate.
  - Fees/costs: Origination fees recognized upfront in noninterest revenue; origination costs expensed as incurred.
  - No allowance or charge-off policies apply; nonaccrual policies do apply.
  - References: Note 3 for fair value option elections; Notes 2 and 3 for loans at fair value classified as trading assets.
text:
Charge-offs  
Consumer loans are generally charged off or charged down 
to the lower of the amortized cost or the net realizable 
value of the underlying collateral (i.e., fair value less 
estimated costs to sell), with an offset to the allowance for 
loan losses, upon reaching specified stages of delinquency 
in accordance with standards established by the  FFIEC. 
Residential real estate loans, unmodified credit card loans 
and scored business banking loans are generally charged 
off no later than  180 days  past due.  Scored auto and 
modified credit card loans are charged off no later than  120 
days  past due.  
Certain consumer loans are charged off or charged down to 
their net realizable value earlier than the FFIEC charge-off 
standards  in the f ollowing  circumstances:  
•Loans modified in a TDR that are determined t o be 
collateral-dependent.  
•Loans to borrowers who have experienced an event that 
suggests a loss is either known or highly certain are 
subject to accelerated charge-off standards (e.g., 
JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K 225residential real estate and auto loans are charged off or 
charged down within  60 days of receiving notification of 
a bankruptcy filing). 
•Auto loans upon repossession of the automobile.  
Other than in  certain limited circumstances,  the Firm 
typically does not recognize charge-offs on the government-
guaranteed portion of loans.  
Wholesale loans are charged off when it is highly certain 
that a loss has been realized. The determination of whether 
to recognize a charge-off includes many factors, including 
the prioritization of  the Firm’s claim in bankruptcy, 
expectations of the workout/restructuring of the loan and 
valuation of the borrower’s equity or the loan collateral.  
When a loan is charged down to the lower of its amortized 
cost or the estimated net realizable value of the underlying 
collateral, the determination of the fair value of the 
collateral depends on the type of collateral (e.g., securities, 
real estate). In cases where the collateral is in the form of 
liquid securities, the fair value is based on quoted market 
prices or broker quotes. For illiquid securities or other 
financial assets, the fair value of the collateral is generally 
estimated using a discounted cash flow model.  
For residential real estate loans, collateral values are based 
upon external valuation sources. When it becomes likely 
that a borrower is either unable or unwilling to pay,  the 
Firm utilizes a broker’s price opinion, appraisal and/or an 
automated valuation model of the home based on an 
exterior-only valuation (“exterior opinions”), which is then 
updated at least every  12 months , or more frequently 
depending on various market factors. As soon as practicable 
after  the Firm receives the property in satisfaction of a debt 
(e.g., by taking legal title or physical possession), the Firm 
generally obtains an appraisal based on an inspection that 
includes the interior of the home (“interior appraisals”). 
Exterior opinions and interior appraisals are discounted 
based upon  the Firm’s experience with actual liquidation 
values as compared with the estimated values provided by 
exterior opinions and interior appraisals, considering state-
specific factors.  
For commercial real estate loans, collateral values are 
generally based on appraisals from internal and external 
valuation sources. Collateral values are typically updated 
every  six to twelve months , either by obtaining a new 
appraisal or by performing an internal analysis, in 
accordance with  the Firm’s policies.  The Firm also considers 
both borrower- and market-specific factors, which may 
result in obtaining appraisal updates or broker price 
opinions at more frequent intervals.

title: Loans held-for-sale
heading: 8.19.1.2 Loans held-for-sale
start_phrase: Loans held-for-sale are measured at the lower of cost or fair value, with valuation changes recorded in noninterest revenue.
summary:
- Charge-off policies:
  - Consumer loans: residential real estate and auto loans are charged off/charged down within 60 days of bankruptcy notification; auto loans are charged off upon repossession. Government‑guaranteed portions are generally not charged off except in limited cases.
  - Wholesale loans: charged off when a loss is highly certain, considering bankruptcy claim priority, expected workout/restructuring, and borrower equity/collateral valuation.
  - Charge-downs to the lower of amortized cost or estimated net realizable collateral value; collateral fair value determined by asset type.

- Collateral valuation methods:
  - Liquid securities: quoted market prices or broker quotes.
  - Illiquid securities/financial assets: discounted cash flow models.
  - Residential real estate: external valuation sources; use exterior-only opinions/AVMs when repayment concern arises (updated at least every 12 months or more often); obtain interior appraisals after taking possession; apply discounts based on realized liquidation experience and state factors.
  - Commercial real estate: internal/external appraisals with updates every 6–12 months; borrower and market factors may prompt more frequent updates or broker price opinions.

- Loans held-for-sale (HFS):
  - Measured at lower of cost or fair value; valuation changes recorded in noninterest revenue.
  - Consumer HFS valued on a portfolio basis; wholesale HFS individually.
  - Interest accrued at contractual rate.
  - Origination fees/costs and purchase discounts/premiums deferred in a contra account until sale and included in lower-of-cost-or-FV adjustments and gain/loss on sale.
  - Not subject to the Firm’s allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies; subject to nonaccrual policies.

- Loans at fair value (fair value option):
  - Measured at fair value with changes in noninterest revenue.
  - Interest accrued at contractual rate; fair value changes recognized in noninterest revenue.
  - Origination fees recognized upfront in noninterest revenue; origination costs expensed as incurred.
  - Not subject to the Firm’s allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies; subject to nonaccrual policies.
  - Cross-references to Notes 2 and 3 for additional details and trading asset classifications.
text:
Loans held-for-sale are measured at the lower of cost or fair 
value, with valuation changes recorded in noninterest 
revenue. For consumer loans, the valuation is performed on 
a portfolio basis. For wholesale loans, the valuation is 
performed on an individual loan basis.  
Interest income on loans held-for-sale is accrued and 
recognized based on the contractual rate of interest.  
Loan origination fees or costs and purchase price discounts 
or premiums are deferred in a contra loan account until the 
related loan is sold. The deferred fees or costs and 
discounts or premiums are an adjustment to the basis of the 
loan and therefore are included in the periodic 
determination of the lower of cost or fair value adjustments 
and/or the gain or loss recognized at the time of sale.  
Because these loans are recognized at the lower of cost or 
fair value,  the Firm’s allowance for loan losses and charge-
off policies do not apply to these loans. However, loans 
held-for-sale are subject to the nonaccrual policies 
described above.

title: Loans at fair value
heading: 8.19.1.3 Loans at fair value
start_phrase: Loans for which the fair value option has been elected are measured at fair value, with changes in fair value recorded in noninterest revenue.
summary:
- Charge-off policies:
  - Consumer loans: Residential real estate and auto loans are charged off or down within 60 days of bankruptcy notification; auto loans are also charged off upon repossession.
  - Government-guaranteed loans: Generally no charge-offs on the guaranteed portion, except in limited circumstances.
  - Wholesale loans: Charged off when loss realization is highly certain, considering bankruptcy claim priority, workout/restructuring expectations, and borrower equity/collateral valuation.

- Collateral valuation and charge-downs:
  - Loans charged down to the lower of amortized cost or estimated net realizable collateral value.
  - Liquid securities collateral valued using quoted prices or broker quotes; illiquid assets via discounted cash flow models.
  - Residential real estate: Uses external valuation sources; when default likely, relies on exterior opinions (broker price opinions, appraisals, AVMs) updated at least every 12 months; interior appraisals obtained upon taking possession; values discounted based on liquidation experience and state-specific factors.
  - Commercial real estate: Appraisals from internal/external sources; values updated every 6–12 months via new appraisals or internal analyses, with more frequent updates possible based on borrower/market conditions.

- Loans held-for-sale:
  - Measured at lower of cost or fair value; valuation changes recorded in noninterest revenue.
  - Consumer portfolios valued on a portfolio basis; wholesale on an individual loan basis.
  - Interest income accrued at contractual rates.
  - Origination fees/costs and purchase discounts/premiums deferred and included in lower-of-cost-or-fair-value adjustments and sale gains/losses.
  - Not subject to allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies; subject to nonaccrual policies.

- Loans at fair value (fair value option):
  - Measured at fair value; changes recognized in noninterest revenue.
  - Interest income accrued at contractual rates.
  - Origination fees recognized upfront in noninterest revenue; origination costs expensed as incurred.
  - Not subject to allowance for loan losses or charge-off policies; subject to nonaccrual policies.
  - Cross-references to Notes 2 and 3 for further details and trading asset classifications.
text:
Loans at fair value  
Loans for which the fair value option has been elected are 
measured at fair value, with changes in fair value recorded 
in noninterest revenue.  
Interest income on these loans is accrued and recognized 
based on the contractual rate of interest. Changes in fair 
value are recognized in noninterest revenue. Loan 
origination fees are recognized upfront in noninterest 
revenue. Loan origination costs are recognized in the 
associated expense category as incurred.  
Because these loans are recognized at fair value,  the Firm’s  
allowance for loan losses and charge-off policies do not 
apply to these loans.  However, loans at fair value are 
subject to the nonaccrual policies described above.   
Refer to Note  3 for further information on  the Firm’s 
elections of fair value accounting under the fair value 
option. Refer to Note  2 and Note  3 for further information 
on loans carried at fair value and classified as trading 
assets.  Notes to consolidated financial statements
226 JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K

title: Loan classification changes
heading: 8.19.2 Loan classification changes
start_phrase: Loans in the held-for-investment portfolio that management decides to sell are transferred to the held-for-sale portfolio at the lower of cost or fair value on the date of transfer.
summary:
- Loan classification changes: Criteria and accounting for transferring loans between held‑for‑investment (HFI) and held‑for‑sale (HFS). Transfers to HFS are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value; credit-related losses reduce the allowance for loan losses, while non‑credit losses (e.g., interest rate or FX changes) are recognized in noninterest revenue. Loans retained in HFS and moved back to HFI are recorded at amortized cost and then assessed for impairment under the Firm’s allowance methodology (see Note 13).

- Loan modifications and TDRs: The Firm modifies loans as part of loss mitigation by granting concessions (e.g., rate reductions, term extensions, payment delays, principal forgiveness, or accepting equity/other assets) to borrowers in financial difficulty, which are accounted for as troubled debt restructurings (TDRs). Short‑term or insignificant changes that are not concessions are not TDRs.

- Nonaccrual and return to accrual: Non‑credit card loans modified in a TDR are generally placed on nonaccrual (often already nonaccrual pre‑modification). They may return to accrual after at least six months/six payments of performance and if repayment is reasonably assured based on borrower capacity, collateral values, LTVs, and market factors. In limited cases where the loan is current at modification, nonaccrual may be avoided.

- Impairment measurement for TDRs: TDRs are measured using the Firm’s asset‑specific allowance methodology, incorporating expected re‑default rates, and generally remain subject to asset‑specific allowance for their remaining life, even if performing and back on accrual (see Note 13).

- Foreclosed property: Recognition of assets obtained via restructurings, workouts, or foreclosures (real and personal/commercial property). Foreclosed assets are recorded in other assets at fair value less estimated costs to sell upon receipt (e.g., foreclosure sale or deed‑in‑lieu). Values are reviewed quarterly and adjusted to the lower of cost or fair value, with changes recorded in noninterest revenue; operating costs (e.g., taxes, maintenance) are recorded in other expense.
text:
Loan classification changes  
Loans in the held-for-investment portfolio that 
management decides to sell are transferred to the held-for-
sale portfolio at the lower of cost or fair value on the date 
of transfer. Credit-related losses are charged against the 
allowance for loan losses; non-credit related losses such as 
those due to changes in interest rates or foreign currency 
exchange rates are recognized in noninterest revenue.  
In the event that management decides to retain a loan in 
the held-for-sale portfolio, the loan is transferred to the 
held-for-investment portfolio at amortized cost on the date 
of transfer. These loans are subsequently assessed for 
impairment based on  the Firm’s allowance methodology.  
Refer to Note  13 for a further discussion of the 
methodologies used in establishing  the Firm’s allowance for 
loan losses.

title: Loan modifications
heading: 8.19.3 Loan modifications
start_phrase: The Firm seeks to modify certain loans in conjunction with its loss mitigation activities.
summary:
- Loan classification changes: Loans moved from held-for-investment to held-for-sale are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value at transfer; credit-related losses reduce the allowance for loan losses, while non-credit losses (e.g., interest rate or FX changes) flow through noninterest revenue. Loans retained in held-for-sale and moved back to held-for-investment are transferred at amortized cost and subsequently evaluated for impairment under the Firm’s allowance methodology (see Note 13).

- Loan modifications (TDRs): As part of loss mitigation, the Firm may grant concessions (e.g., interest rate reductions, term extensions, payment deferrals, principal forgiveness, or acceptance of other assets) to borrowers in financial difficulty. Short-term or insignificant changes that are not concessions are not TDRs. With the exception of credit card loans, TDR-modified loans are generally placed on nonaccrual and may return to accrual after at least six months/six payments of performance and if repayment is reasonably assured based on borrower capacity, collateral, LTV, and market factors; certain current loans at modification may avoid nonaccrual. TDRs are measured for impairment using an asset-specific allowance that incorporates expected re-default rates and remains applicable for the life of the loan, even if returned to accrual (see Note 13).

- Foreclosed property: Assets obtained via restructurings, workouts, or foreclosure (including real and personal property) are recognized when received in satisfaction of a loan—typically at foreclosure sale or deed-in-lieu for real estate—and recorded in other assets at fair value less costs to sell. Values are reviewed quarterly and adjusted to the lower of cost or fair value, with subsequent valuation changes recognized in noninterest revenue; related operating costs (e.g., taxes, maintenance) are recorded in other expense.
text:
Loan modifications  
The Firm seeks to modify certain loans in conjunction with 
its loss mitigation activities. Through the modification,  
JPMorgan Chase  grants one or more concessions to a 
borrower who is experiencing financial difficulty in order to 
minimize  the Firm’s economic loss and avoid foreclosure or 
repossession of the collateral, and to ultimately maximize 
payments received by  the Firm from the borrower. The 
concessions granted vary by program and by borrower-
specific characteristics, and may include interest rate 
reductions, term extensions, payment delays, principal 
forgiveness, or the acceptance of equity or other assets in 
lieu of payments. Such modifications are accounted for and 
reported as TDRs. Loans with short-term and other 
insignificant modifications that are not considered 
concessions are not TDRs.  
Loans, except for credit card loans, modified in a TDR are 
generally placed on nonaccrual status, although in many 
cases such loans were already on nonaccrual status prior to 
modification. These loans may be returned to performing 
status (the accrual of interest is resumed) if the following 
criteria are met: (i) the borrower has performed under the 
modified terms for a minimum of six months  and/or six 
payments, and (ii) the Firm has an expectation that 
repayment of the modified loan is reasonably assured based 
on, for example, the borrower’s debt capacity and level of 
future earnings, collateral values, LTV ratios, and other 
current market considerations. In certain limited and well-
defined circumstances in which the loan is current at the 
modification date, such loans are not placed on nonaccrual 
status at the time of modification.  
Loans modified in TDRs are generally measured for 
impairment using  the Firm’s established asset-specific 
allowance methodology, which considers the expected re-
default rates for the modified loans. A loan modified in a 
TDR generally remains subject to the asset-specific 
component of the allowance throughout its remaining life, 
regardless of whether the loan is performing and has been 
returned to accrual status. Refer to Note  13 for further  
discussion of the methodology used to estimate  the Firm’s 
asset-specific allowance.

title: Foreclosed property
heading: 8.19.4 Foreclosed property
start_phrase: The Firm acquires property from borrowers through loan restructurings, workouts, and foreclosures.
summary:
- Loan classification changes: Loans moved from held-for-investment (HFI) to held-for-sale (HFS) are recorded at the lower of cost or fair value at transfer; credit-related losses reduce the allowance for loan losses, while non-credit losses (e.g., interest rate or FX changes) go to noninterest revenue. Loans retained in HFS and moved back to HFI are recorded at amortized cost and then evaluated for impairment under the Firm’s allowance methodology (see Note 13).
- Loan modifications: The Firm modifies loans as part of loss mitigation, granting concessions to borrowers in financial difficulty (e.g., rate reductions, term extensions, payment delays, principal forgiveness, or accepting equity/other assets) to minimize losses and avoid foreclosure; such concessions are treated as Troubled Debt Restructurings (TDRs). Short-term or insignificant changes that are not concessions are not TDRs.
- Nonaccrual and return to accrual: With the exception of credit card loans, TDR-modified loans are generally placed on nonaccrual (often already nonaccrual pre-modification). They may return to accrual after at least six months/six payments of performance and when repayment is reasonably assured based on borrower capacity, collateral/LTV, and market factors. In limited cases where loans are current at modification, they may remain on accrual.
- Impairment measurement of TDRs: TDRs are evaluated using an asset-specific allowance methodology that incorporates expected re-default rates and typically remain subject to this asset-specific allowance for their remaining life, even if returned to accrual (see Note 13).
- Foreclosed property: The Firm recognizes assets obtained via restructurings, workouts, or foreclosures (real and personal property) when it receives title or possession, including at foreclosure sale or deed-in-lieu for real estate. These assets are recorded in other assets at fair value less estimated costs to sell, reviewed quarterly and carried at the lower of cost or fair value; subsequent fair value changes affect noninterest revenue, and operating costs (e.g., taxes, maintenance) are expensed to other expense.
text:
Foreclosed  property  
The Firm acquires property from borrowers through loan 
restructurings, workouts, and foreclosures. Property 
acquired may include real property (e.g., residential real 
estate, land, and buildings) and commercial and personal 
property (e.g., automobiles, aircraft, railcars, and ships).  
The Firm recognizes foreclosed property upon receiving 
assets in satisfaction of a loan (e.g., by taking legal title or 
physical possession). For loans collateralized by real 
property,  the Firm generally recognizes the asset received 
at foreclosure sale or upon the execution of a deed in lieu of 
foreclosure transaction with the borrower.  Foreclosed 
assets are reported in other assets on the Consolidated 
balance sheets and initially recognized at fair value less 
estimated costs to sell.  Each quarter the fair value of the 
acquired property is reviewed and adjusted, if necessary, to 
the lower of cost or fair value. Subsequent adjustments to 
fair value are charged/credited to noninterest revenue. 
Operating expense, such as real estate taxes and 
maintenance, are charged to other expense.  
JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K 227

title: Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio - Introduction
heading: 8.19.6 Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio
start_phrase: Consumer loans, excluding credit card loans, consist primarily of scored residential mortgages, home equity loans and lines of credit, auto and business banking loans, with a focus on serving the prime consumer credit market.
summary: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s consumer (excluding credit card) loan portfolio composition, balances, and credit quality indicators: portfolio focuses on prime borrowers and includes scored residential mortgages, home equity loans/lines (including junior liens), auto and business banking loans, plus prime interest-only and certain payment-option mortgages that may negatively amortize. Retained loans at December 31 were $300.8B in 2022 ($237.6B residential real estate; $63.2B auto and other) and $295.6B in 2021 ($224.8B; $70.8B), with Business Banking PPP loans of $350M (2022) and $5.4B (2021). Delinquency rates are the primary credit quality indicator: >30 days past due signals emerging stress; for residential real estate, >150 days past due indicates likely foreclosure or similar liquidation. Additional indicators include current estimated LTV/combined LTV (loss severity and willingness to pay), refreshed FICO (with <660 higher risk), and geographic distribution for both residential and scored auto/business banking loans (reflecting regional economic and event-driven impacts).
text:
Consumer, excluding credit card loan portfolio
Consumer loans, excluding credit card loans, consist 
primarily of scored residential mortgages, home equity 
loans and lines of credit, auto and business banking loans, 
with a focus on serving the prime consumer credit market. 
The portfolio also includes home equity loans secured by 
junior liens, prime mortgage loans with an interest-only 
payment period, and certain payment-option loans that may 
result in negative amortization.  
The following table provides information about retained 
consumer loans, excluding credit card, by class.  
December 31, (in millions) 2022 2021
Residential real estate $ 237,561 $ 224,795 
Auto and other(a) 63,192  70,761 
Total retained loans $ 300,753 $ 295,556 
(a)At D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2 and 2021, included $350 million  and $5.4 
billion  of loans, respectively, in Business Banking under the PPP. Delinquency rates are the primary credit quality indicator 
for consumer loans. Loans that are more than  30 days  past 
due provide an early warning of borrowers who may be 
experiencing financial difficulties and/or who may be 
unable or unwilling to repay the loan. As the loan continues 
to age, it becomes more clear whether the borrower is likely 
to be unable or unwilling to pay. In the case of residential 
real estate loans, late-stage delinquencies (greater than  
150 days  past due) are a strong indicator of loans that will 
ultimately result in a foreclosure or similar liquidation 
transaction. In addition to delinquency rates, other credit 
quality indicators for consumer loans vary based on the 
class of loan, as follows:  
•For residential real estate loans, the current estimated 
LTV ratio, or the combined LTV ratio in the case of junior 
lien loans, is an indicator of the potential loss severity in 
the event of default. Additionally, LTV or combined LTV 
ratios can provide insight into a borrower’s continued 
willingness to pay, as the delinquency rate of high-LTV 
loans tends to be greater than that for loans where the 
borrower has equity in the collateral. The geographic 
distribution of the loan collateral also provides insight as 
to the credit quality of the portfolio, as factors such as 
the regional economy, home price changes and specific 
events such as natural disasters, will affect credit 
quality. The borrower’s current or “refreshed” FICO 
score is a secondary credit quality indicator for certain 
loans, as FICO scores are an indication of the borrower’s 
credit payment history. Thus, a loan to a borrower with a 
low FICO score (less than  660) is considered to be of 
higher risk than a loan to a borrower with a higher FICO 
score. Further, a loan to a borrower with a high LTV 
ratio and a low FICO score is at greater risk of default 
than a loan to a borrower that has both a high LTV ratio 
and a high FICO score.
•For scored auto and business banking loans, geographic 
distribution is an indicator of the credit performance of 
the portfolio. Similar to residential real estate loans, 
geographic distribution provides insights into the 
portfolio performance based on regional economic 
activity and events.Notes to consolidated financial statements
230 JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K

start_phrase: The Firm’s proprietary modification programs as well as government programs, including U.S. GSE programs, generally provide various concessions to financially troubled borrowers including, but not limited to, interest rate reductions, term or payment extensions and delays of principal and/or interest payments that would otherwise have been required under the terms of the original agreement.
summary:

title: Credit card loan portfolio - Introduction
heading: 8.19.7 Credit card loan portfolio
start_phrase: The credit card portfolio segment includes credit card loans originated and purchased by the Firm.
summary: Introduces the Firm’s credit card loan portfolio and its credit quality framework, emphasizing delinquency rates (30+ and 90+ days past due) as the primary indicator, with geographic distribution also informative; borrower credit scores (FICO) are treated as a lagging, secondary indicator, refreshed at least quarterly on a statistically significant random sample, and the Firm generally originates to prime borrowers though scores may decline over time. Presents delinquency data for retained credit card loans at December 31, 2022 and 2021, split between within the revolving period and converted to term loans (TDRs). 2022: total retained loans $185,175 million ($184,379 million revolving; $796 million term); 30+ days past due ratio 1.45% total (1.40% revolving; 12.56% term); 90+ days past due ratio 0.68% total (0.67% revolving; 4.52% term). 2021: total retained loans $154,296 million; 30+ ratio 1.04% total (0.99% revolving; 8.71% term); 90+ ratio 0.50% total (0.48% revolving; 2.74% term).
text:
Credit card loan portfolio
The credit card portfolio segment includes credit card loans 
originated and purchased by  the Firm. Delinquency rates 
are the primary credit quality indicator for credit card loans 
as they provide an early warning that borrowers may be 
experiencing difficulties  (30 days  past due); information on 
those borrowers that have been delinquent for a longer 
period of time  (90 days  past due) is also considered. In 
addition to delinquency rates, the geographic distribution of 
the loans provides insight as to the credit quality of the 
portfolio based on the regional economy.
While the borrower’s credit score is another general 
indicator of credit quality,  the Firm does not view credit 
scores as a primary indicator of credit quality because the  
borrower’s credit score tends to be a lagging indicator. The distribution of such scores provides a general indicator of 
credit quality trends within the portfolio; however, the score  
does not capture all factors that would be predictive of 
future credit performance. Refreshed FICO score 
information, which is obtained at least quarterly, for a 
statistically significant random sample of the credit card 
portfolio is indicated in the following table. FICO is 
considered to be the industry benchmark for credit scores.
The Firm generally originates new credit card accounts  to 
prime consumer borrowers. However, certain cardholders’ 
FICO scores may decrease over time, depending on the 
performance of the cardholder and changes in the credit 
score calculation.

text:
Loan modifications  
The Firm may offer loan modification programs granting 
concessions to credit card borrowers who are experiencing 
financial difficulty.  The Firm grants concessions for most of 
the credit card loans under long-term programs. These 
modifications involve placing the customer on a fixed 
payment plan, generally for  60 months, and typically 
include reducing the interest rate on the credit card. 
Substantially all modifications under  the Firm’s long-term 
programs are considered to be TDRs. Loans with short-term 
or other insignificant modifications that are not considered 
concessions are not TDRs.  
If the cardholder does not comply with the modified 
payment terms, then the credit card loan continues to age 
and will ultimately be charged-off in accordance with  the 
Firm’s standard charge-off policy . In most cases,  the Firm 
does not reinstate the borrower’s line of credit.

title: Wholesale loan portfolio - Introduction
heading: 8.19.8 Wholesale loan portfolio
start_phrase: Wholesale loans include loans made to a variety of clients, ranging from large corporate and institutional clients to high-net-worth individuals.
summary: This section defines JPMorgan Chase’s wholesale loan portfolio and its primary credit quality indicator—internal risk ratings—based on probability of default (PD) and loss given default (LGD), informed by obligor debt capacity, earnings, repayment sources, contingencies, management strength, and industry/geography; ratings are reviewed by Credit Risk Management, qualitatively align with S&P/Moody’s (BBB-/Baa3 and above deemed investment grade), and non‑investment‑grade loans are classified as noncriticized or criticized (performing and nonaccrual) consistent with U.S. regulatory categories (special mention, substandard, doubtful). The tables show retained wholesale loans of $603.7B at Dec 31, 2022 (vs $560.4B in 2021), with 70.47% investment grade (vs 73.17%), total criticized at 2.60% (vs 2.39%), and criticized nonaccrual at 0.33% (vs 0.37%); 2022 balances include investment‑grade secured by real estate $99.6B, commercial and industrial $76.3B, and other $249.6B, and non‑investment‑grade totals of $178.3B (real estate $27.2B, C&I $91.4B, other $59.7B). Additional tables provide origination‑year and revolving/term composition for secured real estate and C&I loans; a footnote notes $127M of SBA‑guaranteed PPP nonaccruals excluded in 2021 (not material in 2022).
text:
Wholesale loan portfolio
Wholesale loans include loans made to a variety of clients, 
ranging from large corporate and institutional clients to 
high-net-worth individuals.
The primary credit quality indicator for wholesale loans is 
the internal risk rating assigned to each loan. Risk ratings 
are used to identify the credit quality of loans and 
differentiate risk within the portfolio. Risk ratings on loans 
consider the PD and the LGD.  The PD is the likelihood that a 
loan will default. The LGD is the estimated loss on the loan 
that would be realized upon the default of the borrower and 
takes into consideration collateral and structural support 
for each credit facility.  
Management considers several factors to determine an 
appropriate internal risk rating, including the obligor’s debt 
capacity and financial flexibility, the level of the obligor’s 
earnings, the amount and sources for repayment, the level 
and nature of contingencies, management strength, and the 
industry and geography in which the obligor operates.  The 
Firm’s  internal risk ratings generally align with the 
qualitative characteristics (e.g., borrower capacity to meet 
financial commitments and vulnerability to changes in the 
economic environment) defined by S&P and Moody’s, 
however the quantitative characteristics (e.g., PD and LGD) 
may differ as they reflect internal historical experiences and 
assumptions.  The Firm  generally considers internal ratings 
with qualitative characteristics equivalent to BBB-/Baa3 or 
higher as investment grade, and these ratings have a lower 
PD and/or lower LGD than non-investment grade ratings.  Noninvestment-grade ratings are further classified as 
noncriticized and criticized, and the criticized portion is 
further subdivided into performing and nonaccrual loans, 
representing management’s assessment of the collectibility 
of principal and interest. Criticized loans have a higher PD 
than noncriticized loans.  The Firm’s definition of criticized 
aligns with the U.S. banking regulatory definition of 
criticized exposures, which consist of special mention, 
substandard and doubtful categories.   
Risk ratings are reviewed on a regular and ongoing basis by 
Credit Risk Management and are adjusted as necessary for 
updated information affecting the obligor’s ability to fulfill 
its obligations.
As noted above, the risk rating of a loan considers the 
industry in which the obligor conducts its operations. As 
part of the overall credit risk management framework,  the 
Firm focuses on the management and diversification of its 
industry and client exposures, with particular attention paid 
to industries with an actual or potential cre dit concern. 
Refer to Note  4 for further detail on industry 
concentrations.Notes to consolidated financial statements

title: Note 13 – Allowance for credit losses - Introduction
heading: 8.20 Note 13 – Allowance for credit losses
start_phrase: The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents management's estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of the Firm's financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
summary: Introduction to the Firm’s allowance for credit losses, defined as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining life of financial assets measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments. It comprises: allowance for loan losses (for scored and risk-rated retained loan portfolios, presented separately on the Consolidated balance sheets), allowance for lending-related commitments (presented in accounts payable and other liabilities), and allowance for credit losses on investment securities (reflected in investment securities). All changes flow through the provision for credit losses on the income statement. The allowance is judgmental and reviewed at least quarterly by the CRO, CFO, and Controller, with potential for significant changes based on macroeconomic conditions, forecasts, and other factors. Policies for loan losses and lending-related commitments follow; policies for investment securities are in Note 10.
text:
Note 13 – Allowance for credit losses
The Firm’s allowance for credit losses represents 
management's estimate of expected credit losses over the 
remaining expected life of  the Firm's financial assets 
measured at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet 
lending-related commitments. The allowance for credit 
losses comprises:
•the allowance for loan losses, which covers  the Firm’s 
retained loan portfolios (scored and risk-rated) and is 
presented separately on the Consolidated balance sheets,  
•the allowance for lending-related commitments, which is 
presented on the Consolidated balance sheets in accounts 
payable and other liabilities, and  
•the allowance for credit losses on investment securities, 
which is reflected in investment securities on the 
Consolidated balance sheets.  
The income statement effect of all changes in the allowance 
for credit losses is recognized in the provision for credit 
losses. 
Determining the appropriateness of the allowance for credit 
losses is complex and requires significant judgment by 
management about the effect of matters that are inherently 
uncertain. At least quarterly, the allowance for credit losses 
is reviewed by the CRO, the CFO and the Controller of  the 
Firm. Subsequent evaluations of credit exposures, 
considering the macroeconomic conditions, forecasts and 
other factors then prevailing, may result in significant 
changes in the allowance for credit losses in future periods.  
The Firm’s policies used to determine its allowance for loan 
losses and its allowance for lending-related commitments 
are described in the following paragraphs. Refer to Note  10 
for a description of the policies used to determine the 
allowance for credit losses on investment securities.

title: Methodology for allowances for loan losses and lending-related commitments
heading: 8.20.1 Methodology for allowances for loan losses and lending-related commitments
start_phrase: The allowance for loan losses and allowance for lending-related commitments represents expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of retained loans and lending-related commitments that are not unconditionally cancellable.
summary:
This section explains the Firm’s framework for estimating and recording expected credit losses across its financial assets and certain commitments.

- Scope and components: The allowance for credit losses covers (1) allowance for loan losses on retained loan portfolios, (2) allowance for lending-related commitments presented in accounts payable and other liabilities, and (3) allowance on investment securities (see Note 10). All changes flow through the provision for credit losses on the income statement.
- Governance and judgment: The allowance involves significant management judgment, reflecting macroeconomic conditions and forecasts, and is reviewed at least quarterly by the Firm’s CRO, CFO, and Controller. Allowances may change materially with evolving conditions.
- Methodology for loans and lending-related commitments:
  - Measures expected credit losses over the instruments’ remaining expected life for loans and non–unconditionally cancellable commitments.
  - No allowance is recorded for unconditionally cancellable commitments (e.g., credit cards future draws).
  - Accrued interest: Expected losses on credit card loan interest are included in the loan loss allowance; no allowance on other accrued interest receivables because they are written off by 90 days past due via reversal of interest income.
  - Expected life considers contractual term, prepayments, cancellation features, and extension/call options. For funded credit card loans, expected life and payment allocation reflect CARD Act rules (payments applied first to higher-rate balances).
  - Expected credit loss estimates include anticipated recoveries of amounts previously charged off (which can result in a negative allowance).
- Collective vs. individual assessment:
  - Exposures with similar risk characteristics are assessed collectively (portfolio-based component); those without are assessed individually (asset-specific component).
  - Consumer portfolio risk characteristics: product type, delinquency, FICO, geography, and current LTV for collateralized loans.
  - Wholesale portfolio risk characteristics: internal risk rating, delinquency, tenor, collateral level/type, line of business, geography, industry, credit enhancement, product, facility purpose, and payment terms.
  - Portfolio-based component typically covers consumer loans, performing risk-rated loans, and certain lending-related commitments.
  - Asset-specific component applies to modified PCD loans, loans modified or expected to be modified in a TDR, collateral-dependent loans, and risk-rated loans on nonaccrual.
- Portfolio-based quantitative approach: Starts with modeling transitions in delinquency or risk ratings over the expected life, applying credit loss factors to exposure at default. These factors incorporate probability of default and loss given default (loss severity).
text:
Methodology for allowances for loan losses and lending-
related commitments
The allowance for loan losses and allowance for lending-
related commitments represents expected credit losses 
over the remaining expected life of retained loans and 
lending-related commitments that are not unconditionally 
cancellable.  The Firm does not record an allowance for 
future draws on unconditionally cancellable lending-related 
commitments (e.g. , credit cards). Expected losses related to 
accrued interest on credit card loans are considered in  the 
Firm’s allowance for loan losses.  However,  the Firm does 
not record an allowance on other accrued interest 
receivables, due to its policy to write  these receivables off 
no later than  90 days past due by reversing interest 
income.  
The expected life of each instrument is determined by 
considering its contractual term, expected prepayments, 
cancellation features, and certain extension and call 
options. The expected life of funded credit card loans is 
generally estimated by considering expected future 
payments on the credit card account, and determining how 
much of those amounts should be allocated to repayments 
of the funded loan balance (as of the balance sheet date) versus other account activity. This allocation is made using 
an approach that incorporates the payment application 
requirements of the Credit Card Accountability 
Responsibility and Disclosure Act of 2009, generally paying 
down the highest interest rate balances first.  
The estimate of expected credit losses includes expected 
recoveries of amounts previously charged off or expected to 
be charged off, even if such recoveries result in a negative 
allowance.

title: Collective and Individual Assessments
heading: 8.20.2 Collective and Individual Assessments
start_phrase: When calculating the allowance for loan losses and the allowance for lending-related commitments, the Firm assesses whether exposures share similar risk characteristics.
summary:
- Defines the Firm’s allowance for credit losses as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining expected life of financial assets at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
- Identifies three components and their balance sheet presentation: (1) allowance for loan losses (separate line), (2) allowance for lending-related commitments (accounts payable and other liabilities), and (3) allowance for credit losses on investment securities (within investment securities).
- States that all changes in the allowance flow through the provision for credit losses in the income statement.
- Emphasizes the judgmental and complex nature of estimating the allowance; governance includes at least quarterly reviews by the Firm’s CRO, CFO, and Controller, with allowances sensitive to macroeconomic conditions and forecasts.
- Notes that policies for loan losses and lending-related commitments are detailed here, while policies for investment securities are in Note 10.
- Methodology for loans and lending-related commitments:
  - Covers expected credit losses over the remaining expected life for retained loans and commitments that are not unconditionally cancellable.
  - No allowance is recorded for future draws on unconditionally cancellable commitments (e.g., credit cards).
  - Expected losses on accrued interest for credit card loans are included in the allowance; other accrued interest receivables are written off no later than 90 days past due by reversing interest income, so no allowance is recorded on them.
  - Expected life reflects contractual term, expected prepayments, cancellation features, and extension/call options; for funded credit card loans, expected life is estimated using payment allocation rules under the CARD Act (highest interest rate balances paid first).
  - Expected recoveries of amounts previously charged off are included and can result in a negative allowance.
- Collective vs. individual assessment:
  - Exposures sharing similar risk characteristics are assessed collectively; significant judgment is applied in defining risk pools.
  - Key consumer risk characteristics: product type, delinquency, current FICO, geography, and current LTV for collateralized loans.
  - Key wholesale risk characteristics: internal risk rating, delinquency, tenor, collateral type/level, line of business, geography, industry, credit enhancement, product type, facility purpose, and payment terms.
  - Most exposures are collectively assessed (portfolio-based component), covering consumer loans, performing risk-rated loans, and certain lending-related commitments.
  - Individual (asset-specific) assessments apply to modified PCD loans, loans modified or expected to be modified in a TDR, collateral-dependent loans, and risk-rated loans on nonaccrual.
- Portfolio-based component mechanics (quantitative framework):
  - Starts with estimating transitions in delinquency status or risk ratings over the instrument’s expected life.
  - Applies credit loss factors to estimated exposure at default; factors reflect probability of default and loss given default.
text:
Collective and Individual Assessments
When calculating the allowance for loan losses and the 
allowance for lending-related commitments,  the Firm 
assesses whether exposures share similar risk 
characteristics. If similar risk characteristics exist,  the Firm 
estimates expected credit losses collectively, considering 
the risk associated with a particular pool and the probability 
that the exposures within the pool will deteriorate or 
default. The assessment of risk characteristics is subject to 
significant management judgment. Emphasizing one 
characteristic over another or considering additional 
characteristics could affect the allowance.  
•Relevant risk characteristics for the consumer portfolio 
include product type, delinquency status, current FICO 
scores, geographic distribution, and, for collateralized 
loans, current LTV ratios.   
•Relevant risk characteristics for the wholesale portfolio 
include risk rating, delinquency status, tenor, level and 
type of collateral, LOB,  geography, industry, credit 
enhancement, product type, facility purpose, and 
payment terms.  
The majority of  the Firm’s credit exposures share risk 
characteristics with other similar exposures, and as a result 
are collectively assessed for impairment (“portfolio-based 
component”). The portfolio-based component covers 
consumer loans, performing risk-rated loans and certain 
lending-related commitments.  
If an exposure does not share risk characteristics with other 
exposures,  the Firm generally estimates expected credit 
losses on an individual basis, considering expected 
repayment and conditions impacting that individual 
exposure (“asset-specific component”). The asset-specific 
component covers modified PCD loans, loans modified or 
reasonably expected to be modified in a TDR, collateral-
dependent loans, as well as, risk-rated loans that have been 
placed on nonaccrual status.

title: Portfolio-based component
heading: 8.20.3 Portfolio-based component
start_phrase: The portfolio-based component begins with a quantitative calculation that considers the likelihood of the borrower changing delinquency status or moving from one risk rating to another.
summary:
- Overview and scope: Describes the Firm’s allowance for credit losses (ACL) as management’s estimate of expected losses over the remaining expected life of financial assets at amortized cost and certain off-balance sheet lending-related commitments.
- Components and presentation: 
  - Allowance for loan losses (retained, scored and risk-rated loan portfolios) presented separately on the Consolidated balance sheets.
  - Allowance for lending-related commitments presented in accounts payable and other liabilities.
  - Allowance for credit losses on investment securities reflected within investment securities (methodology referenced to Note 10).
  - All changes flow through the provision for credit losses in the income statement.
- Governance and judgment: ACL is complex, uncertain, and reviewed at least quarterly by the CRO, CFO, and Controller; subsequent macroeconomic changes may materially impact future ACL levels.
- Methodology for loans and lending-related commitments:
  - Covers expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of loans and non–unconditionally cancellable commitments.
  - No allowance for future draws on unconditionally cancellable commitments (e.g., credit cards).
  - Credit card accrued interest losses included in loan loss allowance; other accrued interest receivables written off by 90 days past due, so no allowance recorded.
  - Expected life determined using contractual term, prepayments, cancellation features, and certain extension/call options; credit card life estimated via payment allocation consistent with the CARD Act (higher-rate balances paid first).
  - Expected losses include anticipated recoveries of prior or future charge-offs, potentially resulting in negative allowance.
- Collective vs. individual assessments:
  - Exposures with similar risk characteristics are collectively assessed; otherwise, assessed individually.
  - Consumer risk characteristics: product type, delinquency, current FICO, geography, and LTV for collateralized loans.
  - Wholesale risk characteristics: risk rating, delinquency, tenor, collateral level/type, line of business, geography, industry, credit enhancement, product type, purpose, and payment terms.
  - Most exposures are collectively assessed (portfolio-based component); individual assessments apply to modified PCD loans, TDRs (or expected TDRs), collateral-dependent loans, and nonaccrual risk-rated loans.
- Portfolio-based component:
  - Quantitative expected loss over instrument life via credit loss factors (probability of default and loss severity) applied to exposure at default.
  - Factors derived from five internal macroeconomic scenarios (central, relative adverse, extreme adverse, relative upside, extreme upside) over an eight-quarter forecast, then a one-year straight-line reversion to long-run historical information.
  - Scenarios are produced through a governed process incorporating Firm outlook, SME input, and market consensus.
  - Qualitative adjustments address model imprecision, emerging risks, trends, and uncertainties (economic/political conditions, underwriting quality, borrower behavior, concentrations, industry/product/portfolio factors).
  - Significant management judgment; results are sensitive to inputs and assumptions.
- Asset-specific component:
  - Individual evaluation for collateral-dependent loans and larger nonaccrual wholesale loans; smaller loans may be aggregated with relevant factors.
  - Measurement generally equals amortized cost minus present value of expected cash flows discounted at original EIR; changes flow through the allowance.
  - For collateral-dependent loans, fair value of collateral less costs to sell determines charge-offs or negative allowance for recoveries.
  - TDRs: incorporates concessions, forgone interest/principal, and redefault risk.
    - Residential real estate: product-specific PDs using credit characteristics with housing price and unemployment assumptions, plus Firm’s redefault experience.
    - Credit cards: projected delinquencies and charge-offs by modification program based on Firm history.
    - Wholesale: management’s expectation of repayment under modified terms.
  - Estimation is highly judgmental given uncertainties in severities, valuations, default/redefault rates, payment timing/prepayments, economic duration, borrower/industry/portfolio dynamics, and insolvency outcomes.
text:
Portfolio-based component
The portfolio-based component begins with a quantitative 
calculation that considers the likelihood of the borrower 
changing delinquency status or moving from one risk rating 
to another. The quantitative calculation covers expected 
credit losses over an instrument’s expected life and is 
estimated by applying credit loss factors to  the Firm’s 
estimated exposure at default. The credit loss factors 
incorporate the probability of borrower default as well as 
loss severity in the event of default. They are derived using Notes to consolidated financial statements
242 JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-Ka weighted average of five internally developed 
macroeconomic scenarios over an eight-quarter forecast 
period, followed by a single year straight-line interpolation 
to revert to long run historical information for periods 
beyond the eight-quarter forecast period. The five 
macroeconomic scenarios consist of a central, relative 
adverse, extreme adverse, relative upside and extreme 
upside scenario, and are updated by  the Firm’ s central 
forecasting team. The scenarios take into consideration  the 
Firm’s  macroeconomic outlook, internal perspectives from 
subject matter experts across  the Firm , and market 
consensus and involve a governed process that incorporates 
feedback from senior management  across LOBs, Corporate 
Finance and Risk Management.
The quantitative calculation is adjusted to take into 
consideration model imprecision, emerging risk 
assessments, trends and other subjective factors that are 
not yet reflected in the calculation. These adjustments are 
accomplished in part by analyzing the historical loss 
experience, including during stressed periods, for each 
major product or model. Management applies judgment in 
making this adjustment, including taking into account 
uncertainties associated with the economic and political 
conditions, quality of underwriting standards, borrower 
behavior, credit concentrations or deterioration within an 
industry, product or portfolio, as well as other relevant 
internal and external factors affecting the credit quality of 
the portfolio. In certain instances, the interrelationships 
between these factors create further uncertainties.
The application of different inputs into the quantitative 
calculation, and the assumptions used by management to 
adjust the quantitative calculation, are subject to significant 
management judgment, and emphasizing one input or 
assumption over another, or considering other inputs or 
assumptions, could affect the estimate of the allowance for 
loan losses and the allowance for lending-related 
commitments.

title: Asset-specific component
heading: 8.20.4 Asset-specific component
start_phrase: To determine the asset-specific component of the allowance, collateral-dependent loans (including those loans for which foreclosure is probable) and larger, nonaccrual risk-rated loans in the wholesale portfolio segment are generally evaluated individually, while smaller loans (both scored and risk-rated) are aggregated for evaluation using factors relevant for the respective class of assets.
summary:
- Describes the Firm’s methodology for estimating the allowance for loan losses and lending-related commitments, anchored in a quantitative framework that averages five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios (central, relative adverse, extreme adverse, relative upside, extreme upside) over an eight-quarter forecast, followed by a one-year straight-line reversion to long-run historical conditions. Scenarios are governed and updated by a central forecasting team with inputs from subject matter experts, market consensus, and senior management across businesses and risk functions.
- Explains qualitative adjustments layered onto the quantitative estimate to capture model imprecision, emerging risks, trends, and factors not yet reflected in models. These rely on historical loss experience (including stressed periods) and management judgment about economic/political conditions, underwriting quality, borrower behavior, credit concentrations, and industry/product/portfolio dynamics, acknowledging compounding uncertainties among these factors.
- Emphasizes sensitivity of the allowance to management’s assumptions and inputs; different weightings or alternative assumptions can materially change estimated reserves.
- Details the asset-specific component: collateral-dependent loans and larger nonaccrual risk-rated wholesale loans are evaluated individually; smaller loans are pooled. Measurement generally uses the present value of expected cash flows discounted at the original effective rate; for collateral-dependent loans, fair value of collateral less costs to sell determines charge-offs or negative allowances for recoveries.
- Outlines treatment of loans modified or expected to be modified in TDRs: incorporates modification effects (forgone interest, principal forgiveness, other concessions) and redefault risk. Residential real estate uses product-specific PDs tied to borrower credit characteristics and assumptions on home prices and unemployment, informed by industry data and the Firm’s redefault experience; credit cards use projected delinquencies and charge-offs by modification type; wholesale relies on management’s view of repayment capacity under modified terms.
- Highlights that estimating future cash flows is highly judgmental, depending on loss severities, asset valuations, default/redefault rates, payment timing and prepayments, macroeconomic duration, borrower/industry/portfolio conditions, insolvency outcomes, and other economic factors; many assumptions are subjective and require significant management judgment.
text:
Asset-specific component  
To determine the asset-specific component of the 
allowance, collateral-dependent loans (including those 
loans for which foreclosure is probable) and larger, 
nonaccrual risk-rated loans in the wholesale portfolio 
segment are generally evaluated individually, while smaller 
loans (both scored and risk-rated) are aggregated for 
evaluation using factors relevant for the respective class of 
assets.  
The Firm generally measures the asset-specific allowance as 
the difference between the amortized cost of the loan and 
the present value of the cash flows expected to be collected, 
discounted at the loan’s original effective interest rate. 
Subsequent changes in impairment are generally 
recognized as an adjustment to the allowance for loan 
losses. For collateral-dependent loans, the fair value of 
collateral less estimated costs to sell is used to determine 
the charge-off amount for declines in value (to reduce the 
amortized cost of the loan to the fair value of collateral) or 
the amount of negative allowance that should be recognized (for recoveries of prior charge-offs associated 
with improvements in the fair value of collateral). 
The asset-specific component of the allowance for loans 
that have been or are expected to be modified in TDRs 
incorporates the effect of the modification on the loan’s 
expected cash flows (including forgone interest, principal 
forgiveness, as well as other concessions), and also the 
potential for redefault. For residential real estate loans 
modified in or expected to be modified in TDRs,  the Firm 
develops product-specific probability of default estimates, 
which are applied at a loan level to compute expected 
losses. In developing these probabilities of default,  the Firm 
considers the relationship between the credit quality 
characteristics of the underlying loans and certain 
assumptions about housing prices and unemployment, 
based upon industry-wide data.  The Firm also considers its 
own historical loss experience to-date based on actual 
redefaulted modified loans. For credit card loans modified 
in or expected to be modified in TDRs, expected losses 
incorporate projected delinquencies and charge-offs based 
on the Firm’s historical experience by type of modification 
program. For wholesale loans modified or expected to be 
modified in TDRs, expected losses incorporate 
management’s expectation of the borrower’s ability to 
repay under the modified terms.  
Estimating the timing and amounts of future cash flows is 
highly judgmental as these cash flow projections rely upon 
estimates such as loss severities, asset valuations, default 
rates (including redefault rates on modified loans), the 
amounts and timing of interest or principal payments 
(including any expected prepayments) or other factors that 
are reflective of current and expected market conditions. 
These estimates are, in turn, dependent on factors such as 
the duration of current overall economic conditions, 
industry, portfolio, or borrower-specific factors, the 
expected outcome of insolvency proceedings as well as, in 
certain circumstances, other economic factors. All of these 
estimates and assumptions require significant management 
judgment and certain assumptions are highly subjective.  
JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K 243
