title: Discussion of changes in the allowance
heading: 8.20.6 Discussion of changes in the allowance
start_phrase: The allowance for credit losses as of D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 2 was $22.2 billion , reflecting a net addition of $3.5 billion from D e c e m b e r 3 1 , 2 0 2 1, consis ting of:
summary:
- Reports JPMorgan Chase’s allowance for credit losses at December 31, 2022 of $22.2 billion, a net increase of $3.5 billion from December 31, 2021.
- Breaks down the increase: $2.3 billion in wholesale (driven by a deteriorating macroeconomic outlook and loan growth, mainly in CB and CIB) and $1.2 billion in consumer (largely Card Services, due to higher balances and weaker outlook, partly offset by reduced borrower-behavior uncertainty as pandemic effects recede).
- Explains that the macroeconomic outlook worsened due to a Q4 2022 central scenario now assuming a mild recession and heavier weighting to adverse scenarios from Q1 2022 amid higher inflation, tighter monetary policy, and geopolitical risks (including the war in Ukraine).
- Describes methodology: allowance estimated using a weighted average of five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios; adverse scenarios imply a U.S. unemployment peak of 5.6% in Q2 2024 and U.S. real GDP 1.2% lower by the end of Q2 2024 versus the central case.
- Presents central scenario assumptions:
  - As of Dec 31, 2022: U.S. unemployment 3.8% (2Q23), 4.3% (4Q23), 5.0% (2Q24); YoY U.S. real GDP growth 1.5% (2Q23), 0.4% (4Q23), 0.0% (2Q24).
  - As of Dec 31, 2021: U.S. unemployment 4.2% (2Q22), 4.0% (4Q22), 3.9% (2Q23); YoY U.S. real GDP growth 3.1% (2Q22), 2.8% (4Q22), 2.1% (2Q23).
  - Notes that unemployment reflects quarterly averages and GDP growth is year-over-year change in real GDP levels.
- States that future changes to forecasts will flow through the provision for credit losses.
- Provides cross-references to further details: Critical Accounting Estimates (pp. 149–152), Consumer Credit Portfolio (pp. 110–115), and Wholesale Credit Portfolio (pp. 116–126).

Discussion of changes in the allowance
The allowance for credit losses as of  D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2 
was $22.2  billion , reflecting a net addition of  $3.5 billion  
from  D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 1, consis ting of:  
•$ 2 . 3  b i l l i o n in wholesale , driven by deterioration in the 
Firm’s macroeconomic outlook and loan growth, 
predominantly in CB and CIB, and
•$ 1 . 2  b i l l i o n in consumer , predominantly driven by Card 
Services, reflecting higher outstanding balances and 
deterioration in the Firm’s macroeconomic outlook, 
partially offset by a reduction in the allowance related to 
a decrease in uncertainty associated with borrower 
behavior as the effects of the pandemic gradually recede.  
Deterioration in the Firm’s macroeconomic outlook included 
both updates to the central scenario in the fourth quarter of 
2022, which now reflects a mild recession, as well as the 
impact of the increased weight placed on the adverse 
scenarios beginning in the first quarter of 2022 due to the 
effects associated with higher inflation, changes in 
monetary policy, and geopolitical risks, including the war in 
Ukraine.  
The Firm's allowance for credit losses is estimated using a 
weighted average of five internally developed 
macroeconomic scenarios. The adverse scenarios 
incorporate more punitive macroeconomic factors than the 
central case assumptions provided in the table below, 
resulting in a weighted average U.S. unemployment rate 
peaking at 5.6% in the second quarter of 2024, and a 
1.2% lower U.S. real GDP exiting the second quarter of 
2024 .The Firm’s central case assumptions reflected U.S.

The Firm’s other business segments are also involved with VIEs (both third-party and  Firm -sponsored), but to a lesser extent,

•Asset & Wealth Management: AWM sponsors and manages certain funds that are deemed VIEs. As asset manager of the 
funds, AWM earns a fee based on assets managed; the fee varies with each fund’s investment objective and is competitively 
priced. For fund entities that qualify as VIEs, AWM’s interests are, in certain cases, considered to be significant variable 
interests that result in consolidation of the financial results of these entities.
•Commercial Banking: CB provides financing and lending-related services to a wide spectrum of clients, including certain 
third-party-sponsored entities that may meet the definition of a VIE. CB does not control the activities of these entities and 
does not consolidate these entities.  CB’s maximum loss exposure, regardless of whether the entity is a VIE, is generally 
limited to loans and lending-related commitments which are reported and disclosed in the same manner as any other third-
party transaction.  
•Corporate : Corporate is involved with entities that may meet the definition of VIEs; however these entities are generally 
subject to specialized investment company accounting, which does not require the consolidation of investments, including 
VIEs. In addition, Treasury and CIO invest in securities generally issued by third parties which may meet the definition of 
VIEs (e.g., issuers of asset-backed securities). In general, the Firm does not have the power to direct the significant 
activities of these entities and therefore does not consolidate these entities. Refer to Note 10 for further information on the 
Firm’s investment securities portfolio.
In addition,  CIB also invests in and provides financing and other services to VIEs sponsored by third parties. Refer to pages 
251-252  of this Note  for more information on consolidated VIE assets and liabilities as well as the VIEs sponsored by third

start_phrase: CCB’s Card Services business may securitize originated credit card loans, primarily through the Chase Issuance Trust (the “Trust”).
summary:
The excerpt outlines JPMorgan Chase’s disclosures on variable interest entities (VIEs) in Note 14 of its 2022 Form 10-K. It:
- Defines “Firm-sponsored” VIEs as entities where JPMorgan Chase is the primary beneficiary, uses the VIE to securitize Firm assets, the VIE issues instruments bearing the Firm’s name, or it is a Firm-administered asset-backed commercial paper conduit.
- Summarizes key Firm-sponsored VIEs by segment:
  - Consumer & Community Banking (CCB): credit card securitization trusts; mortgage securitization trusts.
  - Corporate & Investment Bank (CIB): residential and commercial mortgage and other securitization trusts; multi-seller conduits; municipal bond vehicles.
  - Notes other segments’ involvement: AWM sponsors/manages certain fund VIEs (sometimes consolidated); Commercial Banking provides financing to third-party VIEs (not consolidated; exposure limited to loans/commitments); Corporate/Treasury/CIO invest in third-party VIE securities and generally do not consolidate under specialized investment company accounting. References Note 10 for investment securities and pages 251–252 for consolidated VIEs and third-party-sponsored VIEs.
- Details significant Firm-sponsored credit card securitizations (Chase Issuance Trust):
  - Continuing involvement includes servicing, holding an undivided seller’s interest, retaining certain subordinated securities, and maintaining escrow accounts.
  - The Firm consolidates these trusts as primary beneficiary due to power over significant activities (servicing, receivable transfers, modifications) and exposure to potentially significant benefits/losses.
  - Trust assets are restricted to trust investors and are not available to Firm creditors.
  - Minimum undivided interest ~5%; undivided interests held were $6.1 billion (2022) and $7.1 billion (2021); average undivided interest in principal receivables was ~62% (2022) and 57% (2021). No senior securities retained; $1.5 billion of subordinated securities retained at both year-ends; amounts eliminated in consolidation.
- Covers Firm-sponsored mortgage and other securitization trusts:
  - The Firm securitizes originated and purchased residential and commercial mortgages and other consumer loans (primarily in CCB and CIB), may service the loans and/or retain interests.
  - Presents unpaid principal in Firm-sponsored private-label securitization VIEs (both consolidated and with continuing involvement) and JPMorgan Chase’s interests in nonconsolidated VIEs. Continuing involvement includes servicing, retained senior/subordinated interests (including risk retention), recourse/guarantees, and derivatives. Maximum loss on retained/purchased interests is limited to carrying value.

JPMorgan Chase interests in nonconsolidated VIEs totaled $9.6B (trading $1.6B; investment securities $7.3B; other financial assets $0.7B). text:
Credit card securitizations
CCB’s Card  Services business may securitize originated 
credit card loans, primarily through the Chase Issuance 
Trust (the “Trust”).  The Firm’s continuing involvement in 
credit card securitizations includes servicing the 
receivables, retaining an undivided seller’s interest in the 
receivables, retaining certain senior and subordinated 
securities and maintaining escrow accounts.  
The Firm consolidates the assets and liabilities of its 
sponsored credit card trusts as it is  considered to be the 
primary beneficiary of these  securitization trusts based on  
the Firm’s ability to direct the activities of these VIEs 
through its servicing responsibilities and other duties, 
including making decisions as to the receivables that are 
transferred into those trusts and as to any related 
modifications and workouts. Additionally, the nature and 
extent of  the Firm’s other continuing involvement with the trusts, as indicated above, obligates  the Firm to absorb 
losses and gives  the Firm the right to receive certain 
benefits from these VIEs that could potentially be 
significant.  
The underlying securitized credit card receivables and other 
assets of the securitization trusts are available only for 
payment of the beneficial interests issued by the

of $6.1 billion  and $7.1 billion , respectively.  The Firm 
maintained an average undivided interest in principal

title: Residential mortgage
heading: 8.21.3 Residential mortgage
start_phrase: The Firm securitizes residential mortgage loans originated by CCB, as well as residential mortgage loans purchased from third parties by either CCB or CIB.
summary:
- The Firm securitizes residential mortgage loans originated or purchased by CCB and those purchased by CIB, with CCB generally retaining servicing. When CCB services the loans (e.g., oversees modifications and workouts), the Firm can direct the VIE’s significant activities and may retain interests upon securitization.
- CIB underwrites and trades securities from Firm‑sponsored securitizations and may retain or reacquire senior, subordinated, or residual interests, including those required by credit risk retention rules. Together with CCB’s servicing and positions held by CIB, Treasury and CIO, or CCB, the Firm may be deemed the primary beneficiary of certain trusts.
- The Firm does not consolidate residential mortgage securitizations when it is not the servicer (and thus lacks power over significant activities) or does not hold a potentially significant beneficial interest.
- For commercial mortgage securitizations, CIB originates and securitizes loans and may retain unsold interests, but the Firm generally does not service these trusts. Control over significant activities typically resides with the servicer or a “controlling class” of investors, and the Firm generally does not retain the controlling class in its sponsored transactions. Treasury and CIO may invest in these securitizations.
- The Firm conducts re‑securitizations by transferring debt securities to VIEs, often involving U.S. GSEs and government agency‑backed residential mortgage securities. Consolidation depends on the Firm’s role and economic interest.
- Transfers to re‑securitization VIEs totaled $16.1 billion (2022), $53.9 billion (2021), and $46.1 billion (2020).
- Most re‑securitizations are client‑driven with shared decision‑making and significant client economic interests; accordingly, the Firm generally does not consolidate these VIEs.
- No private‑label securities were transferred to re‑securitization VIEs in 2020–2022, and any retained interests in such Firm‑sponsored VIEs were not material.
- For third‑party‑sponsored re‑securitizations (typically purchased in the secondary market), the Firm lacks unilateral decision‑making power or demonstrates shared power, and therefore does not consolidate these VIEs.
text:
Residential mortgage
The Firm securitizes residential mortgage loans originated 
by CCB, as well as residential mortgage loans purchased 
from third parties  by either CCB or CIB. CCB generally 
retains servicing for all residential mortgage loans  it 
originated or purchased , and for certain mortgage loans 
purchased by  CIB. For securitizations of loans serviced by  
CCB, the Firm has the power to direct the significant 
activities of the VIE because it is responsible for decisions 
related to loan modifications and workouts.  CCB may also 
retain an interest upon securitization.
In addition,  CIB engages in underwriting and trading 
activities involving securities issued by Firm -sponsored 
securitization trusts. As a result,  CIB at times retains senior 
and/or subordinated interests (including residual interests 
and amounts required to be held pursuant to credit risk 
retention rules) in residential mortgage securitizations at 
the time of securitization, and/or reacquires positions in the 
secondary market in the normal course of business. In 
certain instances, as a result of the positions retained or 
reacquired by  CIB or held by  Treasury and CIO or CCB, when 
considered together with the servicing arrangements 
entered into by  CCB, the Firm is deemed to be the primary 
beneficiary of certain securitization trusts. 
The Firm does not consolidate residential mortgage 
securitizations  (Firm -sponsored or third-party-sponsored) 
when it is not the servicer (and therefore does not have the 
power to direct the most significant activities of the trust) 
or does not hold a beneficial interest in the trust that could 
potentially be significant to the trust.

title: Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations
heading: 8.21.4 Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations
start_phrase: CIB originates and securitizes commercial mortgage loans, and engages in underwriting and trading activities involving the securities issued by securitization trusts.
summary:
- Residential mortgage securitizations: The Firm securitizes loans originated or purchased by CCB and some purchased by CIB. CCB typically retains servicing, which gives it power over significant activities (e.g., modifications/workouts), and may retain interests. CIB underwrites/trades related securities and may retain or reacquire senior/subordinated (including risk-retention) interests. Considering retained positions and CCB servicing, the Firm may be the primary beneficiary of certain trusts. The Firm does not consolidate trusts when it is not the servicer or lacks a potentially significant beneficial interest.

- Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations: CIB originates, securitizes, underwrites, and trades commercial mortgage securitizations, sometimes retaining unsold senior/subordinated (including risk-retention) interests. The Firm generally does not service these deals. Control typically resides with the servicer or a “controlling class” of investors, and the Firm generally does not hold the controlling class; Treasury and CIO may invest.

- Re-securitizations: The Firm transfers debt securities into VIEs (largely U.S. GSE and government agency-sponsored, backed by residential mortgages) in exchange for new interests; consolidation depends on the Firm’s role and interests. Transfers totaled approximately $16.1 billion (2022), $53.9 billion (2021), and $46.1 billion (2020). Most transactions are client-driven with shared decision-making, so the Firm typically does not consolidate these VIEs. No private-label securities were transferred in 2020–2022; any retained interests in such VIEs were not material as of year-end 2022 and 2021. The Firm may invest in third-party re-securitizations via the secondary market but does not consolidate them due to lack of unilateral power or shared power in their design.
text:
Commercial mortgages and other consumer securitizations
CIB originates and securitizes commercial mortgage loans, 
and engages in underwriting and trading activities involving 
the securities issued by securitization trusts.  CIB may retain 
unsold senior and/or subordinated interests (including 
amounts required to be held pursuant to credit risk 
retention rules) in commercial mortgage securitizations at 
the time of securitization but, generally, the Firm does not 
service commercial loan securitizations. Treasury and CIO 
may choose to invest in these securitizations as well. For 
commercial mortgage securitizations the power to direct 
the significant activities of the VIE generally is held by the 
servicer or investors in a specified class of securities 
(“controlling class”).  The Firm generally does not retain an 
interest in the controlling class in its sponsored commercial 
mortgage securitization transactions.

title: Re-securitizations - Introduction
heading: 8.21.5 Re-securitizations
start_phrase: The Firm engages in certain re-securitization transactions in which debt securities are transferred to a VIE in exchange for new beneficial interests.
summary: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s re-securitization activities involving transfers of debt securities to VIEs—primarily U.S. GSE and government agency-sponsored trusts backed by residential mortgages—including consolidation conclusions. Most transactions are client-driven with shared decision-making and significant client economic interests, so the Firm generally does not consolidate these VIEs. The Firm also buys beneficial interests in third-party-sponsored re-securitizations (often in the secondary market) without unilateral power over key activities, and therefore does not consolidate those VIEs. No private-label securities were transferred to re-securitization VIEs in 2020–2022, and retained interests in any Firm-sponsored VIEs were not material as of December 31, 2022 and 2021. A table reports principal amounts of securities transferred to re-securitization VIEs: $16,128 million (2022), $53,923 million (2021), and $46,123 million (2020).

Re-securitizations
The Firm engages in certain re-securitization transactions in 
which debt securities are transferred to a VIE in exchange 
for new beneficial interests. These transfers occur in 
connection with both U.S. GSEs and government agency 
sponsored VIEs, which are backed by residential mortgages. 
The Firm’s consolidation analysis is largely dependent on

Most re-securitizations with which the Firm is involved are 
client-driven transactions in which a specific client or group 
of clients is seeking a specific return or risk profile. For

circumstances, the Firm does not have the unilateral ability 
to direct the most significant activities of the re-

the initial design of the trust, or the Firm was involved with 
an independent third-party sponsor and demonstrated 
shared power over the creation of the trust; therefore, the 
Firm does not consolidate the re-securitization VIE.

title: Multi-seller conduits
heading: 8.21.6 Multi-seller conduits
start_phrase: Multi-seller conduit entities are separate bankruptcy remote entities that provide secured financing, collateralized by pools of receivables and other financial assets, to customers of the Firm.
summary:
- Discloses the Firm’s interests in nonconsolidated re-securitization VIEs tied to U.S. GSEs and government agencies: $2.58 billion at December 31, 2022, and $1.95 billion at December 31, 2021; the Firm did not consolidate any U.S. GSE/government agency or Firm-sponsored private-label re-securitization VIEs in those periods.
- Explains multi-seller conduits:
  - Bankruptcy-remote entities that provide secured financing to customers, funded via highly rated commercial paper (CP) repaid from underlying asset cash flows.
  - Credit risk mitigated through deal-specific credit enhancements (e.g., seller overcollateralization) sized as multiples of expected losses.
  - Each asset pool has a minimum 100% deal-specific liquidity facility from JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.; the Firm also provides uncommitted program-wide liquidity and ~10% program-wide credit enhancement via standby letters of credit.
  - The Firm consolidates its Firm-administered conduits due to power over key activities and potentially significant economic interests (fees and exposures from liquidity and credit enhancement).
  - The Firm makes markets in and invests in conduit CP; it held $13.8 billion (2022) and $13.7 billion (2021), eliminated in consolidation; holdings reflect funding strategy, not market illiquidity; no obligation to purchase beyond risk retention requirements.
  - Deal-specific and program-wide facilities are eliminated in consolidation; unfunded lending-related commitments to certain clients were $10.6 billion (2022) and $13.4 billion (2021), reported off-balance sheet.
- Describes municipal bond vehicles (tender option bond trusts):
  - Trusts purchase highly rated municipal bonds and issue puttable floating-rate certificates (floaters) and inverse floating-rate residuals (residuals) to finance at short-term rates.
  - Customer TOB trusts have residuals held by third parties; non-customer TOBs have residuals retained by the Firm; the Firm sponsors all non-customer TOBs.

  - Liquidity provider obligations are conditional and limited by specified events.
text:
Multi-seller conduits
Multi-seller conduit entities are separate bankruptcy 
remote entities that provide secured financing, 
collateralized by pools of receivables and other financial 
assets, to customers of  the Firm. The conduits fund their 
financing facilities through the issuance of highly rated 
commercial paper. The primary source of repayment of the 
commercial paper is the cash flows from the pools of assets. 
In most instances, the assets are structured with deal-
specific credit enhancements provided to the conduits by 
the customers (i.e., sellers) or other third parties. Deal-
specific credit enhancements are generally structured to 
cover a multiple of historical losses expected on the pool of 
assets, and are typically in the form of overcollateralization 
provided by the seller. The deal-specific credit 
enhancements mitigate  the Firm’s potential losses on its 
agreements with the conduits.
To ensure timely repayment of the commercial paper, and 
to provide the conduits with funding to provide financing to 
customers in the event that the conduits do not obtain 
funding in the commercial paper market, each asset pool 
financed by the conduits has a minimum 100% deal-
specific liquidity facility associated with it provided by  
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. also 
provides the multi-seller conduit vehicles with uncommitted 
program-wide liquidity facilities and program-wide credit 
enhancement in the form of standby letters of credit. The 
amount of program-wide credit enhancement required is 
based upon commercial paper issuance and approximates  
10%  of the outstanding balance of commercial paper.
The Firm consolidates its  Firm -administered multi-seller 
conduits, as  the Firm has both the power to direct the 
significant activities of the conduits and a potentially 
significant economic interest in the conduits. As 
administrative agent and in its role in structuring 
transactions,  the Firm makes decisions regarding asset 
types and credit quality, and manages the commercial 
paper funding needs of the conduits.  The Firm’s interests 
that could potentially be significant to the VIEs include the 
fees received as administrative agent and liquidity and 
program-wide credit enhancement provider, as well as the 
potential exposure created by the liquidity and credit 
enhancement facilities provided to the conduits.In the normal course of business,  JPMorgan Chase makes 
markets in and invests in commercial paper issued by  the 
Firm -administered multi-seller conduits.  The Firm held 
$13.8 billion  and $13.7 billion  of the commercial paper 
issued by  the Firm -administered multi-seller conduits at  
D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2 and 2021 , respectively, which have 
been eliminated in consolidation.  The Firm’s investments 
reflect  the Firm’s funding needs and capacity and were not 
driven by market illiquidity.  Other than the amounts 
required to be held pursuant to credit risk retention rules,  
the Firm is not obligated under any agreement to purchase 
the commercial paper issued by  the Firm -administered 
multi-seller conduits.
Deal-specific liquidity facilities, program-wide liquidity and 
credit enhancement provided by the Firm have been 
eliminated in consolidation. The Firm or the Firm-
administered multi-seller conduits provide lending-related 
commitments to certain clients of the Firm-administered 
multi-seller conduits. The unfunded commitments were  
$10.6 billion  and $13.4 billion  at D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2 and 
2021 , respectively, and are reported as off-balance sheet 
lending-related commitments in other unfunded 
commitments to extend credit.  Refer to Note  28 for more 
information on off-balance sheet lending-related 
commitments.

title: Municipal bond vehicles - Introduction
heading: 8.21.7 Municipal bond vehicles
start_phrase: Municipal bond vehicles or tender option bond (“TOB”) trusts allow institutions to finance their municipal bond investments at short-term rates.
summary: Introduces JPMorgan Chase’s use of municipal bond vehicles known as tender option bond (TOB) trusts, which purchase highly rated single-issuer municipal bonds and finance them by issuing puttable floating-rate certificates (floaters) and inverse floating-rate residual interests (residuals). Distinguishes customer TOB trusts (residual held by a third-party investor and sponsored by a third party) from non-customer TOB trusts (residual retained and sponsored by the Firm). Describes the Firm’s roles: J.P. Morgan Securities LLC may act as remarketing agent (setting periodic variable rates, initial placement, and remarketing; floaters held by the Firm were not material in 2022 and 2021) and, along with JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., often serves as sole liquidity/tender option provider. Outlines liquidity obligations and limits via Termination Events (issuer or credit enhancer bankruptcy/failure to pay, bond taxability, immediate downgrade below investment grade) and mitigants (high bond credit quality, excess collateralization, reimbursement agreements with residual holders), and the process if floaters are tendered and cannot be remarketed. Notes TOB trusts are variable interest entities and the Firm consolidates non-customer TOB trusts because, as residual holder, it has decision-making power and exposure to potentially significant benefits and losses.
text:
Municipal bond vehicles
Municipal bond vehicles or tender option bond (“TOB”) 
trusts allow institutions to finance their municipal bond 
investments at short-term rates. In a typical TOB 
transaction, the trust purchases highly rated municipal 
bond(s) of a single issuer and funds the purchase by issuing 
two types of securities: (1) puttable floating-rate 
certificates (“floaters”) and (2) inverse floating-rate 
residual interests (“residuals”). The floaters are typically 
purchased by money market funds or other short-term 
investors and may be tendered, with requisite notice, to the 
TOB trust. The residuals are retained by the investor 
seeking to finance its municipal bond investment.  TOB 
transactions where the residual is held by a third-party 
investor are typically known as customer TOB trusts, and 
non-customer TOB trusts are transactions where the 
Residual is retained by  the Firm. Customer TOB trusts are 
sponsored by a third party.  The Firm serves as sponsor for 
all non-customer TOB transactions.  The Firm may provide 
various services to a TOB trust, including  remarketing 
agent, liquidity or tender option provider, and/or sponsor.
J.P. Morgan Securities LLC may serve as a remarketing 
agent on the floaters for TOB trusts. The remarketing agent 
is responsible for establishing the periodic variable rate on 
the floaters, conducting the initial placement and 
remarketing tendered floaters. The remarketing agent may, 
but is not obligated to, make markets in floaters. Floaters 
held by the Firm were not material during 2022  and 2021 .
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. or J.P. Morgan Securities LLC 
often serves as the sole liquidity or tender option provider 
for the TOB trusts. The liquidity provider’s obligation to 
perform is conditional and is limited by certain events Notes to consolidated financial statements
250 JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K
(“Termination Events”), which include bankruptcy or failure 
to pay by the municipal bond issuer or credit enhancement 
provider, an event of taxability on the municipal bonds or 
the immediate downgrade of the municipal bond to below 
investment grade. In addition, the liquidity provider’s 
exposure is typically further limited by the high credit 
quality of the underlying municipal bonds, the excess 
collateralization in the vehicle, or, in certain transactions, 
the reimbursement agreements with the Residual holders.
Holders of the floaters may “put,” or tender, their floaters 
to the TOB trust. If the remarketing agent cannot 
successfully remarket the floaters to another investor, the liquidity provider either provides a loan to the TOB trust for 
the TOB trust’s purchase of the floaters, or it directly 
purchases the tendered floaters.  
TOB trusts are considered to be variable interest entities.  
The Firm consolidates non-customer TOB trusts because as 
the Residual holder,  the Firm has the right to make 
decisions that significantly impact the economic 
performance of the municipal bond vehicle, and it has the 
right to receive benefits and bear losses that could 
potentially be significant to the municipal bond vehicle.

title: VIEs sponsored by third parties - Introduction
heading: 8.21.8 VIEs sponsored by third parties
start_phrase: The Firm enters into transactions with VIEs structured by other parties.
summary:
VIEs sponsored by third parties  
The Firm enters into transactions with VIEs structured by 
other parties. These include, for example, acting as a 
derivative counterparty, liquidity provider, investor, 
underwriter, placement agent, remarketing agent, trustee 
or custodian. These transactions are conducted at arm’s-
length, and individual credit decisions are based on the 
analysis of the specific VIE, taking into consideration the 
quality of the underlying assets. Where  the Firm does not 
have the power to direct the activities of the VIE that most 
significantly impact the VIE’s economic performance, or a 
variable interest that could potentially be significant,  the 
Firm generally does not consolidate the VIE, but it records 
and reports these positions on its Consolidated balance 
sheets in the same manner it would record and report 
positions in respect of any other third-party transaction.

title: Tax credit vehicles
heading: 8.21.8.1 Tax credit vehicles
start_phrase: The Firm holds investments in unconsolidated tax credit vehicles, which are limited partnerships and similar entities that own and operate affordable housing, energy, and other projects.
summary:
- Describes the Firm’s involvement with variable interest entities (VIEs) sponsored by third parties in roles such as derivative counterparty, liquidity provider, investor, underwriter, placement/remarketing agent, trustee, or custodian. Transactions are at arm’s length, and the Firm generally does not consolidate these VIEs unless it has power over significant activities or a potentially significant variable interest; otherwise, positions are recorded like other third‑party transactions.
- Explains investments in unconsolidated tax credit vehicles (primarily VIE limited partnerships for affordable housing, energy, and other projects). A third party controls significant activities; the Firm participates as a limited partner and earns returns mainly via tax credits. Maximum loss exposure was $30.2 billion (2022) and $26.8 billion (2021), including unfunded commitments of $10.6 billion and $9.4 billion, respectively. The Firm may withhold capital until projects qualify for credits. References are made to Notes 25 and 28.
- Details customer municipal bond vehicles (tender option bond, or TOB, trusts). The Firm may act as remarketing agent and/or provide liquidity or tender option facilities. In some cases it has reimbursement agreements giving recourse to residual holders upon termination; it does not intend to protect residual holders from losses. The Firm does not consolidate these trusts due to lack of decision‑making power. Maximum exposure as liquidity provider was $5.8 billion (2022) and $6.8 billion (2021); fair value of assets held by such VIEs was $8.2 billion (2022) and $10.5 billion (2021).
- Outlines loan securitizations of residential mortgages, credit card receivables, commercial mortgages, and other consumer loans conducted to meet investor demand and provide liquidity. For non‑consolidated trusts, transfers are accounted for as sales when isolation, transferee’s pledge/exchange rights, and lack of effective control criteria are met. Gains/losses are recognized based on proceeds versus carrying value and reported in noninterest revenue.
text:
Tax credit vehicles  
The Firm holds investments in unconsolidated tax credit 
vehicles, which are limited partnerships and similar entities 
that own and operate affordable housing, energy, and other 
projects.  These entities are primarily considered VIEs. A 
third party is typically the general partner or managing 
member and has control over the significant activities of the 
tax credit vehicles, and accordingly  the Firm does not 
consolidate tax credit vehicles.  The Firm generally invests in 
these partnerships as a limited partner and earns a return 
primarily through the receipt of tax credits allocated to the 
projects. The maximum loss exposure, represented by 
equity investments and funding com mitments, was  $30.2 
billion  and $26.8 billion , of which  $10.6 billion  and $9.4 
billion  was unfunded at  D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2 and 2021 , 
respectively.  The Firm assesses each project and to reduce 
the risk of loss, may withhold varying amounts of its capital 
investment until the project qualifies for tax credits. Refer 
to Note  25 for further information on affordable housing 
tax credits  and Note  28 for more information on off-balance 
sheet lending-related commitments.

The Firm may provide various services to customer TOB 
trusts, including  remarketing agent, liquidity or tender 
option provider. In certain customer TOB transactions,  the 
Firm, as liquidity provider, has entered into a 
reimbursement agreement with the Residual holder. In 
those transactions, upon the termination of the vehicle,  the 
Firm has recourse to the third-party Residual holders for 
any shortfall.  The Firm does not have any intent to protect 
Residual holders from potential losses on any of the 
underlying municipal bonds.  The Firm does not consolidate 
customer TOB trusts, since  the Firm does not have the 
power to make decisions that significantly impact the 
economic performance of the municipal bond vehicle.

title: Loan securitizations - Introduction
heading: 8.21.9 Loan securitizations
start_phrase: The Firm has securitized and sold a variety of loans, including residential mortgages, credit card receivables, commercial mortgages and other consumer loans.
summary: Introduces JPMorgan Chase’s loan securitizations, covering asset types (residential mortgages, credit card receivables, commercial mortgages, other consumer loans) and purposes (meeting investor demand, generating liquidity). Describes sale accounting for securitizations when the trust is not consolidated, requiring: legal isolation of assets from the Firm’s creditors, the transferee/beneficial interest holder’s ability to pledge or exchange the assets, and the Firm’s lack of effective control (no repurchase before maturity and no unilateral right to require asset return). For sales, gain or loss equals proceeds received (cash, beneficial interests, servicing assets) minus carrying value, with results reported in noninterest revenue.
text:
Loan securitizations
The Firm has securitized and sold a variety of loans, 
including residential mortgages, credit card receivables,  
commercial mortgages and other consumer loans. The 
purposes of these securitization transactions were to satisfy 
investor demand and to generate liquidity for  the Firm.
For loan securitizations in which  the Firm is not required to 
consolidate the trust,  the Firm records the transfer of the 
loan receivable to the trust as a sale when all of the 
following accounting criteria for a sale are met: (1) the 
transferred financial assets are legally isolated from  the 
Firm’s creditors; (2) the transferee or beneficial interest 
holder can pledge or exchange the transferred financial 
assets; and (3)  the Firm does not maintain effective control 
over the transferred financial assets (e.g.,  the Firm cannot 
repurchase the transferred assets before their maturity and 
it does not have the ability to unilaterally cause the holder 
to return the transferred assets).
For loan securitizations accounted for as a sale,  the Firm 
recognizes a gain or loss based on the difference between 
the value of proceeds received (including cash, beneficial 
interests, or servicing assets received) and the carrying 
value of the assets sold. Gains and losses on securitizations 
are reported in noninterest revenue.Notes to consolidated financial statements

title: Goodwill - Introduction
heading: 8.22.1 Goodwill
start_phrase: Goodwill is recorded upon completion of a business combination as the difference between the purchase price and the fair value of the net assets acquired, and can be adjusted up to one year from the acquisition date as more information is obtained about the fair value of assets acquired and liabilities assumed.
summary: This section defines goodwill as the excess of purchase price over the fair value of net assets in business combinations, adjustable for up to one year post-acquisition, not amortized, and tested for impairment annually in the fourth quarter or upon adverse indicators; goodwill is allocated to reporting units aligned with management structure. It provides a table of goodwill by segment—Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Commercial Banking, Asset & Wealth Management, and Corporate—with totals of $51,662m (2022), $50,315m (2021), and $49,248m (2020), and notes a qualitative impairment assessment for Corporate goodwill acquired in 2021 under U.S. GAAP. A reconciliation table shows changes from business combinations ($1,426m in 2022; $1,073m in 2021; $1,412m in 2020) and other adjustments (predominantly foreign currency), with prior-period revisions. Listed acquisitions driving goodwill include, in 2022: Global Shares (AWM), Frosch Travel Group and Figg (CCB), Renovite Technologies and Volkswagen Payments (CIB); in 2021: Nutmeg (Corporate), OpenInvest and Campbell Global (AWM), Frank and The Infatuation (CCB); in 2020: cxLoyalty (CCB) and 55ip (AWM).
text:
Goodwill
Goodwill is recorded upon completion of a business 
combination as the difference between the purchase price 
and the fair value of the net assets acquired, and can be 
adjusted up to one year from the acquisition date as more 
information is obtained about the fair value of assets 
acquired and liabilities assumed. Subsequent to initial 
recognition, goodwill is not amortized but is tested for 
impairment during the fourth quarter of each fiscal year, or 
more often if events or circumstances, such as adverse 
changes in the business climate, indicate that there may be 
an impairment.
The goodwill associated with each business combination is 
allocated to the related reporting units, which are generally 
determined based on how the Firm’s businesses are 
managed and how they are reviewed.  The following table 
presents goodwill attributed to the reportable business

title: Goodwill impairment testing
heading: 8.22.1.1 Goodwill impairment testing
start_phrase: The Firm’s goodwill was not impaired at December 31, 2022, 2021 and 2020 .
summary:
- Scope: Note 15 covers accounting, balances, changes, and testing for goodwill, plus recognition and valuation of mortgage servicing rights (MSRs).

- Goodwill policy:
  - Recognized in business combinations as purchase price over fair value of net assets; measurement period adjustments allowed up to one year.
  - Not amortized; tested for impairment annually in Q4 or more frequently if indicators arise.
  - Allocated to reporting units aligned with how the firm manages and reviews its businesses.

- Goodwill balances and changes:
  - Total goodwill at Dec 31: $51.7B (2022), $50.3B (2021), $49.2B (2020).
  - By segment (2022): Consumer & Community Banking largest ($32.1B), followed by Asset & Wealth Management ($7.9B), Corporate & Investment Bank ($8.0B), Commercial Banking ($3.0B), Corporate ($0.6B). Corporate’s 2021 goodwill assessed qualitatively per U.S. GAAP.
  - Rollforward shows increases primarily from acquisitions and minor foreign currency adjustments.
  - Notable acquisitions contributing to goodwill:
    - 2022: Global Shares (AWM), Frosch Travel, Figg (CCB), Renovite, Volkswagen Payments (CIB).
    - 2021: Nutmeg (Corporate), OpenInvest, Campbell Global (AWM), Frank, The Infatuation (CCB).
    - 2020: cxLoyalty (CCB), 55ip (AWM).

- Goodwill impairment testing:
  - No impairment recognized in 2020–2022.
  - Test compares each reporting unit’s fair value to its carrying value; impairment recognized up to the amount of goodwill if carrying exceeds fair value.
  - Carrying value proxy: allocated capital plus goodwill and other intangibles, with capital levels informed by peers, regulatory requirements, and the firm’s budget process.
  - Valuation primarily via income approach (discounted cash flows with terminal value), using cost of equity derived from CAPM and adjusted for unit-specific risks; checks include comparison to peers’ cost of equity and market trading/transaction multiples.
  - Aggregate reporting unit fair values also compared to firm market capitalization, considering control premium, execution risk differences, and short-term market volatility.
  - Potential future impairment drivers: weaker performance, higher credit losses, higher capital requirements, adverse economic/market or regulatory changes, higher estimated market cost of equity.

- Mortgage servicing rights (MSRs):
  - Represent fair value of expected future cash flows from servicing performing loans for others; value declines over time as servicing cash flows are received (offsetting servicing and ancillary fee income).
  - Recognized when purchased or when loans are sold/securitized with servicing retained.
  - Measured at fair value under the firm’s U.S. GAAP election and managed as a single class/aggregate pool.
  - Fair value estimated using an option-adjusted spread model across multiple interest-rate scenarios with a prepayment model; discounted at risk-adjusted rates.
  - Key inputs: portfolio characteristics, contractual fees, prepayment and delinquency assumptions, servicing costs, late charges/ancillary revenue, and other economic factors.
  - Assumptions validated against observable market data, recent market activity, and actual portfolio experience.
text:
Goodwill impairment testing
The Firm’s goodwill was not impaired at December 31, 
2022, 2021 and 2020 .
The goodwill impairment test is generally performed by 
comparing the current fair value of  each reporting unit with 
its carrying value. If the fair value is in excess of the 
carrying value, then the  reporting unit’s goodwill is 
considered not to be impaired. If the fair value is less than 
the carrying value, then an impairment charge is recognized for the amount by which the  reporting unit’s carrying value 
exceeds its fair value, up to the amount of  goodwill  
allocated to that reporting unit. 
The Firm uses the reporting units’ allocated capital plus 
goodwill and other intangible assets as a proxy for the 
carrying values of equity for the reporting units in the 
goodwill impairment testing. Reporting unit equity is 
determined on a similar basis as the allocation of capital to 
the LOBs which takes into consideration a variety of factors 
including c apital levels of similarly rated peers and 
applicable regulatory capital requirements. Proposed LOB 
capital levels are incorporated into the Firm’s annual 
budget process, which is reviewed by the Firm’s Board of 
Directors  and Operating Committee . Allocated capital is 
further reviewed at least annually and updated as needed.
The primary method the Firm uses to estimate the fair value 
of its reporting units is the income approach. This approach 
projects cash flows for the forecast period and uses the 
perpetuity growth method to calculate terminal values. 
These cash flows and terminal values, which are based on 
the reporting units’ annual budgets and forecasts are then 
discounted using an appropriate discount rate. The discount 
rate used for each reporting unit represents an estimate of 
the cost of equity for that reporting unit and is determined 
considering the Firm’s overall estimated cost of equity 
(estimated using the Capital Asset Pricing Model), as 
adjusted for the risk characteristics specific to each 
reporting unit (for example, for higher levels of risk or 
uncertainty associated with the business or management’s 
forecasts and assumptions). To assess the reasonableness 
of the discount rates used for each reporting unit, 
management compares the discount rate to the estimated 
cost of equity for publicly traded institutions with similar 
businesses and risk characteristics. In addition, the 
weighted average cost of equity (aggregating the various 
reporting units) is compared with the Firm’s overall 
estimated cost of equity to ensure reasonableness. The 
valuations derived from the discounted cash flow analysis 
are then compared with market-based trading and 
transaction multiples for relevant competitors. Trading and 
transaction comparables are used as general indicators to 
assess the overall reasonableness of the estimated fair 
values, although precise conclusions generally cannot be 
drawn due to the differences that naturally exist between 
the Firm’s businesses and competitor institutions. 
The Firm also takes into consideration a comparison 
between the aggregate fair values of the Firm’s reporting 
units and JPMorgan Chase’s market capitalization. In 
evaluating this comparison, the Firm considers several 
factors, including (i) a control premium that would exist in a 
market transaction, (ii) factors related to the level of 
execution risk that would exist at the Firmwide level that do 
not exist at the reporting unit level and (iii) short-term 
market volatility and other factors that do not directly 
affect the value of individual reporting units.
JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K 255Unanticipated declines in business performance, increases 
in credit losses, increases in capital requirements, as well as 
deterioration in economic or market conditions, adverse 
regulatory or legislative changes or increases in the 
estimated market cost of equity, could cause the estimated 
fair values of  the Firm’s reporting units  to decline in the 
future, which could result in a material impairment charge 
to earnings in a future period related to some portion of the 
associated goodwill.

title: Mortgage servicing rights
heading: 8.22.2 Mortgage servicing rights
start_phrase: MSRs represent the fair value of expected future cash flows for performing servicing activities for others.
summary:
- Highlights risk that adverse business performance, credit losses, higher capital requirements, economic/market deterioration, regulatory changes, or higher estimated cost of equity could reduce reporting units’ fair values and trigger future goodwill impairments.
- Defines mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) as the fair value of expected future servicing cash flows; MSRs are recognized when servicing is retained on loan sales/securitizations or purchased from third parties.
- States the Firm elects fair value accounting for MSRs under U.S. GAAP and manages them as a single class/aggregate pool.
- Describes MSR valuation via an option-adjusted spread (OAS) model that projects cash flows across interest-rate scenarios using the Firm’s prepayment model and discounts at risk‑adjusted rates; key inputs include servicing fees, prepayments, delinquency, servicing costs, late/ancillary fees, discount rates, and economic factors; estimates are benchmarked to observable market data and actual experience.
- Explains MSR fair value sensitivity to interest rates: values typically decrease when rates fall due to higher prepayments; the Firm uses combinations of derivatives and securities (e.g., MBS and fixed‑receive swaps) to hedge MSR interest‑rate risk with the intent to offset valuation changes.
- Provides MSR activity for 2020–2022: ending fair value rose to $7.973B in 2022 (from $5.494B in 2021 and $3.276B in 2020); details originations, purchases, dispositions (including excess MSRs exchanged for SMBS), cash flow realization, and valuation changes attributable to market rates and other modeling inputs.
- Notes unrealized gains/losses from MSRs included in income and reports third‑party mortgage loans serviced and servicer advances (generally reimbursable and senior in cash flow priority, thus minimal credit risk, though advances may be unrecoverable if not made per rules).
- Presents components of mortgage fees and related income for 2020–2022: production revenue declined in 2022, while net mortgage servicing revenue improved due to MSR valuation increases offset by derivative and other risk‑management results; total CCB mortgage fees and related income decreased to $1.236B in 2022.
- Cautions that valuation sensitivities are not linear; provides 2022 vs. 2021 key assumption levels and shocks: weighted‑average CPR (6.12% vs. 9.90%) and OAS (5.77% vs. 6.44%), with quantified fair value impacts under adverse changes; OAS includes operational risk and regulatory capital.
text:
Mortgage servicing rights
MSRs represent the fair value of expected future cash flows 
for performing servicing activities for others. The fair value 
considers estimated future servicing fees and ancillary 
revenue, offset by estimated costs to service the loans, and 
generally declines over time as net servicing cash flows are 
received, effectively amortizing the MSR asset against 
contractual servicing and ancillary fee income. MSRs are 
either purchased from third parties or recognized upon sale 
or securitization of mortgage loans if servicing is retained.
As permitted by U.S. GAAP,  the Firm has elected to account 
for its MSRs at fair value.  The Firm treats its MSRs as a 
single class of servicing assets based on the availability of 
market inputs used to measure the fair value of its MSR 
asset and its treatment of MSRs as one aggregate pool for 
risk management purposes.  The Firm estimates the fair 
value of MSRs using an option-adjusted spread (“OAS”) 
model, which projects MSR cash flows over multiple interest 
rate scenarios in conjunction with  the Firm’s prepayment 
model, and then discounts these cash flows at risk-adjusted 
rates. The model considers portfolio characteristics, 
contractually specified servicing fees, prepayment 
assumptions, delinquency rates, costs to service, late 
charges and other ancillary revenue, and other economic 
factors.  The Firm  compares fair value estimates and 
assumptions to observable market data where available, 
and also considers recent market activity and actual 
portfolio experience.  Notes to consolidated financial statements
256 JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-KThe fair value of MSRs is sensitive to changes in interest 
rates, including their effect on prepayment speeds. MSRs 
typically decrease in value when interest rates decline 
because declining interest rates tend to increase 
prepayments and therefore reduce the expected life of the 
net servicing cash flows that comprise the MSR asset. 
Conversely, securities (e.g., mortgage-backed securities), 
and certain derivatives (e.g., those for which  the Firm receives fixed-rate interest payments) increase in value 
when interest rates decline.  JPMorgan Chase uses 
combinations of derivatives and securities to manage the 
risk of changes in the fair value of MSRs. The intent is to 
offset any interest-rate related changes in the fair value of 
MSRs with changes in the fair value of the related risk 
management instruments.

title: Premises and equipment
heading: 8.23 Note 16 – Premises and equipment
start_phrase:
Premises and equipment, including leasehold 
improvements, are carried at cost less accumulated 
depreciation and amortization.
summary:
- Note 16 – Premises and equipment:
  - Premises, equipment, and leasehold improvements are recorded at cost less accumulated depreciation/amortization.
  - Depreciation is recognized on a straight-line basis over estimated useful lives.
  - Leasehold improvements are amortized straight-line over the shorter of the remaining lease term or the improvements’ useful life.
  - Certain costs to acquire/develop internal-use software are capitalized and amortized straight-line over the software’s expected useful life once ready for use.
  - Assets are reviewed for impairment when events or changes in circumstances indicate carrying values may not be fully recoverable.

- Note 17 – Deposits:
  - Breakdown of noninterest-bearing and interest-bearing deposits by U.S. and non-U.S. offices at December 31, 2022 and 2021.
  - Total deposits: $2,340.2 billion (2022) vs. $2,462.3 billion (2021).
  - U.S. offices: $1,921.2 billion (2022) vs. $2,071.5 billion (2021). Non-U.S. offices: $418.9 billion (2022) vs. $390.8 billion (2021).
  - Certain structured notes elected at fair value are included within deposits; prior-period amounts revised to conform to current presentation.
  - Time deposits meeting/exceeding insured limits: $142.5 billion (2022) vs. $93.5 billion (2021); all non-U.S. time deposits typically exceed the insured limit.
  - Maturity schedule of interest-bearing time deposits at 12/31/2022 totals $154.6 billion, with $150.7 billion maturing in 2023 and smaller amounts maturing through after 5 years across U.S. and non-U.S. offices.
text:
Premises and equipment, including  leasehold 
improvements, are carried at cost less accumulated 
depreciation and amortization.  JPMorgan Chase  computes 
depreciation using the straight-line method over the 
estimated useful life of an asset. For leasehold 
improvements,  the Firm uses the straight-line method 
computed over the lesser of the remainder of the lease 
term, or estimated useful life of the improvements.  
JPMorgan Chase  capitalizes certain costs associated with 
the acquisition or development of internal-use software. 
Once the software is ready for its intended use, these costs 
are amortized on a straight-line basis over the software’s 
expected useful life.  
Impairment is assessed periodically when events or changes 
in circumstances indicate that the carrying value of an asset 
may not be fully recove rable.Note 17 –

start_phrase:

summary:
- Scope: JPMorgan Chase, as lessee, has noncancellable leases primarily for premises and equipment, largely operating leases used for business purposes. Lease terms generally are 20 years or less and include options to extend or terminate when reasonably certain to be exercised. Leases do not restrict dividends, financing, or entering new leases.
- Accounting policy: For leases over 12 months, the Firm recognizes a lease liability and corresponding right‑of‑use (ROU) asset at commencement, measured at the present value of future minimum payments using a collateralized borrowing rate. Lease liabilities are in accounts payable and other liabilities; ROU assets are in premises and equipment and include prepayments and initial direct costs, net of incentives. Rental expense is recognized on a straight‑line basis in occupancy expense.
- Non‑lease components: Certain leases have escalation clauses tied to maintenance, utilities, and taxes. For real estate leases, the Firm elected not to separate lease and non‑lease components; payments therefore include both.
- Balances at December 31:
  - 2022: ROU assets $7,782 million; lease liabilities $8,183 million; weighted average remaining lease term 8.4 years; weighted average discount rate 3.55%.
  - 2021: ROU assets $7,888 million; lease liabilities $8,328 million; weighted average remaining lease term 8.5 years; weighted average discount rate 3.40%.
- Cash flow and non‑cash activity:

text:
Firm as lessee
A t  D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 22, JPMorgan Chase and its 
subsidiaries were obligated under a number of 
noncancellable leases, predominantly operating leases for 
premises and equipment used primarily for business 
purposes. These leases generally have terms of  20 years  or 
less, determined based on the contractual maturity of the 
lease, and include periods covered by options to extend or 
terminate the lease when  the Firm is reasonably certain 
that it will exercise those options. All leases with lease 
terms greater than twelve months are reported as a lease 
liability with a corresponding right-of-use (“ROU”) asset. 
None of these lease agreements impose restrictions on  the 
Firm’s ability to pay dividends, engage in debt or equity 
financing transactions or enter into further lease 
agreements. Certain of these leases contain escalation 
clauses that will increase rental payments based on 
maintenance, utility and tax increases, which are non-lease 
components.  The Firm elected not to separate lease and 
non-lease components of a contract for its real estate 
leases. As such, real estate lease payments represent 
payments on both lease and non-lease components.  
Operating lease liabilities and ROU assets are recognized at 
the lease commencement date based on the present value 
of the future minimum lease payments over the lease term. 
The future lease payments are discounted at a rate that 
estimate s the Firm’s collateralized borrowing rate for 
financing instruments of a similar term and are included in 
accounts payable and other liabilities. The operating lease 
ROU asset, included in premises and equipment, also 
includes any lease prepayments made, plus initial direct 
costs incurred, less any lease incentives received. Rental 
expense associated with operating leases is recognized on a 
straight-line basis over the lease term, and generally 
included in occupancy expense in the Consolidated 
statements of income.  The following tables provide information related to  the

title: Firm as lessor
heading: 8.25.2 Firm as lessor
start_phrase:
The Firm provides auto and equipment lease financing to its 
customers through lease arrangements with lease terms

summary:
- Scope: The Firm, acting as a lessor, provides auto and equipment lease financing, predominantly through auto operating leases.
- Accounting policies: Assets subject to operating leases are recorded in other assets and depreciated on a straight-line basis over the lease term to estimated residual value; depreciation is included in technology, communications and equipment expense. Lease income is recognized on a straight-line basis in other income.
- Impairment: Leased assets are periodically assessed; if carrying amount exceeds undiscounted lease cash flows plus estimated residual value, an impairment loss is recognized.
- Residual value risk: Monitored via projections at origination and periodic reviews; mitigated through arrangements with certain manufacturers or lessees.

text:
Firm as lessor
The Firm provides auto and equipment lease financing to its 
customers through lease arrangements with lease terms 
that may contain renewal, termination and/or purchase 
options. The Firm’s lease financings are predominantly auto 
operating leases. These assets subject to operating leases 
are recognized in other assets on  the Firm’s Consolidated 
balance sheets and are depreciated on a straight-line basis 
over the lease term to reduce the asset to its estimated 
residual value. Depreciation expense is included in 
technology, communications and equipment expense in the 
Consolidated statements of income.  The Firm’s lease 
income is generally recognized on a straight-line basis over 
the lease term and is included in other income in the 
Consolidated statements of income.  
On a periodic basis,  the Firm assesses leased assets for 
impairment, and if the carrying amount of the leased asset 
exceeds the undiscounted cash flows from the lease 
payments and the estimated residual value upon disposition 
of the leased asset, an impairment loss is recognized.  
The risk of loss on auto and equipment leased assets 
relating to the residual value of the leased assets is 
monitored through projections of the asset residual values 
at lease origination and periodic review of residual values, 
and is mitigated through arrangements with certain 
manufacturers or lessees.

start_phrase:
Basic earnings per share (“EPS”) is calculated using the

summary:
- Focus: Note 23 explains JPMorgan Chase’s earnings per share (EPS) methodology and results for 2022, 2021, and 2020.
- Basic EPS method: Uses the two-class method, allocating all earnings (distributed and undistributed) between common stock and participating securities.
- Participating securities: Unvested RSUs that receive nonforfeitable dividends during vesting; treated as a separate class for basic EPS and not included as incremental shares in diluted EPS.
- Diluted EPS method: Reflects contingently issuable shares (e.g., awards requiring future service). Calculated under both the two-class and treasury stock methods; the more dilutive result is reported. For all periods shown, the two-class method was more dilutive.
- 2022 results:

text:
Earnings per share
Basic earnings per share (“EPS”) is calculated using the 
two-class method. Under the two-class method, all earnings 
(distributed and undistributed) are allocated to common 
stock and participating securities. JPMorgan Chase  grants 
RSUs under its share-based compensation programs, 
predominantly all of which entitle recipients to receive 
nonforfeitable dividends during the vesting period on a 
basis equivalent to dividends paid to holders of the Firm’s 
common stock. These unvested RSUs meet the definition of 
participating securities based on their respective rights to 
receive nonforfeitable dividends, and they are treated as a 
separate class of securities in computing basic EPS. 
Participating securities are not included as incremental 
shares in computing diluted EPS; refer to Note 9 for 
additional information.
Diluted EPS incorporates the potential impact of 
contingently issuable shares, including awards which 
require future service as a condition of delivery of the 
underlying common stock. Diluted EPS is calculated under 
both the two-class and treasury stock methods, and the 
more dilutive amount is reported. For each of the periods 
presented in the table below, diluted EPS calculated under 
the two-class method was more dilutive.

text:
Income taxes  
JPMorgan Chase  and its eligible subsidiaries file a 
consolidated U.S. federal income tax return. JPMorgan 
Chase uses the asset and liability method to provi de for 
income taxes on all transactions recorded in the 
Consolidated Financial Statements. This method requires 
that income taxes reflect the expected future tax 
consequences of temporary differences between the 
carrying amounts of assets or liabilities for book and tax 
purposes. Accordingly, a deferred tax asset or liability for 
each temporary difference is determined based on the tax 
rates that the Firm expects to be in effect when the 
underlying items of income and expense are realized. 
JPMorgan Chase’s expense for income taxes includes the 
current and deferred portions of that expense. A valuation 
allowance is established to reduce deferred tax assets to 
the amount the Firm expects to realize.
Due to the inherent complexities arising from the nature of  
the Firm’s businesses, and from conducting business and 
being taxed in a substantial number of jurisdictions, 
significant judgments and estimates are required to be 
made. Agreement of tax liabilities between  JPMorgan Chase 
and the many tax jurisdictions in which  the Firm files tax 
returns may not be finalized for several years. Thus,  the 
Firm’s final tax-related assets and liabilities may ultimately 
be different from those currently reported.

Significant exams include: U.S. (2011–2013, amended returns; 2014–2018, original and amended returns), New York State (2012–2014), New York City (2015–2017), and U.K. (2011–2020), all in field examination stages.

title: Intercompany funds transfers
heading: 8.33.2 Intercompany funds transfers
start_phrase:
Restrictions imposed by U.S. federal law prohibit JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, N.A., and its subsidiaries, from lending to 
JPMorgan Chase & Co. (“Parent Company”) and certain of 
its affiliates unless the loans are secured in specified 
amounts.
summary:
- Scope: Note 26 covers restricted cash, other restricted assets, and intercompany funds transfers; Note 27 outlines regulatory capital requirements for JPMorgan Chase & Co. and key subsidiaries.

- Restricted cash and other restricted assets:
  - Certain Firm assets are restricted by U.S. and non-U.S. regulators (including OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC) due to the activities of subsidiaries, reserve requirements at certain non-U.S. central banks, and broker-dealer rules.
  - Restricted cash totaled $26.8B at Dec 31, 2022 ($19.7B in 2021), comprising:
    - Segregated for the benefit of securities and cleared derivative customers: $18.7B (2021: $14.6B).
    - Cash reserves at non-U.S. central banks/other purposes: $8.1B (2021: $5.1B).
    - Largely held as deposits with banks ($25.4B in 2022; $18.4B in 2021) and cash/due from banks ($1.4B; $1.3B).
  - Other restricted assets:
    - Cash and securities pledged with clearing organizations for customers: $42.4B (2021: $47.5B).
    - Securities restricted for customer activity: $31.7B (2021: $30.0B).

- Intercompany funds transfers and dividend restrictions:
  - U.S. law restricts lending by JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and its subsidiaries to the Parent Company and affiliates; “covered transactions” must be secured and on safe and sound terms, generally limited to 10% of a bank subsidiary’s total capital per affiliate (20% in aggregate), unless collateralized with cash or U.S. government obligations.
  - Corporate structure: Key subsidiaries are JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and JPMorgan Chase Holdings LLC (IHC). The IHC holds most non-bank subsidiaries, owns other assets, provides intercompany loans to the Parent, and receives substantially all net proceeds from Parent securities issuances.
  - Parent’s main funding/income sources: dividends from the Bank and dividends/credit from the IHC.
  - Regulators (Federal Reserve, OCC, FDIC) can limit or prohibit dividends if deemed unsafe or unsound. The IHC is barred from paying dividends or extending credit to the Parent if capital/liquidity thresholds are breached or if otherwise limited by management/Board.
  - As of Jan 1, 2023, banking subsidiaries could pay about $34B in aggregate dividends to their bank holding companies without prior regulatory approval, with capacity supplemented by 2023 earnings.

- Regulatory capital (Note 27):
  - The Federal Reserve sets capital requirements for the consolidated holding company; the OCC sets similar requirements for the principal insured depository institution (IDI), JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.
  - Under Basel III, capital adequacy is assessed under two approaches—Standardized and Advanced—with binding requirements based on the lower of the two.
  - Minimum risk-based capital requirements include CET1, Tier 1, and Total capital, incorporating:
    - For the consolidated BHC: minimums plus a GSIB surcharge of 3.5% and a Stress Capital Buffer (SCB) of 4.0% for Standardized ratios (vs. a fixed 2.5% conservation buffer for Advanced). In 2021, the SCB was 3.2% (implying lower 2021 requirements).
    - For IDIs: a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer; no GSIB surcharge.
  - As of Dec 31, 2022:
    - Standardized BHC requirements: CET1 12.0%, Tier 1 13.5%, Total 15.5; IDI: 7.0%, 8.5%, 10.5, respectively.
    - Advanced BHC requirements: CET1 10.5%, Tier 1 12.0%, Total 14.0; IDI: 7.0%, 8.5%, 10.5.
    - Well-capitalized thresholds (apply to IDIs): CET1 6.5%, Tier 1 8.0%, Total 10.0%.
  - Leverage-based requirements:
    - Tier 1 leverage minimum: 4.0% (BHC and IDI); well-capitalized IDI: 5.0% (no BHC well-cap threshold).
    - Supplementary leverage ratio (SLR) minimums: 5.0% for BHCs and 6.0% for IDIs (3.0% base plus buffers of 2.0% BHC/3.0% IDI); no BHC well-cap threshold.
text:
Intercompany funds transfers 
Restrictions imposed by U.S. federal law prohibit  JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, N.A., and its subsidiaries, from lending to 
JPMorgan Chase  & Co. (“Parent Company”) and certain of 
its affiliates  unless the loans are secured in specified 
amounts. Such secured loans  provided by any banking 
subsidiary to the Parent Company or to any particular 
affiliate, together with certain other transactions with such 
affiliate (collectively referred to as “covered transactions”), 
must be made on terms and conditions that are consistent 
with safe and sound banking practices. In addition, unless 
collateralized with cash or US Government debt obligations, 
covered transactions are generally limited to  10%  of the 
banking subsidiary’s total capital, as determined by the risk-
based capital guidelines; the aggregate amount of covered 
transactions between  any banking subsidiary and all of its 
affiliates is limited to 20%  of the banking subsidiary’s total 
capital.
The Parent Company’s two principal subsidiaries are 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and JPMorgan Chase Holdings 
LLC, an intermediate holding company (the “IHC”). The IHC 
generally holds the stock of JPMorgan Chase’s subsidiaries 
other than JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and its subsidiaries. 
The IHC also owns other assets and provides intercompany 
loans to the Parent Company. The Parent Company is 
obligated to contribute to the IHC substantially all the net 
proceeds received from securities issuances (including 
issuances of senior and subordinated debt securities and of 
preferred and common stock).
The principal sources of income and funding for the Parent 
Company are dividends from JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. 
and dividends and extensions of credit from the IHC. In 
addition to dividend restrictions set forth in statutes and 
regulations,  the Federal Reserve, the OCC and the FDIC have 
authority under the Financial Institutions Supervisory Act to 
prohibit or to limit the payment of dividends by the banking 
organizations they supervise, including  the Parent Company 
and its subsidiaries that are banks or bank holding 
companies, if, in the banking regulator’s opinion, payment 
of a dividend would constitute an unsafe or unsound 
practice in light of the financial condition of the banking 
organization.  The IHC is prohibited from paying dividends or 
extending credit to the Parent Company if certain capital or 
liquidity “thresholds” are breached or if limits are otherwise 
imposed by the Parent Company’s management or Board of 
Directors.
At J a n u a r y  1 ,  2 0 2 3 ,  t h e  P a r e n t  C o m p a n y ’ s  b a n k i n g  
subsidiaries could pay, in the aggregate, approximately  $34 
billion  in dividends to  their respective bank holding 
companies without the prior approval of  their relevant 
banking regulators. The capacity to pay dividends in  2023  
will be supplemented by  the banking subsidiaries’ earnings 
during the year.

title: Regulatory capital - Introduction
heading: 8.34 Note 27 – Regulatory capital
start_phrase:
The Federal Reserve establishes capital requirements, 
including well-capitalized requirements, for the 
consolidated financial holding company.
summary: Overview of JPMorgan Chase’s regulatory capital framework and requirements: The Federal Reserve sets consolidated holding company capital rules and the OCC sets similar minimums for the Firm’s principal IDI, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., under Basel III. Risk-weighted assets are calculated under two approaches—Basel III Standardized and Basel III Advanced—and capital adequacy is measured against the lower of the two. Required metrics include CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, Tier 1 leverage, and the Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR); failure to meet minimums may prompt Federal Reserve action. As of Dec 31, 2022, BHC risk-based requirements were CET1/Tier 1/Total of 12.0%/13.5%/15.5% (Standardized) and 10.5%/12.0%/14.0% (Advanced); IDI requirements were 7.0%/8.5%/10.5% under both. Well-capitalized thresholds were CET1 NA/6.5% (BHC/IDI), Tier 1 6.0%/8.0%, and Total 10.0%/10.0%. BHC ratios include minimums plus a 3.5% GSIB surcharge (Method 2) and either a 4.0% SCB (Standardized) or 2.5% capital conservation buffer (Advanced); the countercyclical buffer was 0%. For 2021, BHC Standardized requirements were 11.2%/12.7%/14.7% with a 3.2% SCB. IDIs include a fixed 2.5% conservation buffer and are not subject to the GSIB surcharge. Leverage-based requirements were Tier 1 leverage 4.0% (BHC/IDI) and SLR 5.0% (BHC)/6.0% (IDI); IDI well-capitalized thresholds were 5.0% Tier 1 leverage and 6.0% SLR; the SLR includes a 3.0% minimum plus buffers of 2.0% (BHC) and 3.0% (IDI), and the Federal Reserve does not set well-capitalized leverage thresholds for BHCs.
text:
Regulatory capital
The Federal Reserve establishes capital requirements, 
including well-capitalized requirements, for the 
consolidated financial holding company. The  Office of the 
Comptroller of the Currency (“OCC”) establishes similar 
minimum capital requirements and standards for the Firm’s 
principal IDI subsidiary, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. 
The capital rules under Basel III establish minimum capital 
ratios and overall capital adequacy standards for  large and 
internationally active U.S. bank holding companies and 
banks , including the Firm and its IDI subsidiaries, including 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. Two comprehensive approaches 
are prescribed for calculating  RWA: a standardized 
approach (“Basel III Standardized”), and an advanced 
approach (“Basel III Advanced”).  For each of the risk-based 
capital ratios, the capital adequacy of the Firm and 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A.  is evaluated against the lower of 
the Standardized or Advanced approaches compared to 
their respective regulatory capital ratio requirements.    
The three components of regulatory capital under the Basel 
III rules are as illustrated below:
Under the risk-based capital and leverage-based guidelines 
of the Federal Reserve, JPMorgan Chase is required to 
maintain minimum ratios  for CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital, 
Total capital, Tier 1 leverage and the SLR . Failure to meet

Reserve to take action. IDI subsidiaries are also subject to

title: CECL regulatory capital transition
heading: 8.34.1 CECL regulatory capital transition
start_phrase:
Until December 31, 2021, the Firm’s capital reflected a two 
year delay of the effects of CECL provided by the Federal 
Reserve Board in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
summary:
- Describes JPMorgan Chase’s CECL regulatory capital transition: a COVID-related two-year delay ended Dec 31, 2021; beginning Jan 1, 2022, the $2.9 billion CECL capital benefit is being phased out 25% per year over three years, with $2.2 billion remaining in CET1 at Dec 31, 2022. A parallel 25% phase-out in 2022 also applies to other CECL transition items affecting Tier 2 capital, adjusted average assets, total leverage exposure, and RWA.
- Presents risk-based capital metrics under Basel III Standardized and Advanced approaches, and leverage-based metrics, for both JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., as of Dec 31, 2022 and 2021. All reported metrics reflect CECL transition provisions.
- Confirms both the parent company and the bank subsidiary were well-capitalized and met all applicable capital requirements at year-end 2022 and 2021.
- Key figures at Dec 31, 2022:
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co. (Standardized): CET1 capital $218.9B; RWA $1,653.5B; CET1 ratio 13.2%; Tier 1 ratio 14.9%; Total capital ratio 16.8%.
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co. (Advanced): RWA $1,609.8B; CET1 ratio 13.6%; Tier 1 ratio 15.3%; Total capital ratio 16.4%.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (Standardized): CET1 capital $269.7B; RWA $1,597.1B; CET1 ratio 16.9%; Tier 1 ratio 16.9%; Total capital ratio 18.1%.
  - JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (Advanced): RWA $1,475.6B; CET1 ratio 18.3%; Tier 1 ratio 18.3%; Total capital ratio 18.7%.
- Year-over-year highlights (2022 vs. 2021):
  - Parent CET1 ratios were stable-to-slightly mixed (Standardized 13.2% vs 13.1%; Advanced 13.6% vs 13.8%).
  - Bank CET1 ratios remained strong but eased on the Advanced basis (18.3% vs 19.2%), flat on Standardized (16.9%).
  - RWA increased for both entities on both approaches.
- Leverage metrics (3-month average at quarter-end):
  - JPMorgan Chase & Co.: Adjusted average assets $3.70T (vs $3.78T); Tier 1 leverage ratio 6.6% (vs 6.5%); SLR 5.6% (vs 5.4%); total leverage exposure $4.37T (vs $4.57T).

- Notes that additional CECL accounting guidance is in Note 1.
