summary: Introduces JPMorgan Chase’s off–balance sheet lending-related financial instruments and guarantees, explaining that contractual amounts reflect maximum possible credit risk but typically overstate expected exposure due to refinancing, extension, cancellation, or expiry; the Firm maintains an allowance for credit losses and can reduce/cancel consumer lines (e.g., close credit cards at 60+ days past due; reduce/close HELOCs on property value or credit declines). Provides a maturity-by-type table of contractual amounts and carrying values at December 31, 2022 and 2021: total lending-related $1.327 trillion (carrying value $2.817 billion) vs $1.262 trillion ($2.624 billion); consumer $854.8 billion including $821.3 billion credit card (includes commercial card), and wholesale $472.0 billion comprising $440.4 billion other unfunded credit, $27.4 billion standby letters of credit/financial guarantees, and $4.1 billion other LCs. Other guarantees/commitments include $283.4 billion securities lending indemnification (with $298.5 billion collateral held), $59.2 billion derivatives qualifying as guarantees, $117.0 billion unsettled resale/securities borrowed, $66.4 billion unsettled repo/securities loaned, $191.1 billion exchange and clearing house guarantees, and $820 million loans sold with recourse. Amounts are presented net of risk participations; consumer and wholesale commitments are predominantly U.S.; carrying values represent the allowance/guarantee liability or fair value, and 2022 wholesale carrying values include net markdowns on held-for-sale positions related to unfunded bridge financing commitments.
text:
Note 28 – Off–balance sheet lending-related 
financial instruments, guarantees, and 
other commitments
JPMorgan Chase  provides lending-related financial 
instruments (e.g., commitments and guarantees) to address 
the financing needs of its customers and clients. The 
contractual amount of these financial instruments 
represents the maximum possible credit risk to  the Firm 
should the customer or client draw upon the commitment 
or the Firm be required to fulfill its obligation under the 
guarantee, and should the customer or client subsequently 
fail to perform according to the terms of the contract. Most 
of these commitments and guarantees have historically 
been refinanced, extended, cancelled, or expired without 
being drawn or a default occurring. As a result, the total 
contractual amount of these instruments is not, in  the 
Firm’s view, representative of its expected future credit 
exposure or funding requirements.  To provide for expected credit losses in wholesale and 
certain consumer lending-related commitments, an 
allowance for credit losses on lending-related commitments 
is maintained.  Refer to Note  13 for further information 
regarding the allowance for credit losses on lending-related 
commitments . The following table summarizes the 
contractual amounts and carrying values of off-balance 
sheet lending-related financial instruments, guarantees and 
other commitments at  D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2 and 2021 . The 
amounts in the table below for credit card and home equity 
lending-related commitments represent the total available 
credit for these products.  The Firm has not experienced, 
and does not anticipate, that all available lines of credit for 
these products will be utilized at the same time.  The Firm 
can reduce or cancel credit card lines of credit by providing 
the borrower notice or, in some cases as permitted by law, 
without notice.  In addition,  the Firm typically closes credit 
card lines when the borrower is  60 days  or more past due.  
The Firm may reduce or close HELOCs when there are 
significant decreases in the value of the underlying 
property, or when there has been a demonstrable decline in 
the creditworthiness of the borrower.  Notes to consolidated financial statements

title: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
heading: 8.35.1 Other unfunded commitments to extend credit
start_phrase: Other unfunded commitments to extend credit generally consist of commitments for working capital and general corporate purposes, extensions of credit to support commercial paper facilities and bond financings in the event that those obligations cannot be remarketed to new investors, as well as committed liquidity facilities to clearing organizations.

title: Guarantees - Introduction
heading: 8.35.2 Guarantees
start_phrase: U.S. GAAP requires that a guarantor recognize, at the inception of a guarantee, a liability in an amount equal to the fair value of the obligation undertaken in issuing the guarantee.
summary: Overview of the Firm’s U.S. GAAP accounting for guarantees: at inception, the Firm recognizes a liability at the fair value of the non‑contingent obligation (e.g., consideration received or NPV of premiums), recorded in other liabilities with offsetting cash or other assets; this amount is amortized into income as lending and deposit‑related fees over the contract life. Guarantees include standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees, securities lending indemnifications, certain indemnifications in third‑party contracts, certain derivative contracts, and guarantees under the sponsored member repo program. Lending‑related contingent obligations are recognized separately based on expected credit losses, while non‑lending contingent obligations are recognized when probable and reasonably estimable, and not if below the carrying amount of the inception liability (adjusted for amortization); indemnifications in sales agreements are cited as an example, with initial liabilities amortized as risk declines. The contractual amounts and carrying values of guarantees and indemnifications are presented in a table on page 277.
text:
Guarantees  
U.S. GAAP requires that a guarantor recognize, at the 
inception of a guarantee, a liability in an amount equal to 
the fair value of the obligation undertaken in issuing the 
guarantee. U.S. GAAP defines a guarantee as a contract that 
contingently requires the guarantor to pay a guaranteed 
party based upon: (a) changes in an underlying asset, 
liability or equity security of the guaranteed party; or (b) a 
third party’s failure to perform under a specified 
agreement.  The Firm considers the following off–balance 
sheet arrangements to be guarantees under U.S. GAAP: 
standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees, 
securities lending indemnifications, certain indemnification 
agreements included within third-party contractual 
arrangements, certain derivative contracts and the 
guarantees under the sponsored member repo program.  
As required by U.S. GAAP,  the Firm initially records 
guarantees at the inception date fair value of the non-
contingent obligation assumed (e.g., the amount of 
consideration received or the net present value of the 
premium receivable). For these obligations, the Firm 
records this fair value amount in other liabilities with an 
offsetting entry recorded in cash (for premiums received), or other assets (for premiums receivable). Any premium 
receivable recorded in other assets is reduced as cash is 
received under the contract, and the fair value of the 
liability recorded at inception is amortized into income as 
lending and deposit-related fees over the life of the 
guarantee contract. The lending-related contingent 
obligation is recognized based on expected credit losses in 
addition to, and separate from, any non-contingent 
obligation.
Non-lending-related contingent obligations are recognized 
when the liability becomes probable and reasonably 
estimable. These obligations are not recognized if the 
estimated amount is less than the carrying amount of any 
non-contingent liability recognized at inception (adjusted 
for any amortization). Examples of non-lending-related 
contingent obligations include indemnifications provided in 
sales agreements, where a portion of the sale proceeds is 
allocated to the guarantee, which adjusts the gain or loss 
that would otherwise result from the transaction. For these 
indemnifications, the initial liability is amortized to income 
as the Firm’s  risk is reduced (i.e., over time or when the 
indemnification expires).
The contractual amount and carrying value of guarantees 
and indemnifications are included in the table on page 277 .
For additional information on the guarantees, see below.

title: Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees
heading: 8.35.2.1 Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees
start_phrase: Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees are conditional lending commitments issued by the Firm to guarantee the performance of a client or customer to a third party under certain arrangements, such as commercial paper facilities, bond financings, acquisition financings, trade financings and similar transactions.
summary:
- Scope: Discusses other unfunded commitments to extend credit and the Firm’s guarantees under U.S. GAAP, including their nature, recognition, measurement, and presentation.

- Other unfunded commitments: Primarily cover working capital and general corporate purposes, backstops for commercial paper and bond remarketing failures, committed liquidity facilities to clearing organizations, and multipurpose facilities (which may be drawn as standby letters of credit).

- Guarantees under U.S. GAAP:
  - Definition: Contracts requiring payment based on changes in another party’s asset/liability/equity or a third party’s failure to perform.
  - Firm’s guarantee types: Standby letters of credit and other financial guarantees, securities lending indemnifications, certain third‑party indemnifications, certain derivatives, and guarantees under the sponsored member repo program.

- Accounting and recognition:
  - Initial measurement: Recognize at inception the fair value of the non‑contingent obligation (recorded in other liabilities; offset to cash for premiums received or to other assets for premiums receivable). Premium receivables are reduced as cash is received.
  - Income recognition: The initial guarantee liability is amortized to income as lending and deposit‑related fees over the contract life.
  - Lending-related contingent obligations: Recognized separately based on expected credit losses in addition to the non‑contingent amount.
  - Non‑lending-related contingent obligations: Recognized when probable and reasonably estimable; not recognized if less than the remaining non‑contingent liability. Indemnifications in sales agreements are allocated a portion of proceeds and amortized as risk declines.

  - Guarantee liability: $326M in 2022 vs $353M in 2021 (none for other LCs).
  - Total carrying value: $408M (standby/other financial guarantees) and $6M (other LCs) in 2022; $476M and $9M in 2021.
  - Commitments with collateral: $15.3B (standby/other financial guarantees) and $0.8B (other LCs) in 2022; $14.5B and $1.0B in 2021.
  - Credit quality disclosure is based on the Firm’s internal risk ratings.

title: Securities lending indemnifications
heading: 8.35.3 Securities lending indemnifications
start_phrase: Through the Firm’s securities lending program, counterparties’ securities, via custodial and non-custodial arrangements, may be lent to third parties.
summary:
- Securities lending indemnifications: The Firm lends client/counterparty securities to third parties and indemnifies lenders against borrower failure to return securities. To mitigate risk, it requires cash or highly liquid collateral exceeding 100% of securities on loan, marks collateral to market daily, and adjusts for shortfalls/overcollateralization. Upon borrower default, collateral is used to replace securities or credit cash equivalent. Cash collateral may be invested in indemnified resale agreements, also over-collateralized above 100%.

- Derivatives qualifying as guarantees: Includes written put options (typically ≤5 years) and stable value contracts that protect against declines in market value below book value (longer term or no stated maturity, with termination rights for the Firm). Notional amounts generally represent maximum exposure, though stable value exposure is contractually capped at a lower percentage of notional. Fair value reflects the Firm’s assessed probability of performance; exposures are reduced via offsetting or hedging.
  - Key amounts (in millions):
    - Notional derivative guarantees: $59,180 (2022) vs. $55,730 (2021)
    - Stable value contracts notional (with limited exposure): $31,820 (2022) vs. $29,778 (2021)
    - Maximum exposure on stable value contracts: $2,063 (2022) vs. $2,882 (2021)
    - Derivative payables (fair value): $649 (2022) vs. $475 (2021)
  - The Firm also buys and sells credit protection via credit derivatives (see Note 5).

- Unsettled securities financing agreements: The Firm enters into resale/securities borrowed (advance cash, receive securities) and repurchase/securities loaned (receive cash, provide securities) agreements that settle in the future. These generally are not derivatives and are not recorded on the balance sheet until settlement; most have regular-way settlement (see Note 11).

- Loan sales and securitization-related indemnifications:
  - Mortgage repurchase liability: For loans sold or securitized with U.S. GSEs, the Firm provides representations and warranties and may have to repurchase or indemnify if breached.
  - Private-label securitizations: Repurchase demands are evaluated within litigation reserves (see Note 30).

- Loans sold with recourse: The Firm services mortgages and certain commercial loans on both recourse and nonrecourse bases. In nonrecourse servicing, primary risk is temporary servicing advances; in recourse servicing, the Firm shares credit risk with the loan owner (e.g., Fannie Mae).
text:
Securities lending indemnifications  
Through  the Firm’s securities lending program, 
counterparties’ securities, via custodial and non-custodial 
arrangements, may be lent to third parties. As part of this 
program,  the Firm provides an indemnification in the 
lending agreements which protects the lender against the 
failure of the borrower to return the lent securities. To 
minimize its liability under these indemnification 
agreements,  the Firm obtains cash or other highly liquid 
collateral with a market value exceeding  100%  of the value 
of the securities on loan from the borrower. Collateral is 
marked to market daily to help assure that collateralization 
is adequate. Additional collateral is called from the 
borrower if a shortfall exists, or collateral may be released 
to the borrower in the event of overcollateralization. If a 
borrower defaults,  the Firm would use the collateral held to 
purchase replacement securities in the market or to credit 
the lending client or counterparty with the cash equivalent 
thereof.  
The cash collateral held by  the Firm may be invested on 
behalf of the client in indemnified resale agreements, 
whereby  the Firm indemnifies the client against the loss of 
principal invested. To minimize its liability under these 
agreements,  the Firm obtains collateral with a market value 
exceeding  100%  of the principal invested.

title: Derivatives qualifying as guarantees
heading: 8.35.4 Derivatives qualifying as guarantees
start_phrase: The Firm transacts in certain derivative contracts that have the characteristics of a guarantee under U.S. GAAP.
summary:
- Securities lending indemnifications: The Firm lends client and counterparty securities and indemnifies lenders against borrower failures to return securities. It requires cash or highly liquid collateral exceeding 100% of loaned securities’ value, marks collateral to market daily, and adjusts collateral for shortfalls/overages. Upon borrower default, collateral is used to replace securities or credit cash equivalent. Cash collateral may be invested in indemnified resale agreements, also overcollateralized above 100%.

- Derivatives qualifying as guarantees: Includes written put options (typically ≤5 years) and stable value contracts that protect against declines in a reference portfolio’s market value below book value. Notional generally equals maximum exposure, though stable value exposure is contractually limited to a fraction of notional. Fair value reflects the Firm’s assessed probability of performance; risks are mitigated via offsets and hedges. As of Dec 31, 2022 vs. 2021: derivative guarantees notional $59.2B vs. $55.7B; stable value notional $31.8B vs. $29.8B; maximum exposure on limited stable value $2.1B vs. $2.9B; derivative payables fair value $649M vs. $475M. The Firm also buys and sells credit protection (see Note 5).

- Unsettled securities financing agreements: Describes resale/securities borrowed (cash advanced, securities received) and repurchase/securities loaned (cash received, securities provided). These settle in the future, generally are not derivatives, and are recognized on the balance sheet at settlement; predominantly regular-way (see Note 11).

- Loan sales and securitization indemnifications: For mortgage loan sales/securitizations with U.S. GSEs, the Firm provides representations and warranties that may require repurchase or indemnification if breached. Repurchase demands tied to private-label securitizations are evaluated within litigation reserves (see Note 30).

- Loans sold with recourse: The Firm services mortgages and certain commercial loans on both recourse and nonrecourse bases. Nonrecourse risk centers on temporary servicing advances; in recourse servicing, the Firm shares credit risk with the loan owner (e.g., Fannie Mae).
text:
Derivatives qualifying as guarantees  
The Firm transacts in certain derivative contracts that have 
the characteristics of a guarantee under U.S. GAAP. These 
contracts include written put options that require  the Firm 
to purchase assets upon exercise by the option holder at a 
specified price by a specified date in the future.  The Firm 
may enter into written put option contracts in order to meet 
client needs, or for other trading purposes. The terms of 
written put options are typically  five years  or less. 
Derivatives deemed to be guarantees also includes stable 
value contracts, commonly referred to as “stable value 
products”, that require  the Firm to make a payment of the 
difference between the market value and the book value of 
a counterparty’s reference portfolio of assets in the event 
that market value is less than book value and certain other 
conditions have been met. Stable value products are 
transacted in order to allow investors to realize investment 
returns with less volatility than an unprotected portfolio. 
These contracts are typically longer-term or may have no 
stated maturity, but allow  the Firm to elect to terminate the 
contract under certain conditions.  
The notional value of derivative guarantees generally 
represents  the Firm’s maximum exposure. However, 
exposure to certain stable value products is contractually 
limited to a substantially lower percentage of the notional 
amount.  
The fair value of derivative guarantees reflects the 
probability, in  the Firm’s view, of whether  the Firm will be 
required to perform under the contract.  The Firm reduces 
exposures to these contracts by entering into offsetting 
transactions, or by entering into contracts that hedge the 
market risk related to the derivative guarantees.  The following table summarizes the derivatives qualifying

text:
Unsettled securities financing agreements  
In the normal course of business,  the Firm enters into resale 
and securities borrowed agreements. At settlement, these 
commitments result in  the Firm advancing cash to and 
receiving securities collateral from the counterparty.  The 
Firm also enters into repurchase and securities loaned 
agreements. At settlement, these commitments result in  the 
Firm receiving cash from and providing securities collateral 
to the counterparty. Such agreements settle at a future 
date. These agreements generally do not meet the 
definition of a derivative, and therefore, are not recorded 
on the Consolidated balance sheets until settlement date. 
These agreements predominantly have regular-way 
settlement terms. Refer to Note  11 for a further discussion 
of securities financing agreements.

title: Loans sold with recourse
heading: 8.35.6.3 Loans sold with recourse
start_phrase: The Firm provides servicing for mortgages and certain commercial lending products on both a recourse and nonrecourse basis.
summary:
- Overview of indemnification and guarantee exposures across several business activities, risk mitigants (primarily collateralization), accounting presentation, and quantitative disclosures as of December 31, 2022 and 2021.
- Securities lending indemnifications:
  - The firm indemnifies lenders against borrower failure to return securities under custodial and non-custodial programs.
  - Collateral (cash or highly liquid) exceeds 100% of loaned securities and is marked to market daily; collateral is adjusted for shortfalls/overcollateralization.
  - Upon borrower default, collateral is used to purchase replacement securities or credit cash equivalent.
  - Cash collateral may be invested in indemnified resale agreements; these are overcollateralized above 100%.
- Derivatives qualifying as guarantees:
  - Includes written put options (typically ≤5 years) and stable value contracts that protect portfolio book value versus market value.
  - Notional generally represents maximum exposure; for certain stable value products, exposure is contractually limited to a smaller percentage of notional.
  - Fair value reflects probability of performance; exposures are reduced via offsets/hedges.
  - Quantitative data (in millions):
    - Notional: derivative guarantees $59,180 (2022) vs $55,730 (2021); stable value contracts with limited exposure $31,820 (2022) vs $29,778 (2021).
    - Maximum exposure for limited stable value contracts: $2,063 (2022) vs $2,882 (2021).
    - Fair value derivative payables: $649 (2022) vs $475 (2021).
  - Notes that the firm also buys/sells credit protection (see Note 5).
- Unsettled securities financing agreements:
  - Resale/securities borrowed and repurchase/securities loaned commitments that settle in the future are off-balance sheet until settlement and generally have regular-way terms (see Note 11).
- Loan sales and securitization-related indemnifications:
  - Mortgage repurchase liabilities tied to reps and warranties on loans sold to U.S. GSEs.
  - Private-label securitization repurchase demands are evaluated within litigation reserves (see Note 30).
  - Loans serviced with and without recourse: recourse servicing shares credit risk; losses occur when foreclosure proceeds are insufficient.
  - Securitizations are predominantly nonrecourse; UPB of loans sold with recourse and related liability disclosed elsewhere.
- Other off-balance sheet arrangements:
  - General indemnities including tax gross-up for securities issued outside the U.S., software license indemnities, and sale-of-business indemnities; maximum exposure difficult to estimate; loss risk considered remote.
- Merchant charge-backs:
  - As a merchant acquirer, the firm has contingent liabilities for disputed card transactions; mitigants include withholding settlements, reserves, and collateral; a valuation allowance is recognized.
  - Processed volumes: $2,158.4B (2022), $1,886.7B (2021), $1,597.3B (2020).
- Clearing services – client credit risk:
  - As a clearing member with CCPs for ETDs and OTC-cleared derivatives, the firm stands behind client performance, collects/remits initial and variation margin.
  - Exposure arises from client nonperformance; mitigated via margining and the ability to cease clearing; in default, positions are closed out and margin accessed.
  - Reflected on balance sheet as margin receivables from clients and payables to CCPs; client contracts themselves are not recorded.
  - Maximum exposure is difficult to estimate; based on experience and mitigants, risk of material loss is expected to be remote (see Note 5 for the firm’s own derivatives).
text:
Loans sold with recourse  
The Firm provides servicing for mortgages and certain 
commercial lending products on both a recourse and 
nonrecourse basis. In nonrecourse servicing, the principal 
credit risk to  the Firm is the cost of temporary servicing 
advances of funds (i.e., normal servicing advances). In 
recourse servicing, the servicer agrees to share credit risk 
with the owner of the mortgage loans, such as Fannie Mae 
JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K 279or Freddie Mac or a private investor, insurer or guarantor. 
Losses on recourse servicing predominantly occur when 
foreclosure sales proceeds of the property underlying a 
defaulted loan are less than the sum of the outstanding 
principal balance, plus accrued interest on the loan and the 
cost of holding and disposing of the underlying property.  
The Firm’s securitizations are predominantly nonrecourse, 
thereby effectively transferring the risk of future credit 
losses to the purchaser of the mortgage-backed securities 
issued by the trust. The unpaid principal balance of loans 
sold with recourse  as well as  the carrying value of the

title: Indemnification agreements – general
heading: 8.35.7 Indemnification agreements – general

- Explains when losses arise on recourse mortgage servicing (foreclosure proceeds below loan principal, accrued interest, and property disposition costs) and notes that the firm’s securitizations are predominantly nonrecourse, transferring credit risk to MBS investors. Maximum exposure is hard to estimate; management deems loss risk remote.
  - Merchant charge-backs: as a merchant acquirer, the firm retains contingent liability for disputed card transactions; outlines charge-back mechanics, risk mitigants (withholding settlements, reserves, collateral), and a valuation allowance. Reports processed volumes of $2,158.4B (2022), $1,886.7B (2021), and $1,597.3B (2020).
  - Clearing services client credit risk: as a clearing member for clients’ exchange-traded and OTC-cleared derivatives, the firm collects initial and variation margin and faces client nonperformance risk (but not CCP performance risk). On default, positions are closed and margin accessed; any CCP shortfall may fall to the firm as clearing member. text:
Indemnification agreements – general  
In connection with issuing securities to investors outside the 
U.S.,  the Firm may agree to pay additional amounts to the 
holders of the securities in the event that, due to a change 
in tax law, certain types of withholding taxes are imposed 
on payments on the securities. The terms of the securities 
may also give the Firm the right to redeem the securities if 
such additional amounts are payable. The Firm may also 
enter into indemnification clauses in connection with the 
licensing of software to cl ients (“software licensees”) or 
when it sells a business or assets to a third party (“third-
party purchasers”), pursuant to which it indemnifies 
software licensees for claims of liability or damages that 
may occur subsequent to the licensing of the software, or 
third-party purchasers for losses they may incur due to 
actions taken by  the Firm prior to the sale of the business or 
assets. It is difficult to estimate  the Firm’s maximum 
exposure under these indemnification arrangements, since 
this would require an assessment of future changes in tax 
law and future claims that may be made against  the Firm 
that have not yet occurred. However, based on historical 
experience, management expects the risk of loss to be 
remote.

title: Merchant charge-backs
heading: 8.35.8 Merchant charge-backs
start_phrase: Under the rules of payment networks, in its role as a merchant acquirer, the Firm’s Merchant Services business in CIB Payments , retains a contingent liability for disputed processed credit and debit card transactions that result in a charge-back to the merchant.
summary:
- Explains how losses arise on recourse mortgage servicing when foreclosure proceeds are insufficient, noting the firm’s securitizations are predominantly nonrecourse, transferring future credit loss risk to investors; amounts of loans sold with recourse and related recorded liabilities are disclosed elsewhere (page 277).
- Describes off-balance sheet indemnification arrangements, including: tax gross-up provisions for securities issued outside the U.S. (with possible redemption rights), indemnities to software licensees, and indemnities to buyers in business or asset sales; maximum exposure is difficult to estimate, but management deems loss risk remote.
- Details merchant charge-back exposure in the Merchant Services business: the firm’s contingent liability when disputes are resolved in cardholders’ favor, risk mitigants (withholding settlements, reserves, collateral), and recognition of a valuation allowance; reports processed volumes of $2,158.4B (2022), $1,886.7B (2021), and $1,597.3B (2020).
- Outlines clearing services client credit risk as a CCP clearing member for exchange-traded and OTC-cleared derivatives: collection of initial and variation margin, exposure to client nonperformance (not CCP performance), mitigation via margining and service termination, default procedures (close-out and margin use), and potential obligation to cover shortfalls; recognizes margin receivables/payables rather than clients’ underlying positions; maximum exposure is not readily estimable, with risk of loss viewed as remote.
- Notes cross-reference to Note 5 for the firm’s own derivatives accounted for on the consolidated financial statements.
text:
Merchant charge-backs   
Under the rules of payment networks, in its role as a 
merchant acquirer, the Firm’s Merchant Services business 
in CIB Payments , retains a contingent liability for disputed 
processed credit and debit card transactions that result in a 
charge-back to the merchant. If a dispute is resolved in the 
cardholder’s favor, the Firm will (through the cardholder’s 
issuing bank) credit or refund the amount to the cardholder 
and will charge back the transaction to the merchant.  If the 
Firm is unable to collect the amount from the merchant, the 
Firm will bear the loss for the amount credited or refunded 
to the cardholder. The Firm mitigates this risk by 
withholding future settlements, retaining cash reserve 
accounts or obtaining other collateral. In addition, the Firm  
recognizes a valuation allowance that covers the payment 
or performance risk  related to charge-backs. For the years ended D e c e m b e r  3 1 ,  2 0 2 2, 2021  and 2020 , 
the Firm processed an aggregate volume of $2,158.4 
billion , $1,886.7 billion , and $1,597.3 billion , respectively.

title: Clearing Services – Client Credit Risk
heading: 8.35.9 Clearing Services – Client Credit Risk
start_phrase: The Firm provides clearing services for clients by entering into securities purchases and sales and derivative contracts with CCPs, including ETDs such as futures and options, as well as OTC-cleared derivative contracts.
summary:
- Explains when losses arise on recourse mortgage servicing (foreclosure proceeds below outstanding principal, accrued interest, and property carrying/disposal costs).
- Notes the firm’s securitizations are predominantly nonrecourse, transferring future credit loss risk to MBS investors; discloses that unpaid principal of loans sold with recourse and the related recorded liability are detailed elsewhere (page 277).
- Describes general indemnification arrangements:
  - Tax gross-up commitments on securities issued outside the U.S. if withholding taxes change, with potential redemption rights.
  - Indemnities to software licensees and to buyers of businesses/assets for certain post-transaction claims tied to pre-transaction actions.
  - Maximum exposure is hard to estimate; based on history, management considers loss risk remote.
- Details merchant charge-back exposure in the Merchant Services business:
  - As merchant acquirer, the firm may bear losses if it cannot recover from merchants after cardholder disputes.
  - Risk mitigants include withholding settlements, reserve accounts, collateral, and a valuation allowance for charge-back risk.
  - Reports processed volumes: $2,158.4B (2022), $1,886.7B (2021), $1,597.3B (2020).
- Outlines client credit risk from clearing services:
  - Acts as clearing member for clients’ trades with CCPs in exchange-traded and OTC-cleared derivatives.
  - Collects/remits initial and variation margin; exposed to client nonperformance but not CCP performance.
  - Mitigants include appropriate margining and the ability to cease services; upon client default, positions are closed and margin applied; any CCP shortfall may be payable by the firm.
  - Recognizes margin receivables from clients and margin payables to CCPs; clients’ underlying contracts are not on the firm’s balance sheet.
  - Maximum exposure is difficult to estimate; management deems risk of material loss remote.
  - Refers to Note 5 for the firm’s own derivatives.
text:
Clearing Services – Client Credit Risk  
The Firm provides clearing services for clients by entering 
into securities purchases and sales and derivative contracts 
with CCPs, including ETDs such as futures and options, as 
well as OTC-cleared derivative contracts. As a clearing 
member,  the Firm stands behind the performance of its 
clients, collects cash and securities collateral (margin) as 
well as any settlement amounts due from or to clients, and 
remits them to the relevant CCP or client in whole or part. 
There are two types of margin: variation margin is posted 
on a daily basis based on the value of clients’ derivative 
contracts and initial margin is posted at inception of a 
derivative contract, generally on the basis of the potential 
changes in the variation margin requirement for the 
contract.  
As a clearing member,  the Firm is exposed to the risk of 
nonperformance by its clients, but is not liable to clients for 
the performance of the CCPs. Where possible,  the Firm 
seeks to mitigate its risk to the client through the collection 
of appropriate amounts of margin at inception and 
throughout the life of the transactions.  The Firm can also 
cease providing clearing services if clients do not adhere to 
their obligations under the clearing agreement. In the event 
of nonperformance by a client,  the Firm would close out the 
client’s positions and access available margin. The CCP 
would utilize any margin it holds to make itself whole, with 
any remaining shortfalls required to be paid by  the Firm as 
a clearing member.  
The Firm reflects its exposur e to nonperformance risk of the 
client through the recognition of margin receivables from 
clients and margin payables to CCPs; the clients ’ underlying 
securities or derivative contracts are not reflected in  the 
Firm’s Consolidated Financial Statements.  
It is difficult to estimate  the Firm’s maximum possible 
exposure through its role as a clearing member, as this 
would require an assessment of transactions that clients 
may execute in the future. However, based upon historical 
experience, and the credit risk mitigants available to  the 
Firm, management believes it is unlikely that  the Firm will 
have to make any material payments under these 
arrangements and the risk of loss is expected to be remote.  
Refer to Note  5 for information on the derivatives that  the 
Firm executes for its own account  and records in its 
Consolidated Financial Statements.  Notes to consolidated financial statements
280 JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K

title: Exchange & Clearing House Memberships
heading: 8.35.10 Exchange & Clearing House Memberships
start_phrase: The Firm is a member of several securities and derivative exchanges and clearing houses, both in the U.S. and other countries, and it provides clearing services to its clients.
summary:
- The Firm is a member of multiple U.S. and international securities and derivatives exchanges and clearing houses, which can obligate it to cover a pro rata share of losses from another member’s default or, in some cases, from losses on the clearing house’s investments of guarantee fund contributions and initial margin.
- These obligations vary by organization and may be limited to the Firm’s guarantee fund contribution (or a multiple thereof) or may include residual losses after applying the fund. Payments would generally only be required if losses exceed the clearing house’s contractually required resources.
- The Firm often cannot estimate a maximum possible exposure under these memberships, but based on historical experience considers the risk of loss remote. Where estimable, exposures are disclosed in the “Exchange & clearing house guarantees and commitments” line referenced on page 277.
- Under its sponsored member repo program, the Firm sponsors clients to clear eligible repos and resales through FICC and guarantees clients’ obligations to FICC. The Firm secures a lien on clients’ cash or high-quality securities collateral and expects the risk of loss to be remote. The gross maximum exposure (before collateral) is included in the same disclosure line on page 277; Note 11 provides additional credit risk mitigation details.
- The Parent Company may guarantee certain trading and other obligations of its subsidiaries on a contract basis; because these obligations are recorded on the Firm’s balance sheet or as off-balance sheet commitments, no separate liability is recognized. The likelihood of payment under these guarantees is considered remote.
- The Parent Company guarantees certain long-term debt and structured notes of subsidiaries, including all securities issued by 100%-owned JPMorgan Chase Financial Company LLC, which are fully and unconditionally guaranteed by the Parent. These guarantees rank pari passu with the Parent’s unsecured, unsubordinated indebtedness and are not included in the page 277 table; further details are in Note 20.
text:
The Firm is a member of several securities and derivative 
exchanges and clearing houses, both in the U.S. and other 
countries, and it provides clearing services to its clients. 
Membership in some of these organizations requires  the 
Firm to pay a pro rata share of the losses incurred by the 
organization as a result of the default of another member. 
Such obligations vary with different organizations. These 
obligations may be limited to the amount (or a multiple of 
the amount) of  the Firm’s contribution to the guarantee 
fund maintained by a clearing house or exchange as part of 
the resources available to cover any losses in the event of a 
member default. Alternatively, these obligations may also 
include a pro rata share of the residual losses after applying 
the guarantee fund. Additionally, certain clearing houses 
require  the Firm as a member to pay a pro rata share of 
losses that may result from the clearing house’s investment 
of guarantee fund contributions and initial margin, 
unrelated to and independent of the default of another 
m e m b e r .  G e n e r a l l y  a  p a y m e n t  w o u l d  o n l y  b e  r e q u i r e d  
should such losses exceed the resources of the clearing 
house or exchange that are contractually required to 
absorb the losses in the first instance. In certain cases, it is 
difficult to estimate  the Firm’s maximum possible exposure 
under these membership agreements, since this would 
require an assessment of future claims that may be made 
against  the Firm that have not yet occurred. However, 
based on historical experience, management expects the 
risk of loss to  the Firm to be remote.  Where  the Firm’s 
maximum possible exposure can be estimated, the amount 
is disclosed in the table on  page 277 , in the Exchange & 
clearing house guarantees and commitments line.

title: Sponsored member repo program
heading: 8.35.11 Sponsored member repo program
start_phrase: The Firm acts as a sponsoring member to clear eligible overnight and term resale and repurchase agreements through the Government Securities Division of the Fixed Income Clearing Corporation (“FICC”) on behalf of clients that become sponsored members under the FICC’s rules.
summary:
- Exchange and clearing house memberships: The Firm participates in multiple U.S. and international exchanges and clearing houses and may be required to share in losses from other members’ defaults. Obligations vary by organization and may be limited to the Firm’s guarantee fund contribution (or a multiple) or extend to residual losses after the fund is applied. Some clearing houses also require sharing in losses from investments of guarantee fund contributions and initial margin, independent of any member default. Payments would generally only arise if losses exceed resources contractually available to the clearing house. Maximum exposure is often difficult to estimate; management deems the risk of loss remote. Where estimable, amounts are disclosed in the Exchange & clearing house guarantees and commitments table referenced on page 277.

- Sponsored member repo program: The Firm sponsors clients to clear eligible overnight and term repos/reverse repos through FICC, guaranteeing clients’ obligations to FICC. The Firm mitigates this exposure by securing a lien on cash or high-quality securities collateral placed with the clearing house and considers the risk of loss remote. The maximum exposure, before collateral, is reported in the same guarantees and commitments line; Note 11 provides additional collateral details.

- Guarantees of subsidiaries: The Parent Company may guarantee certain trading and other obligations of subsidiaries on a negotiated basis. Because these subsidiary obligations are on the Firm’s balance sheet or are recorded as off-balance sheet commitments, no separate liability is recognized for the guarantees; the risk of required payment is considered remote.

- Parent guarantees of subsidiary debt: The Parent guarantees certain long-term debt and structured notes of subsidiaries, including all securities issued by wholly owned JPMorgan Chase Financial Company LLC (JPMFC), which are fully and unconditionally guaranteed by the Parent. These guarantees rank pari passu with the Parent’s unsecured, unsubordinated indebtedness and are excluded from the table on page 277; see Note 20 for more information.
text:
Sponsored member repo program  
The Firm acts as a sponsoring member to clear eligible 
overnight and term resale and repurchase agreements 
through the Government Securities Division of the Fixed 
Income Clearing Corporation (“FICC”) on behalf of clients 
that become sponsored members under the FICC’s rules.  
The Firm also guarantees to the FICC the prompt and full 
payment and performance of its sponsored member clients’ 
respective obligations under the FICC’s rules. The Firm 
minimizes its liability under these guarantees by  obtaining a 
security interest in the cash or high-quality securities 
collateral that the clients place with the clearing house; 
therefore , the Firm expects the risk of loss to be remote.  
The Firm’s maximum possible exposure, without taking into 
consideration the associated collateral, is included  in the 
Exchange & clearing house guarantees and commitments 
line on  page 277 . Refer to Note  11 for additional 
information on credit risk mitigation practices on resale 
agreements and the types of collateral pledged under 
repurchase agreements.

Guarantees of subsidiaries 
In the normal course of business,  the Parent Company  may 
provide counterparties with guarantees of certain of the

title: Contingencies
heading: 8.37.1 Contingencies
start_phrase: As of December 31, 2022, the Firm and its subsidiaries and affiliates are defendants or respondents in numerous legal proceedings, including private, civil litigations, government investigations or regulatory enforcement matters.
summary:
- Overview of litigation contingencies: The firm and its subsidiaries face numerous legal proceedings worldwide, including private civil suits, class actions, government investigations, and regulatory enforcement matters across all business lines. Claims span common law tort and contract, antitrust, securities, and consumer protection, and are at varying stages.

- Loss estimate: As of December 31, 2022, the firm estimates the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of reserves at $0 to approximately $1.2 billion. Not all matters are estimable. The estimate involves significant judgment due to early case stages, multiple defendants, unresolved issues (e.g., class certification, claim scope), and uncertain outcomes; the range may change and actual losses could differ significantly.

- Material proceedings highlighted:
  - 1MDB litigation (Malaysia): J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA is sued for alleged “dishonest assistance” related to $300 million (2009) and $500 million (2010) payments from 1MDB to an account of 1MDB PetroSaudi Limited. The firm is challenging service and Malaysian court jurisdiction.
  - Amrapali matters (India): The Enforcement Directorate is investigating J.P. Morgan India Private Limited over 2010 and 2012 investments by offshore funds in Amrapali residential projects. Numerous creditor and homebuyer claims are overseen by India’s Supreme Court. In August 2021, the ED fined J.P. Morgan India about $31.5 million (under appeal). The Supreme Court’s 2019 order made preliminary findings of violations by Amrapali and others (including unspecified JPMorgan entities) and directed further ED inquiries under PMLA and FEMA. In May 2020, the ED attached about $25 million from J.P. Morgan India. The firm is cooperating.
  - Federal Republic of Nigeria litigation (UK): JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. operated an escrow/depository account holding about $1.1 billion for the Nigerian government and two oil companies in an oil-field dispute; funds were paid out in 2011 and 2013 per client instructions. In November 2017, Nigeria sued in the English High Court for approximately $875 million related to those payments (allegations description cut off).
text:
Contingencies 
As of December 31, 2022, the Firm and its subsidiaries and 
affiliates are defendants or respondents in numerous legal 
proceedings, including private, civil litigations, government 
investigations or regulatory enforcement matters. The 
litigations range from individual actions involving a single 
plaintiff to class action lawsuits with potentially millions of 
class members. Investigations and regulatory enforcement 
matters involve both formal and informal proceedings, by 
both governmental agencies and self-regulatory 
organizations. These legal proceedings are at varying stages 
of adjudication, arbitration or investigation, and involve 
each of the Firm’s lines of business and several geographies 
and a wide variety of claims (including common law tort 
and contract claims and statutory antitrust, securities and 
consumer protection claims), some of which present novel 
legal theories.
The Firm believes the estimate of the aggregate range of 
reasonably possible losses, in excess of reserves 
established, for its legal proceedings is from $0 to 
approximately $1.2 billion  at December 31, 2022. This 
estimated aggregate range of reasonably possible losses 
was based upon information available as of that date for 
those proceedings in which the Firm believes that an 
estimate of reasonably possible loss can be made. For 
certain matters, the Firm does not believe that such an 
estimate can be made, as of that date. The Firm’s estimate 
of the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses 
involves significant judgment, given:
•the number, variety and varying stages of the 
proceedings, including the fact that many are in 
preliminary stages, 
•the existence in many such proceedings of multiple 
defendants, including the Firm, whose share of liability 
(if any) has yet to be determined, 
•the numerous yet-unresolved issues in many of the 
proceedings, including issues regarding class 
certification and the scope of many of the claims, and 
•the uncertainty of the various potential outcomes of 
such proceedings, including where the Firm has made 
assumptions concerning future rulings by the court or 
other adjudicator, or about the behavior or incentives of 
adverse parties or regulatory authorities, and those 
assumptions prove to be incorrect.
In addition, the outcome of a particular proceeding may be 
a result which the Firm did not take into account in its 
estimate because the Firm had deemed the likelihood of 
that outcome to be remote. Accordingly, the Firm’s 
estimate of the aggregate range of reasonably possible 
losses will change from time to time, and actual losses may 
vary significantly.Set forth below are descriptions of the Firm’s material legal 
proceedings.

title: 1MDB Litigation
heading: 8.37.2 1MDB Litigation
start_phrase: J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA was named as a defendant in a civil litigation filed in May 2021 in Malaysia by 1Malaysia Development Berhad (“1MDB”), a Malaysian state-owned and controlled investment fund.
summary:
- Overview of litigation contingencies: The Firm and its subsidiaries face numerous legal proceedings worldwide—including private civil suits (individual and class actions), government investigations, and regulatory enforcement—spanning all lines of business and involving diverse claims (tort, contract, antitrust, securities, consumer protection), many at early stages and some involving novel legal theories.
- Loss estimate: As of December 31, 2022, the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses in excess of established reserves is estimated at $0 to approximately $1.2 billion, based on matters where an estimate can be made. The Firm cannot estimate losses for certain matters. The estimate is highly judgmental and subject to change due to factors such as case stage, multiple defendants and undetermined liability shares, unresolved issues (including class certification and claim scope), uncertain outcomes, and assumptions about future rulings or counterparty actions; actual losses may differ significantly, including outcomes previously deemed remote.
- Material proceedings summarized:
  - 1MDB litigation (Malaysia): J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA is sued by 1MDB for alleged “dishonest assistance” related to $300 million (2009) and $500 million (2010) paid into an account of 1MDB PetroSaudi Limited at J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA. The Firm is challenging service validity and Malaysian court jurisdiction (application filed September 2022).
  - Amrapali matters (India): India’s Enforcement Directorate is investigating J.P. Morgan India Private Limited over 2010 and 2012 investments by offshore funds formerly managed by JPMorgan entities in Amrapali Group housing projects. Homebuyer petitions are under the supervision of India’s Supreme Court. In August 2021, the ED fined J.P. Morgan India approximately $31.5 million (appeal pending). The Supreme Court (July 2019) made preliminary findings referencing currency control and money-laundering provisions and directed further inquiry under PMLA and FEMA. In May 2020, the ED attached approximately $25 million from J.P. Morgan India; the Firm is cooperating with the PMLA investigation.
  - Federal Republic of Nigeria litigation (UK): JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. operated an escrow/depository account holding about $1.1 billion for Nigeria’s federal government and two oil companies tied to an oil field dispute; funds were paid out in 2011 and 2013 per client directions. In November 2017, Nigeria sued in the English High Court seeking approximately $875 million related to those payments (details in this excerpt are incomplete).
text:
1MDB Litigation . J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA was named as a 
defendant in a civil litigation filed in May 2021 in Malaysia 
by 1Malaysia Development Berhad (“1MDB”), a Malaysian 
state-owned and controlled investment fund. J.P. Morgan 
(Suisse) SA was served in August 2022. The claim alleges 
“dishonest assistance” against J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA in 
relation to payments of $ 3 0 0  m i l l i o n and $ 5 0 0  m i l l i o n, 
from 2009 and 2010, respectively, received from 1MDB 
and paid into an account at J.P. Morgan Suisse (SA) held by 
1MDB PetroSaudi Limited, a joint venture company 
between 1MDB and PetroSaudi Holdings (Cayman) Limited. 
In September 2022, the Firm filed an application 
challenging the validity of service and the Malaysian court’s 
jurisdiction to hear the claim.

title: Federal Republic of Nigeria Litigation
heading: 8.37.4 Federal Republic of Nigeria Litigation
start_phrase: JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. operated an escrow and depository account for the Federal Government of Nigeria (“FGN”) and two major international oil companies.
summary:
- Overview: The firm and its affiliates face numerous legal proceedings globally, including civil litigations, government investigations, and regulatory enforcement across all business lines. Claims span common law tort and contract, antitrust, securities, and consumer protection, with some novel legal theories.
- Loss estimate: As of December 31, 2022, the aggregate range of reasonably possible losses, in excess of reserves, is $0 to approximately $1.2 billion. The estimate involves significant judgment due to early case stages, multiple defendants, unresolved issues (including class certification and claim scope), and uncertain outcomes; it may change and actual losses could differ materially.

Material matters described:
- 1MDB litigation (Malaysia): J.P. Morgan (Suisse) SA accused of “dishonest assistance” regarding $300 million (2009) and $500 million (2010) payments to an account of a 1MDB joint venture. The firm is challenging service and jurisdiction.
- Amrapali (India): ED investigation into J.P. Morgan India’s involvement with offshore fund investments (2010, 2012) in Amrapali housing projects. In 2021, ED fined ~ $31.5 million (under appeal). The Supreme Court made preliminary findings of violations and ordered further inquiries under PMLA and FEMA. In 2020, ED attached ~ $25 million from J.P. Morgan India; the firm is cooperating.
- Federal Republic of Nigeria litigation (UK): Dispute over $1.1 billion escrowed funds related to oil field rights. Nigeria sought ~ $875 million alleging the bank was on notice of client fraud. After a 2022 trial, the High Court dismissed the case in full; appeal permission was denied in November 2022, concluding the matter.
- Foreign exchange (FX) investigations and litigation: Prior settlements with authorities and a 2015 federal antitrust plea; DOL granted ERISA QPAM exemptions during the 10-year disqualification period. The remaining governmental inquiry is before South Africa’s Competition Tribunal. Civilly, a U.S. class action settlement (approved 2018) resolved core claims; additional agreements with certain opt-outs reached in December 2022. A consumer putative class remains. Related actions persist in the U.K., Israel, the Netherlands, Brazil, and Australia; a U.K. action was agreed to be resolved in December 2022; a U.K. class certification appeal is pending; Israel has a settlement in principle subject to court approval.
- Interchange litigation (U.S.): Antitrust claims against Visa/Mastercard and banks over interchange fees. A monetary class settlement was amended in 2018, adding $900 million to $5.3 billion in escrow; approved in 2019, with appeals pending. Based on opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive class action continues with partial class certification (2021). Numerous individual opt-out suits were filed; settlements cover over half of combined Mastercard- and Visa-branded sales volume.
- Jeffrey Epstein litigation (U.S.): Two SDNY suits allege JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. knowingly facilitated Epstein’s sex trafficking by providing banking services until 2013—one putative class by an alleged victim (filed November 2022) and one by the U.S. Virgin Islands (December 2022). The bank has moved to dismiss both.
- LIBOR and other benchmark matters: Ongoing regulatory inquiries regarding LIBOR/EURIBOR; the Swiss Competition Commission’s EURIBOR investigation continues. The European Commission issued a 2016 decision against the firm and others for EURIBOR-related antitrust violations; the firm has appealed.
text:
Federal Republic of Nigeria Litigation.  JPMorgan Chase Bank, 
N.A. operated an escrow and depository account for the 
Federal Government of Nigeria (“FGN”) and two major 
international oil companies. The account held 
approximately $1.1 billion  in connection with a dispute 
among the clients over rights to an oil field. Following the 
settlement of the dispute, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. paid 
out the monies in the account in 2011 and 2013 in 
accordance with directions received from its clients. In 
November 2017, the Federal Republic of Nigeria (“FRN”) 
commenced a claim in the English High Court for 
approximately $ 8 7 5  m i l l i o n in payments made out of the 
accounts. The FRN alleged that the payments were 
JPMorgan Chase & Co./2022 Form 10-K 283instructed as part of a complex fraud not involving 
JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., but that JPMorgan Chase Bank, 
N.A. was or should have been on notice that the payments 
may be fraudulent. A trial was held between February and 
April 2022. In June 2022, the Court decided the case in 
favor of JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. and dismissed it in full. 
In November 2022, the Court refused permission to the 
FRN to appeal the dismissal, and the matte r was concl uded.

title: Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation
heading: 8.37.5 Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation
start_phrase: The Firm previously reported settlements with certain government authorities relating to its foreign exchange (“FX”) sales and trading activities and controls related to those activities.
summary:
- FRN v. JPMorgan (UK “Quincecare” case): After a February–April 2022 trial, the court ruled for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. in June 2022; the court denied the Federal Republic of Nigeria permission to appeal in November 2022, concluding the matter.
- Foreign exchange (FX) investigations and litigation: The Firm previously settled with various authorities and pleaded guilty in 2015 to a federal antitrust violation; the DOL granted ERISA QPAM exemptions during the 10‑year disqualification period. The only remaining governmental inquiry is before South Africa’s Competition Tribunal. Civil matters include a 2018 U.S. class action settlement (final approval granted; opt‑out claims largely resolved in Dec 2022), a pending U.S. consumer putative class action, and multiple non‑U.S. actions (U.K., Israel, Netherlands, Brazil, Australia), with a U.K. settlement reached in Dec 2022, a U.K. CAT certification appeal ongoing, and an Israel settlement in principle pending court approval.
- Interchange fee litigation: Merchant claims against Visa, Mastercard, and banks alleging antitrust violations. Following reversal of an initial 2012 settlement, the damages case was re‑settled in 2018 with an additional $900 million (on top of $5.3 billion), approved in Dec 2019; appeals are pending and $700 million was returned to defendants due to opt‑outs. The injunctive case continues, with class certification granted in part in Sept 2021. Many opt‑out merchants filed individual suits; settlements have been reached with merchants representing over half of combined Visa/Mastercard sales volume.
- Jeffrey Epstein litigation: Two SDNY suits allege JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. knowingly facilitated Epstein’s activities—one putative class action by an alleged victim (filed Nov 2022) and one by the U.S. Virgin Islands (filed Dec 2022) asserting statutory claims; JPMorgan has moved to dismiss both.
- LIBOR/EURIBOR and other benchmark investigations: Ongoing responses to global inquiries, including a continuing Swiss COMCO EURIBOR investigation. The European Commission issued a 2016 decision against the Firm and others regarding EURIBOR; the Firm has appealed.
text:
Foreign Exchange Investigations and Litigation.  The Firm 
previously reported settlements with certain government 
authorities relating to its foreign exchange (“FX”) sales and 
trading activities and controls related to those activities. 
Among those resolutions, in May 2015, the Firm pleaded 
guilty to a single violation of federal antitrust law. The 
Department of Labor ("DOL") granted the Firm exemptions 
that permit the Firm and its affiliates to continue to rely on 
the Qualified Professional Asset Manager exemption under 
the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (“ERISA”) 
through the ten-year  disqualification period following the 
antitrust plea. The only remaining FX-related governmental 
inquiry is a South Africa Competition Commission matter 
which is currently pending before the South Africa 
Competition Tribunal.
With respect to civil litigation matters, in August 2018, the 
United States District Court for the Southern District of New 
York granted final approval to the Firm’s settlement of a 
consolidated class action brought by U.S.-based plaintiffs, 
which principally alleged violations of federal antitrust laws 
based on an alleged conspiracy to manipulate foreign 
exchange rates and also sought damages on behalf of 
persons who transacted in FX futures and options on 
futures. Although certain members of the settlement class 
filed requests to the Court to be excluded from the class, an 
agreement to resolve their claims was reached in December 
2022. A putative class action remains pending against the 
Firm and other foreign exchange dealers on behalf of 
certain consumers who purchased foreign currencies at 
allegedly inflated rates. In addition, some FX-related 
individual and putative class actions based on similar 
alleged underlying conduct have been filed outside the U.S., 
including in the U.K., Israel, the Netherlands, Brazil and 
Australia. An agreement to resolve one of the UK actions 
was reached in December 2022. In a putative class action 
pending before the U.K. Competition Appeal Tribunal, 
proposed class representatives have appealed the tribunal's 
denial of a request for class certification on an opt-out 
basis. In Israel, a settlement in principle has been reached 
in the putative class action, which remains subject to court 
approval.

title: Interchange Litigation
heading: 8.37.6 Interchange Litigation
start_phrase: Groups of merchants and retail associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, conspired to set the price of credit and debit card interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of antitrust laws.
summary:
- Fraud litigation: Claims that JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. should have been on notice of potentially fraudulent payments; after a Feb–Apr 2022 trial, the court ruled for the bank and dismissed the case; in Nov 2022 the court denied the FRN permission to appeal, concluding the matter.

- Foreign exchange (FX) investigations and litigation: Prior government settlements and a 2015 guilty plea to a federal antitrust violation; DOL granted QPAM exemptions allowing ERISA-related business during the 10-year disqualification period. The only remaining governmental inquiry is a South Africa Competition Commission matter before the Competition Tribunal. Civil cases include a U.S. class action settlement approved in 2018 (with opt-out resolutions reached in Dec 2022), a pending U.S. consumer class action, and non-U.S. actions in the U.K., Israel, the Netherlands, Brazil, and Australia. One U.K. case was resolved in Dec 2022; a U.K. CAT appeal on opt-out class certification is pending; a settlement in principle in Israel awaits court approval.

- Interchange fee litigation: Merchants allege Visa, Mastercard, and certain banks conspired to fix interchange fees. After a 2012 settlement was reversed, the case split into monetary and injunctive tracks. An amended monetary class settlement (2018) added $900 million to about $5.3 billion; approved in 2019 with appeals pending. Due to opt-outs, $700 million was returned to defendants. The injunctive class was certified in part in 2021. Many opt-out merchants brought individual suits; defendants have reached settlements covering over half of combined Visa- and Mastercard-branded sales volume.

- Jeffrey Epstein litigation: Two SDNY lawsuits allege JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. knowingly facilitated Epstein’s misconduct by providing banking services until 2013—one putative class action by an alleged victim (filed Nov 2022) and one by the U.S. Virgin Islands asserting statutory claims (filed Dec 2022). The bank has moved to dismiss both.

- LIBOR and other benchmark rate matters: Ongoing responses to global inquiries related to LIBOR and EURIBOR. The Swiss Competition Commission’s EURIBOR investigation continues. The European Commission issued a 2016 decision finding an antitrust infringement related to EURIBOR; the Firm has appealed.
text:
Interchange Litigation . Groups of merchants and retail 
associations filed a series of class action complaints alleging 
that Visa and Mastercard, as well as certain banks, 
conspired to set the price of credit and debit card 
interchange fees and enacted related rules in violation of 
antitrust laws. In 2012, the parties initially settled the cases 
for a cash payment, but that settlement was reversed on appeal and remanded to the United States District Court for 
the Eastern District of New York.
The original class action was divided into two separate 
actions, one seeking primarily monetary relief and the other 
seeking primarily injunctive relief. In September 2018, the 
parties to the monetary class action finalized an agreement 
which amends and supersedes the prior settlement 
agreement. Pursuant to this settlement, the defendants 
collectively contributed an additional $ 9 0 0  m i l l i o n to the 
approximately $ 5 . 3  b i l l i o n previously held in escrow from 
the original settlement. In December 2019, the amended 
settlement agreement was approved by the District Court. 
Certain merchants appealed the District Court’s approval 
order, and those appeals are pending. Based on the 
percentage of merchants that opted out of the amended 
class settlement, $ 7 0 0  m i l l i o n has been returned to the 
defendants from the settlement escrow in accordance with 
the settlement agreement. The injunctive class action 
continues separately, and in September 2021, the District 
Court granted plaintiffs’ motion for class certification in 
part, and denied the motion in part.
Of the merchants who opted out of the amended damages 
class settlement, certain merchants filed individual actions 
raising similar allegations against Visa and Mastercard, as 
well as against the Firm and other banks. While some of 
those actions remain pending, the defendants have reached 
settlements with the merchants who opted out representing 
over half of the combined Mastercard-branded and Visa-
branded payment card sales volume.

title: Jeffrey Epstein Litigation
heading: 8.37.7 Jeffrey Epstein Litigation

summary:

Some opting-out merchants filed individual suits; many have been settled, covering over half of combined Visa/Mastercard sales volume.
- Jeffrey Epstein litigation: Two SDNY lawsuits allege JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. facilitated Epstein’s unlawful conduct by providing banking services until 2013—one a putative class action by a victim (filed November 2022), and one by the U.S. Virgin Islands (filed December 2022).
